㘨.def: deep; profound, empty; hollow, quiet; peaceful

senses: to make one, to unite; single, the same
一.story: One stroke. In the Laozi it is a number and a name. As a name: hold to the One and do not leave it (10); the sage holds the One and is the model of the world (22); the unseen, the unheard, and the untouched merge into one (14); heaven, earth, spirits, valleys, and kings got the One (39); the Dao gives birth to one, one to two, two to three (42). Wang Bi calls it “the beginning of number and the limit of things”.
一.gap: “The One” with capitals suggests the God of the philosophers or a Neoplatonic source. 一 is also the plain numeral and a horizontal line, and the Dao is said to come before it.
一.shuowen: 惟初太始，道立於一，造分天地，化成萬物。
一.shuowenEn: At the very first, in the great beginning, the Dao was set up in the One; it divided heaven and earth and by change completed the ten thousand things.

丈.def: unit of length equal 3.3 meters; gentleman, man, husband

上.def: top; superior, highest; go up, send up
senses: the one above: a superior, a ruler
to go up; to put above
上.story: 上 is a base line with a mark over it; with 下 it is Xu Shen’s example of a graph that points at an idea. In the Laozi it is the word for the best and for those who rule. The highest good is like water (8). Of the highest ruler, those below know only that he exists (17). The highest de is not de-like (38). The highest officer hears the Dao and walks it (41). To wish to be above the people one must go below them (66). To know not-knowing is 上 (71). The people starve because those above eat too much in taxes (75).
上.gap: English uses different words for “upper”, “best”, and “the authorities”. 上 is all three, so each praise of the highest is also a remark about those on top.
上.shuowenEn: High. This is the ancient form of 上; a graph that points at the matter.

下.def: under, underneath, below; down; inferior; bring down
senses: 天下: all under heaven, the world

parts.m: the mark below it (shape only; not the word “divine”)

下.story: The early graph is a long line with a short mark under it; 上 is the reverse. In the postface to the Shuowen, Xu Shen gives 上 and 下 as his examples of 指事, graphs that point at an idea. In the Laozi the low place is the place of power. Water stays where people hate to be (8). High and low lean on each other (2); the high has the low as its base (39). The great state is the low reach of the river (61). In passage 66, 下 is a verb and a skill: the River and the sea are 善下, good at being below, and so they are kings.
下.gap: English “below” and “under” are prepositions and carry a sense of defeat (“underling”, “beneath me”). 下 can be an action that one does well, and in this book it is where things gather.
下.shuowenEn: The bottom. A graph that points at the matter.

且.def: moreover, also (post-subject); about to, will soon (pre-verb)

並.def: equal to; side by side; also, what is more; both

中.def: central; center, middle; in the midst of; hit (target); attain

senses: the main thing; to preside over
主.story: The Shuowen reads the graph as a lamp with its flame, the dot at the top; the character 炷, a wick, keeps that sense. From the one light in the room came the head of the house and the lord of a state. The Laozi uses the word with care. The Dao feeds all things and does not act the 主 (34). The soldier’s saying in passage 69 is “I do not dare to be the host; I would rather be the guest”. The lord of ten thousand chariots must not treat his person lightly (26).
主.gap: “Lord” brings in feudal Europe and the God of the English Bible. 主 is also the plain word for a host at a dinner and the owner of a dog.

parts.m: in the modern shape, like “king”; in the old form, the lamp stand

乃.def: then; really, indeed; as it turned out, after all; namely

久.def: long time (ago); time passage, grow late
senses: to stay, to keep in place (old sense)
久.shuowen: 以後灸之，象人兩脛後有距也。
久.shuowenEn: To apply heat from behind; it shows a person’s two shins with something set against them from behind.
久.story: Many scholars take this graph as the first way of writing 灸, to burn moxa on the skin: a slow treatment in which the herb stays in place. It was then used for “a long time”. In the Laozi, 久 is what Dao and its followers have and what force lacks. Heaven is long and earth is lasting (7). A storm wind does not last a morning; if heaven and earth cannot make things last, how can people? (23). Know what is enough and you can be long and lasting (44). With the mother of the state one can be long and lasting (59). Dao itself is 久 (16).
久.gap: “Eternal” and “forever” are outside time. 久 is inside time: a thing that stays put for a long while.

之.def: marks preceding phrase as modifier of following phrase; it, him her, them; go to

乘.def: ride, ascend; avail oneself of; numerary adjunct for vehicles

也.def: also; classical final particle of strong affirmation or identity

亂.def: confusion, state of chaos; create chaos, revolt
senses: to confuse, to throw into disorder
the closing section of a song
亂.shuowenEn: To put in order. From 乙; 乙 is that which orders it. From 𤔔.
亂.story: The Shuowen defines disorder as “to put in order”. The graph is commonly explained as two hands that work at a tangle of silk on a frame, and the oldest texts use the word in both directions: a tangle, and the untangling. The Analects quotes King Wu on his ten ministers who 亂, that is, who govern well. In the Laozi the word is the state to avoid: the people’s heart not in 亂 (3); loyal ministers appear when the state is in dark 亂 (18); ritual is the head of 亂 (38); order a thing before it is in 亂 (64).
亂.gap: English “chaos” is a Greek void and “disorder” is a mere absence. 亂 is a tangle of threads: a thing with structure that has gone wrong, and that hands can work on.

事.def: affair, matter, business; to serve; accident, incident
senses: work, service, a task; an office
an affair, a matter, an event
事.shuowenEn: An office, a duty. From 史 (a scribe, an officer); the sound is from 之, abbreviated.
事.story: At first one word with 史, the officer who holds a record, and 吏, the clerk: a hand that carries out a charge. In the Laozi the sage manages affairs by not-forcing (2); the task goes through and the people say it happened of itself (17); one makes the Way one’s work (23); and the world is won by having no business, 無事 (48, 57).
事.gap: “Thing” and “matter” are too slack. 事 is something that has to be done by someone.

senses: wú: not to have (early writing for 無)
亡.shuowenEn: To flee. From a person and 乚 (a nook, a hiding place).

parts.m: what is left of a person (in the Shuowen’s reading)

亡.story: In the Shuowen’s account 亡 is a person who has gone into a corner and cannot be found; the early forms are read in other ways too. The word runs from “absent” through “lost” to “dead” and “destroyed”. It is the core of 忘 (to forget), 盲 (blind), 望 (to look out for one who is away), and 喪 (mourning). The last line of Laozi 33 turns on it: one who dies and is not 亡 has long life. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 忘 there: “is not forgotten”.
亡.gap: English “perish” is final and grand. 亡 is first only “not here”, which is why a dead person may be said not to be it.

senses: to cross; a crossing, a meeting point
to exchange, to hand over; mutual
交.shuowenEn: Crossed shins. From 大 (a person); it shows the form of crossing.
交.story: A person with crossed legs, and then everything that crosses or is exchanged. In the Changes, heaven and earth 交 and all things go through. In the Laozi a great state is the 交 of all under heaven, the place where it meets (61), and when ghosts and sage do not harm each other, 德 comes home 交, from both sides (60).
交.gap: English needs “confluence”, “exchange”, “relations”, and “intercourse”. The one Chinese word keeps them joined.

什.def: file of ten soldiers; mixed, miscellaneous

senses: to be close, to treat as kin
the kernel of a nut or seed
feeling in a limb (不仁: numb)
仁.shuowenEn: To be close, to treat as kin. From 人 (person) and 二 (two).
仁.story: The word for what passes between two people. Confucius made it the centre of his teaching; Mencius told kings that a humane ruler has no enemy who can stand against him. It is warm and graded: most for kin, less for those far away. Guodian bamboo texts are reported to write it with a body over a heart. The Laozi treats it with suspicion. Heaven and earth are not 仁 (5). When the great Dao is left, 仁 and duty appear (18). Cut off 仁, and the people return to family love (19). The highest 仁 acts, and has no motive for acting (38). One line uses it without blame: in giving, 仁 is good (8).
仁.gap: “Benevolence” is Victorian charity from above. “Humanity” is too wide. 仁 is close, kin-like warmth that has degrees. The Laozi objects to the degrees and to the display.

介.def: forerunner, herald, harbinger; to lie between; sea shell; to wear armor

付.def: give, deliver, pay, hand over; entrust

代.def: replace, replacement (of person or generation); era, generation

以.def: by means of; thereby, therefore; consider as; in order to

任.def: trust to, rely on, appoint; to bear, duty, office; allow

企.def: plan a project; stand on tiptoe
senses: to lift the heels, to stand on tiptoe
to look out for, to long for
modern: to plan (企圖), enterprise (企業)
企.shuowenEn: To lift the heels. From 人 (person); 止 gives the sound.
企.story: 企 puts a person on top of a foot, and the Shuowen’s gloss is “to lift the heels”. A person rises on the toes to see over a wall or to be seen over a crowd, so the word grew toward hope and ambition: to look out for a thing that is still far away. The modern compound 企業, “enterprise”, was made in Japan in the nineteenth century and came back into Chinese. Laozi 24 uses the first, bodily sense for its opening joke: the one on tiptoe is taller and does not stand. Mawangdui silk text A is reported to write 炊 in this place.
企.gap: English “tiptoe” suggests quiet or stealth. 企 is about height and reach: the heels leave the ground so that the eyes can go farther.

senses: to crouch, to lie face down
to lie hidden, to wait in ambush
the hottest weeks of summer (三伏)
伏.shuowenEn: To keep watch. From 人 (person) and 犬 (dog).
伏.story: A person with a dog, low to the ground and waiting. From that posture come the senses “to hide”, “to submit”, and “to ambush”. In passage 58 disaster 伏 inside good fortune: it is present now, flat and patient, and not a later stage. The line is the source of a common saying, 禍福相倚, “disaster and fortune lean on each other”.
伏.gap: “Lurks” makes it sinister and “hides” makes it passive. 伏 is a trained stillness with intent in it.

senses: to strike; to attack a state
伐.shuowen: 擊也。从人持戈。一曰敗也。
伐.shuowenEn: To strike. A person who holds a dagger-axe. Another sense: to ruin.
伐.story: A person and a halberd. The word for a campaign against a state became a word for bragging: to attack with one’s own merits. The Laozi uses that sense three times: not self-praising, so there is merit (22); the self-praiser has no merit (24); achieve the result and do not boast (30).
伐.gap: English “boast” is only vain. 伐 keeps the violence: self-praise as an assault on the listener.

伯.def: older brother; father's elder brother; senior male 'sire'; feudal rank 'count'

似.def: resemble, similar to; as if, seem

位.def: throne; position, post; rank, status; seat

作.def: make; work; compose, write; act, perform
senses: to rise, to get up, to stir
to make, to do, to begin work
作.shuowenEn: To get up. From 人 (person) and 乍.

parts.m: suddenly, to start; also the sound

作.story: First a body that gets up, then a work that is started. The ten thousand things 作, arise, and the sage does not refuse them (2); they arise together and “I watch their return” (16); the difficult things of the world must 作 from the easy (63). In passage 37, after things have changed of themselves, wanting 作: it stirs, or the things want to act.
作.gap: English separates “arise” (it happens) from “make” (someone does it). 作 does not.

使.def: cause, send on a mission, order; envoy, messenger, ambassador

供.def: supply, provide for; offer in worship

senses: to insult, to treat with scorn
侮.shuowenEn: To wound. From 人 (person), with 𣫭 for the sound.
侮.story: Contempt that is acted out. It is the last rung of passage 17: the ruler whom the people scorn. The debater Song Xing, of the same century, made a doctrine of it: 見侮不辱, “to be insulted is no disgrace”.
侮.gap: “Despise” is a feeling held inside. 侮 is shown, and it hurts: the Shuowen says “to wound”.

senses: custom, the ways of a place
俗.shuowenEn: What is practised. From 人 (a person), with 谷 (valley) for the sound.
俗.story: The habits that a community shares. In passage 20 the speaker is set against 俗人, ordinary people, who are bright and sharp while the speaker is dim. In passage 80 the people take joy in their customs, and the word is warm.
俗.gap: “Custom” is neutral and “vulgar” is a sneer. 俗 can be either, and the Laozi uses both tones.

senses: to rear, to protect, to keep safe
保.shuowenEn: To rear. From 人 (person) and a short form of 𤓽, the ancient form of 孚.

parts.m: here: what remains of a child and the hand that holds it

保.story: The early form is commonly explained as an adult who carries a child on the back. In passage 62 the Dao is the good person’s treasure, 寶, and that by which the not-good person is 保, kept: the two words have one sound. Passage 15 says that one who 保 this Dao does not wish to be full.
保.gap: “Protect” suggests a guard and a threat. 保 is nearer to being carried.

senses: to keep faith; true to one’s word
a token, a message (later: a letter)
信.shuowenEn: Sincere, real. From 人 (person) and 言 (speech). A joined-meaning character.
信.story: A person beside a word. To be 信 is to be someone whose word holds, and the same graph names the trust that others then give. The Laozi uses it in both directions. In words, the good is 信 (8). When trust is not enough, there is no trust in return (17). Within Dao there is something real, and within that there is 信, a token that can be tested (21). The sage trusts the trustworthy and trusts the untrustworthy also (49). Light promises mean little 信 (63). True words are not beautiful (81).
信.gap: “Faith” has become religious, “sincerity” is a feeling, and “trust” is the other person’s response. 信 is all three as one fact: word and deed agree.

senses: to repair, to keep in order
to tend, to cultivate (the person, a teaching)
修.shuowenEn: To adorn. From 彡 (strokes of hair or ornament), with 攸 for the sound.
修.story: 修 is regular care for a thing that is already there: to brush it, to mend it, to keep it fit. 修身, “to keep the person in order”, was shared by all the early schools. Passage 54 uses the verb five times, for body, household, village, state, and realm, and each time the object is only 之, “it”.
修.gap: “Cultivate” brings a field and a crop. 修 is nearer to maintenance: how a person keeps a boat, a wall, or a road.

senses: a granary, a storehouse for grain
倉.shuowen: 榖藏也。倉黃取而藏之，故謂之倉。从食省，口象倉形。
倉.shuowenEn: A store for grain. One gathers it in haste and stores it, hence the name. From an abbreviated 食 (food); the 口 pictures the shape of the granary.
倉.story: The granary was the heart of a farming state: tax grain went in after the harvest and came out to feed the army, the court, and, in a good state, the hungry in a bad year. An empty 倉 in spring meant famine. The Laozi names it once: the granaries are very empty (53).
倉.gap: A modern reader has no granary and does not fear the spring. For this text an empty store is the plainest sign of misrule.

倚.def: rely on, depend on; lean heavily

senses: made by people; artifice; acquired by effort
偽.shuowenEn: Deceit. From 人 (person), with 爲 for the sound. (The Shuowen writes the graph in its fuller form, 僞.)
偽.story: A person plus “to make”. For Xunzi it is a proud word: what is good in people is made, not born. For the Laozi it is what appears when cleverness comes out (18). The Guodian slips are reported to have it in passage 19 as a thing to cut off.
偽.gap: “Hypocrisy” judges a motive. 偽 only says “made”; it is the reader who decides if made is false.

傷.shuowenEn: A cut, a wound. From 人 (person), with a short form of 𥏻 for the sound.
傷.story: A wound on a person. Passage 60 uses the word four times in forty-eight characters: the spirits do not 傷 people, the sage also does not, and the two do not 傷 each other. Passage 74 warns that one who chops in place of the master carpenter seldom fails to 傷 the hand.
傷.gap: “Harm” is abstract. 傷 is a cut in flesh.

儉.shuowenEn: To bind, to restrain. From 人 (person), with 僉 for the sound.
儉.story: 儉 is the conduct of a person who holds in: few wants, little display, small cost to others. Confucians praised it in ritual and in a ruler’s household. The Laozi uses the word only in passage 67, as the second of three precious things: 儉故能廣, sparing and so able to be wide. Wang Bi explains that when cost is spared the world does not run short. Passage 59 praises a related quality with another word, 嗇, the farmer’s care in storing. The opposite is 奢, lavish, “stretched open”. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to write the word with the graph 檢.
儉.gap: “Economy” is bookkeeping, “moderation” is a mean between extremes, “frugality” is about money. 儉 is a general drawing-in of the self, so that there is more room around it.

兆.def: omen; million; mega; also trillion. China = million; Japan and Taiwan = trillion
senses: the cracks on a heated turtle shell or bone, read in divination
omen, sign; to show a sign
the first trace of a thing to come
a very large number (a million; in old counts more)
兆.shuowenEn: The splits of a scorched turtle shell. From 卜 (to divine); 兆 is a picture. (The Shuowen enters the word under the fuller graph 𠧞.)
兆.story: Shang and Zhou diviners put a hot point to a prepared shell or bone and read the cracks that appeared. 卜 pictures one such crack with its branch; 兆 is the pattern to be read. From there the word came to mean any sign of what is to come. The Laozi uses it as a verb with 未, “not yet”: in passage 20 the speaker is still, 未兆, like an infant that has not yet smiled; in passage 64 a thing that is 未兆 is easy to plan for. The sense is earlier than “early”: no sign has appeared at all. As a part it gives the sound in 跳, 逃, and 桃.
兆.gap: “Omen” in English suggests a message from a god or from fate. 兆 is more physical: a crack, a first visible line. “Before it begins” loses the picture of the diviner and the shell.

senses: former; those who went before, the dead

parts.m: upper part in the Shuowen’s analysis: to go; commonly explained as a foot

先.story: A foot above a person: one who has stepped ahead. From there come “first”, “earlier”, and the dead who went before, 先人. The Laozi distrusts the front place. Dao looks like the forebear of the high god (4). The sage puts the body behind, and it is 先 (7). To stand before the people, put the body behind them (66). One of the speaker’s three guarded things is not daring to go ahead of all under heaven (67).
先.gap: English “first” is a rank and a prize. 先 is a position on a road, with others behind.

光.shuowen: 明也。从火在人上，光明意也。
光.shuowenEn: Brightness. Fire above a person: the idea of light.
光.story: A person who holds fire overhead. 光 is light that goes out and is seen. The Laozi is wary of it: soften the light (4, 56); be bright and do not dazzle (58). In passage 52 it may be used, and then one goes back to 明, the clear state that it came from.
光.gap: English “light” covers both the beam and the brightness. The Chinese line needs them apart: 光 is the beam.

senses: to bear on the shoulder; to be equal to
克.shuowenEn: The shoulder; to shoulder. It shows the form of carved wood under a roof.
克.story: The first sense is to be equal to a load. From there: to be able, to master, to win. In passage 59 one who has stored 德 in layers has “nothing not 克”: nothing that such a person is not equal to.
克.gap: “Conquer” puts an enemy in the line. 克 needs only a weight.

兌.def: cash; exchange, barter; weight; trigram ☱; hexagram ䷹
senses: an opening, a hole; the mouth
a trigram and hexagram of the Changes: lake, mouth, joy
兌.shuowenEn: To speak; to be pleased. From 儿 (a person’s legs), with 㕣 for the sound.
兌.story: Commonly explained as a person with open mouth. It gives its sound, and something of its sense, to 說 (to speak; to please), 悅 (joy), 稅 (tax), 脫 (to shed), and 銳 (sharp). In the Laozi it is the opening that one blocks: 塞其兌，閉其門 (52, 56). Readers of the Changes also heard the trigram of the lake and the mouth.
兌.gap: “Openings” or “apertures” is anatomy. 兌 also carries speech, pleasure, and exchange: everything that passes out through a mouth.

senses: a rhinoceros, or a great wild ox (the identity is debated)
兕.story: The Shuowen lists the animal under an old picture-graph and describes it as like a wild ox and dark in colour, apart from 犀, the rhinoceros of the far south. Shang kings hunted it. Its horn made drinking cups and its hide made armour. In passage 50 it is the first danger of the road: it finds no place to thrust its horn.
兕.gap: “Rhinoceros” puts the scene in Africa or India for an English reader. The 兕 belonged to the plains and marshes of ancient China.

入.shuowenEn: To go inside. It shows things that come down together from above.
入.story: Two strokes that lean together and point up, like a wedge or a root tip. Its partner is 出, to come out. The Laozi pairs them for birth and death: 出生入死, “to come out is life, to go in is death” (50). In passage 43, that which has no substance 入, enters, where there is no gap.

全.shuowenEn: Complete. From 入 and 工. (The Shuowen enters the word under the older graph 仝.)
全.story: The Shuowen glosses the word “complete”; it is commonly added that the form with jade stood for a piece of jade with no flaw. In the Warring States it was a word of survival and of strategy: to keep one’s life whole, to take a state whole. The proverb of passage 22 says the bent is what stays 全. Our text of passage 16 has it in the great chain: even-handed, then whole; whole, then heaven.
全.gap: “Perfect” and “complete” add an ideal. 全 only says that no piece has been broken off.

senses: a term of respect for an old man
公.shuowen: 平分也。从八从厶。八猶背也。韓非曰：背厶爲公。
公.shuowenEn: To share out evenly. From 八 and 厶. 八 is like “to turn the back”. Han Fei said: to turn the back on the private (厶) is 公.
公.story: The word joins three ideas that English keeps apart: fair, public, and noble. The Legalists set 公 against 私, the private, and built the state on the first. In passage 16 it comes from having room for all things, and it leads on to heaven.
公.gap: “Impartial” is cool; “public” is institutional; “duke” is a rank. A Chinese reader hears all three.

共.def: together with, all, total; to share

兵.shuowen: 械也。从廾持斤，并力之皃。
兵.shuowenEn: Implements (of war). From two hands that hold an axe; the look of strength joined.
兵.story: Two hands grip an axe. The word began as the weapon, passed to the men who carry weapons, and then to war as a whole: the 兵法 of Sunzi is “the method of war”. The Laozi names it often and never with praise. One does not force the world with 兵 (30); 兵 are tools of ill omen (31); strong 兵 do not win (76); when armies meet, the one that grieves wins (69).
兵.gap: English must choose “weapons”, “soldiers”, or “war”. 兵 is all three, so a sentence about tools is also about men.

senses: to hold two at once; both, together
to combine, to join under one hand
兼.shuowen: 并也。从又持秝。兼持二禾，秉持一禾。
兼.shuowenEn: To join. From a hand (又) that holds 秝 (two grain plants). 兼 holds two stalks; 秉 holds one.

parts.m: two grain plants in a row

兼.story: One hand around two stalks of grain. The Warring States used the word for the swallowing of states, and the Mohists for care that takes in everyone. The Laozi uses it once: a great state wants no more than to 兼畜人, to gather people in and feed them (61). The character is the sound-part of 謙, “modest”, and 廉, “a clean edge”.
兼.gap: “Unite” is too noble and “annex” too harsh. 兼 is neutral: two things in one grip.

冥.shuowen: 幽也。从日从六，冖聲。日數十。十六日而月始虧幽也。
冥.shuowenEn: Hidden, dark. From 日 (sun) and 六 (six), with 冖 for the sound. The count of the sun is ten; on the sixteenth day the moon begins to wane toward darkness.
冥.story: The Shuowen reads the calendar in it: ten and six, the day after full moon, when the dark starts to come back. With 窈, the depth of a cave, it makes the passage’s second word for the unseen: 窈兮冥兮, and within it there is essence (21).
冥.gap: “Dark” in English leans toward evil or ignorance. 冥 is the dark of depth and of the moon’s return.

senses: ill-omened: the diviner’s verdict, opposite of 吉
凶.shuowen: 惡也。象地穿交陷其中也。
凶.shuowenEn: Bad. It pictures a hole in the ground and a thing that has fallen into it.
凶.story: One of the two commonest words on the oracle bones and in the Book of Changes: this course is 吉, that one is 凶. The Shuowen sees a pitfall. In passage 16, to rise wildly without knowledge of the constant is 凶; in passage 30, after a great army there are 凶 years.
凶.gap: “Evil” makes it a moral judgement. 凶 is about outcomes: this path has a hole in it.

出.def: go out, send out; stand; produce

刃.shuowenEn: The hard part of a knife. It shows a knife that has an edge.

parts.m: a mark that points at the edge

刃.story: A knife with one added stroke that points at the place that cuts: a character of the “pointing” kind, like 本 (a tree marked at the root) and 末 (a tree marked at the tip). It gives its sound to 忍, to endure, and 認, to recognise. In the Laozi it occurs once: the weapon finds no place to lodge its 刃 in the one who holds life well (50).
刃.gap: English “blade” is the whole flat of the knife. 刃 is only the line that cuts.

分.def: divide; small unit of time etc.

利.shuowen: 銛也。从刀。和然後利，从和省。《易》曰：「利者，義之和也。」
利.shuowenEn: Sharp. From 刀 (knife). After harmony comes gain; the graph takes a part of 和. The Changes says: “Gain is the harmony of what is right.”
利.story: A knife beside grain: the common explanation is a blade that cuts the crop, and so both “sharp” and “harvest, gain”. The Shuowen prefers a moral reading, with 禾 as a short form of 和, harmony. 利 was one of the most contested words of the Warring States. For the Mohists it was the measure of right action: that which benefits the world. Mencius set it against rightness. Sunzi uses it for the advantage that a general seeks. The Laozi uses both senses: “sharp tools” (36, 57), and water that “benefits the ten thousand things and does not contend” (8). In passage 11 it is the gain that substance gives.
利.gap: English separates “sharp”, “profit”, and “benefit”. In 利 the edge is still in the word: gain is a thing that is cut and taken.

senses: to cut to a pattern (cloth, timber)
to make, to shape; to regulate, to control
an institution, a system; a rule
制.shuowen: 裁也。从刀从未。未，物成有滋味，可裁斷。一曰止也。
制.shuowenEn: To cut out. From 刀 (knife) and 未. 未 is a thing grown ripe and full of flavour, which can be cut. Another sense: to stop.

parts.m: a tree in full leaf; what is ripe for cutting (Shuowen)

制.story: 制 is the cut that makes something: the tailor’s cut that turns cloth into a robe, the carpenter’s that turns timber into a frame. From it came “to regulate” and the noun for the institutions of a state. The Laozi uses the craft sense and the political sense at once: “the great cutting does not sever” (28); “when the cutting begins, there are names” (32).
制.gap: “System” and “regulation” hide the knife. In 制 it is still visible.

senses: the unbroken line of the Book of Changes (partner of 柔)
剛.shuowenEn: To cut through by force. From 刀 (knife), with 岡 for the sound.

parts.m: sound gāng; by itself, a ridge

剛.story: The hardness of a blade. With 柔, soft, it forms one of the basic pairs of Chinese thought. The Laozi always gives the victory to the other side: the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong (36); the soft overcomes the hard (78).
剛.gap: “Hard” is neutral in English and “firm” is praise. 剛 has an edge: it is the hardness that cuts and can snap.

senses: to cut apart, to hack off
割.shuowenEn: To strip, to cut apart. From 刀 (knife); 害 gives the sound.
割.story: 割 is the butcher’s and the conqueror’s cut: meat from the bone, a strip of land from a neighbour. Warring States treaties are full of 割地, “cut land”. The Laozi uses it twice for what the sage’s shaping does not do: “the great cutting does not sever” (28), and the sage is “square and does not cut” (58).
割.gap: English “cut” is neutral. 割 hurts; its sound part is the word for harm.

劌.def: to cut, injure, stab, stick on

功.shuowen: 以勞定國也。从力从工，工亦聲。
功.shuowenEn: To settle the state by toil. From 力 (strength) and 工 (work); 工 also gives the sound.

parts.m: strength; commonly explained as a plow

功.story: 功 is work that a state counts. In the Warring States, rank and land went more and more to recorded merit and less to birth, and 功 became the unit of a career. The Laozi speaks of it always at the moment of completion, and always with a step away: the work done and not dwelt in (2), the work done and the person withdraws (9), the work done and the people say “we are so of ourselves” (17). The one who boasts has no 功 (24).
功.gap: “Work” is too plain and “achievement” too private. 功 is public credit: what others owe you for what you did.

勇.shuowenEn: It is breath, vital energy. From 力 (strength), with 甬 for the sound.
勇.story: The Shuowen defines courage as 气, breath: the surge of energy that carries a body forward. It was the prized quality of the Warring States, rewarded with rank and sung in stories of swordsmen. The Laozi gives it conditions. Courage grows from tenderness, and courage with the tenderness let go is death (67). Courage in daring kills; courage in not-daring keeps alive (73). Confucius drew a similar line: the humane are sure to be brave, and the brave are not sure to be humane.
勇.gap: “Brave” is praise in English with no question asked. 勇 is a raw force of breath and strength; the texts ask what it serves.

senses: to set in motion, to act
動.shuowenEn: To rise, to start up. From 力 (strength), with 重 for the sound.
動.story: Strength beside a weight. In the Laozi the good in movement is timing (8); the bellows, when it moves, gives more and more (5); who can bring the still thing to life by slow movement (15)? People move toward the place of death (50). The Dao has one movement: turning back (40). The short form is 动.
動.gap: English “movement” suggests progress or a cause. The Dao’s 動 goes back to where it came from.

senses: to bear, to be equal to (a load, a task)
to surpass; all, completely (不可勝: more than can be…)
勝.shuowenEn: To bear, to be equal to. From 力 (strength); 朕 gives the sound.
勝.story: 勝 began as the ability to carry: to be equal to a weight. To overcome an opponent is to be more than equal to him. The Laozi uses the word for its reversals: the soft overcomes the hard (36, 78), stillness overcomes heat (45), the female overcomes the male by stillness (61). In passage 31 a victory is to be mourned. In passage 33 the one who overcomes others has force, and the one who overcomes the self is strong.
勝.gap: “Conquer” and “defeat” need an enemy. 勝 can mean only that one is equal to what one carries, which is how the self is “overcome”.

senses: momentum; the lie of the land; a situation’s tendency
勢.shuowen: 盛力權也。从力埶聲。經典通用埶。
勢.shuowenEn: Full force and weight of authority. From 力 (strength), with 埶 for the sound. The classics generally write 埶.
勢.story: A key term of Warring States thought. For the Sunzi it is the energy of a formation, like pent water or round stones on a slope. For Shen Dao and Han Fei it is the power of position that makes a ruler obeyed. The Laozi uses it once, mildly: circumstance completes what the Way has born (51). The silk texts read 器 there.
勢.gap: No one English word covers it: “momentum”, “circumstance”, “position”, and “power” each give a part.

senses: to be worn out, used up (in the Laozi, as commonly read)
勤.story: The plain sense is hard work, and one passage of the Laozi uses it so: the best student hears of Dao and practices it with 勤 (41). In two other places most readers take it as “worn out, exhausted”. Use the valley spirit, and it is not 勤 (6). Block the openings and shut the gates, and to the end of life there is no 勤 (52). The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to write the word in passage 6 as 堇, with no “strength” part.
勤.gap: English must choose between “without effort” and “never used up”. The first is about the user and the second is about the source. The Chinese word can lean either way.

勿.def: must not, do not; without, never

senses: to change others by teaching or example (教化)
to melt, to dissolve; to die (to “change”)
化.shuowenEn: Teaching takes effect. From 𠤎 (a person turned upside down: “to change”) and 人 (a person); 𠤎 also gives the sound.

parts.m: here 𠤎, a person turned over

化.story: Two human figures, one upright and one overturned: a thing becomes its other. Confucians used the word for the moral change that a ruler’s teaching works in the people. The Laozi adds 自: the ten thousand things will 自化, change of themselves, if lords and kings keep to not-doing (37), and “I do not act, and the people change of themselves” (57). The Zhuangzi makes 化 its word for the endless turning of one form of life into the next.
化.gap: “Transform” and “reform” suggest an agent and a goal. 化 can be a process with no agent and no better or worse: ice to water, a living thing to earth.

senses: a carpenter, a worker in wood
a master craftsman of any trade
skill in making (匠心, a craftsman’s mind)
匠.shuowen: 木工也。从匚从斤。斤，所以作器也。
匠.shuowenEn: A worker in wood. From 匚 (a box) and 斤 (an axe). The axe is that with which vessels are made.

parts.m: a box, a vessel that receives things

匠.story: An axe in its box. The word first meant the carpenter and then any master of a craft. The Zhuangzi tells of Carpenter Shi, who whirled his axe and hewed a speck of plaster from a friend’s nose without a scratch. In the Laozi the word appears only in passage 74: a ruler who kills in the place of the one in charge of killing is like a person who hews in the place of the great carpenter, and seldom is the hand not hurt.
匠.gap: “Carpenter” is a trade in English. 大匠 is also a rank: the master whose stroke has no waste. The image is of mastery that cannot be borrowed.

匹.def: bolt of cloth; counter for horses

千.def: thousand; many, numerous; very; (Cant.) a cheater, swindler

博.shuowen: 大通也。从十从尃。尃，布也。
博.shuowenEn: Great and thorough reach. From 十 (ten) and 尃. 尃 is to spread out.
博.story: Breadth, above all of learning. The Confucians prized it: learn broadly, and hold it together with ritual. The Laozi sets it against knowing: those who know are not broad, and the broad do not know (81). The word is used only there in the book.
博.gap: “Erudite” and “well-read” are praise. The Laozi uses 博 for knowledge that has spread out and lost its depth.

危.def: dangerous, precarious; high; 12th lunar mansion, determinative star α Aquarii (Sadalmelik)

卻.shuowenEn: To restrain desire. From 卪 (a kneeling figure; a tally), with 谷 for the sound.
卻.story: 卻 is movement backward: to retreat, to refuse a gift, to turn something away. Later editors doubted the Shuowen’s gloss, “to restrain desire”, and corrected the text; we quote it as it stands. In passage 46 the running horses are 卻, turned back, from the road to the farm. The modern short form is 却.
卻.gap: English “turn back” needs someone who does the turning. The Chinese verb stands without a subject.

厚.story: Thickness as of a mountain. Applied to people it is generosity and depth of feeling; its opposite is 薄, thin. The full-grown person stays in the thick (38). One who holds de in fullness, 含德之厚, is like an infant (55). But thick living can kill: people die early because they feed life too thickly (50, 75).
厚.gap: English “thick” is not praise for a person. 厚 is: solid, kind, deep.

senses: (yā) to press down, to weigh on (later 壓)
(yàn) to be sated, to have had enough
to be sick of, to loathe, to reject
厭.shuowen: 笮也。从厂猒聲。一曰合也。
厭.shuowenEn: To press down. From 厂 (cliff), with 猒 for the sound. Another sense: to fit together.

parts.m: sated: sweet (甘) with dog meat (肰); also the sound

厭.story: The inner part, 猒, is a full stomach: the Shuowen says “to have eaten one’s fill”. Under a cliff it becomes pressure. The one graph wrote both “to press” and “to be sick of”, and the Laozi uses each. The rich are 厭 with drink and food (53). The world pushes the sage forward and does not tire (66). Passage 72 plays on both in one line: do not press on what the people live by; only because there is no pressing, there is no loathing. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 猒 in all three places.
厭.gap: English has no word that is both a weight from above and a disgust from below. “Oppress” and “fed up” together come near.

及.def: extend; reach; come up to; and
senses: to reach, to catch up with
to come to, to extend to
及.shuowenEn: To catch up with. From a hand and a person.

parts.m: a hand that reaches from behind

及.story: A hand takes hold of a person from behind. The wordless teaching and the gain of not-doing are things that few in the world 及 (43). The great trouble that I have is that I have a self; if I had none, what trouble would 及, reach, me (13)?
及.gap: “Attain” sounds like an achievement. 及 is plainer: to come level with someone on the road.

senses: to turn back, to return (later written 返)
反.shuowenEn: To turn over. From 又 (a hand); the 厂 shows the shape of turning over.

parts.m: here the sign of turning over (not “cliff”)

反.story: A hand that turns something over, or is turned. The one gesture gives return, reversal, and opposition, and the Laozi uses all three. The great goes far, and far means 反, return (25). Dark de is deep and far and goes 反, the other way, from things (65). Straight words seem 反, their opposite (78). And the summary: 反 is the movement of the Dao (40).
反.gap: “Return”, “reversal”, and “opposite” are three English words with three feelings: home, change, conflict. 反 is one word, and a reader of Chinese does not have to choose.

senses: to take a trophy ear (in the hunt; after battle)
取.shuowen: 取：捕取也。从又从耳。《周禮》：“獲者取左耳。”
取.shuowenEn: 取 is “to catch and take”. It is made of 又 (a hand) and 耳 (an ear). The Zhouli says: “whoever makes a catch takes the left ear.”
取.story: A hand on an ear. The Shuowen explains it from two customs it quotes: in the royal hunt, whoever caught an animal took its left ear as the tally, and after battle the cut ears of the enemy (聝) were presented as the count. From the trophy the word became the general verb “to take”. The Laozi uses it in two ways. One is the formula of choice: leave that, 取 this (12, 38, 72). The other is the taking of the realm: the one who wants to 取 all under heaven and work on it will not succeed (29); 取 all under heaven by having no business (48, 57); a large state that puts itself below a small one 取 it (61).
取.gap: “Take” is a mild word. 取 began as an act of war, and the Laozi’s phrase “take all under heaven” keeps some of that.

senses: (early) to hand over, later written 授
受.shuowenEn: To hand over to one another. From 𠬪 (two hands), with a reduced 舟 (boat) for the sound.

parts.m: what is left of the object passed between the hands

受.story: Two hands and a thing that passes between them. One graph first served for both giving and receiving. In passage 78 the ruler receives the dirt and the ill omens of the state, as low water receives what runs down.
受.gap: “Accept” and “bear” sound passive or heroic. 受 is a plain act of the hands: someone holds a thing out, and you take it.

senses: the right hand; the right side
to help, to protect (later written 佑)
the west side (facing south); the side of death and war
右.shuowenEn: Hand and mouth help each other. From 又 (the right hand) and 口 (mouth).

parts.m: a hand (the right hand 又 in the old form)

右.story: 右 is the right hand with a mouth: the hand that feeds, or the hand helped by a spoken word. Like 左 it first meant “to help”. In ritual order it is the lower side in peace and the leading side in mourning and war. Laozi 31 notes that the chief general stands on the right, and reads this as the placing of a funeral.
右.gap: English “right” also means correct and just. 右 has none of that; in this passage it is the side of the dead.

司.def: take charge of, control, manage; officer
senses: to have charge of, to manage
an officer; an office (司馬, 司寇, 司空)
司.shuowenEn: A minister who manages affairs outside (the court). From 后 (sovereign) written in reverse.

parts.m: a mouth: the word of command

司.story: The Shuowen reads 司 as the mirror image of 后, the sovereign who issues orders. The officer faces the other way and carries the orders out. In early writing the two were probably one graph that could face either side. The word filled the lists of government posts. In the Laozi it names two offices: 司殺者, the one in charge of killing (74), and in passage 79 司契 and 司徹, the keeper of the tally and the keeper of the tithe.
司.gap: “To preside” sounds grand. 司 is the daily work of a post: a desk, a duty, and a limit.

senses: to share; to be at one with
同.shuowenEn: To join, to meet. From 𠔼 (a cover) and 口 (mouth).
同.story: Many mouths under one cover: an assembly, agreement. In the Laozi it is the word for unity that is not mystical fusion. The two come out together, and together are called dark (1); it shares the dust of the world (4, 56); one who works at the Way is the same as the Way (23); and passage 56 names the result 玄同, the dark sameness.
同.gap: “Become one with” sounds like rapture. 同 is plainer: of the same kind, in the same company.

senses: title, rank; a word as against the thing (實)
名.shuowen: 自命也。从口从夕。夕者，冥也。冥不相見，故以口自名。
名.shuowenEn: To call oneself. From 口 (mouth) and 夕 (evening). Evening is darkness. In the dark people cannot see each other, so each one says a name with the mouth.
名.story: The Shuowen’s picture is one of the best in the dictionary: two people meet at dusk, cannot see faces, and call out who they are. A name is a voice in the dark. In the Warring States, 名 was a central problem of government and logic. Confucius wanted names made correct, so that “ruler” and “father” would bind the people who carried those titles. The debaters of the School of Names tested how names attach to things. Legalist administrators held each officer to the 名 of the post. The word also means fame, and the Laozi asks in passage 44: 名與身孰親, “name or body, which is closer to you?”
名.gap: English “name” is mostly a label for a person or thing. 名 also covers title, role, reputation, and the whole act of dividing the world with words. “Nameless” (無名) in the Laozi is not “anonymous”. It is the state before the world is cut into kinds.

senses: to rule, to be lord of
a polite “you”; 君子: a gentleman
君.shuowenEn: The honoured one. From 尹. He issues commands, so it has a mouth.

parts.m: a hand that holds a staff: one who governs

君.story: A lord, in this graph, is a hand with the staff of office and a mouth that gives orders. 君子, “the lord’s son”, became the Confucian word for a person of noble conduct. In Laozi 26 the word comes twice: stillness is the lord of restlessness, and the restless ruler loses the lord, which means his seat and also his own inner ruler. The Mawangdui copies of passage 26 are reported to use 君子 where the received text has “the sage”.
君.gap: English “lord” is feudal or religious. 君 is any holder of command, and also the faculty in a person that should be in command.

senses: to contain, to hold within, to keep unsaid
the jade put in the mouth of the dead
含.shuowenEn: To hold in the mouth. From 口 (mouth), with 今 for the sound.
含.story: 含 is to keep a thing behind closed lips: not swallowed, not spoken. Passage 55 opens with 含德, “to hold de in the mouth”: power kept in and not shown, as a baby’s strength is all inside. The opposite is in passage 38, where lower 德 is the kind that is held on to and shown.
含.gap: “To have” or “to possess” makes 德 a property. 含 is nearer to holding the breath.

吾.shuowenEn: “I”: what one calls oneself. From 口 (mouth), with 五 for the sound.
吾.story: One of the two common classical words for “I”; the other is 我. 吾 is used mostly as subject or possessor. The speaker of the Laozi says 吾 at moments of plain report or confessed limit: “I do not know whose child it is” (4); “I have great trouble because I have a body” (13); “I see their return” (16); “I do not know its name” (25); “my words are very easy to know” (70). The book has no name of an author in it. It has this voice.
吾.gap: English “I” is always the same word. Classical Chinese has several, and the choice sets a tone; 吾 is plain and unassuming.

味.shuowenEn: Rich flavour. From 口 (mouth), with 未 for the sound.

parts.m: a tree in full leaf; “flavour”; gives the sound

味.story: A mouth beside a tree at its ripest. The Laozi distrusts strong flavour: the five tastes dull the mouth (12). It praises the flat: the Dao, when it comes out of the mouth, is thin and has no 味 (35), and the task is to 味無味, to taste what has no taste (63).
味.gap: “Taste” in English is also judgment, as in “good taste”. 味 stays on the tongue, and then becomes slow, bodily attention.

命.def: life; destiny, fate, luck; an order, instruction
senses: what is given to each: life, span, lot
命.shuowenEn: To cause, to send on a task. From 口 (mouth) and 令 (an order).

parts.m: an order; a person who kneels under a roof or a mouth

命.story: At first the same word as 令, a spoken order. Heaven’s order gave a ruling house its right to rule; in the same way each creature has from heaven its nature and its length of days. 復命 was the envoy’s report when the task was done. In passage 16 each thing goes back to the root and “reports on its charge”. Passage 51 says no one commands (命) the honour paid to the Way; it is always so of itself.
命.gap: “Fate” and “destiny” point to a fixed future. 命 points back to something given at the start.

senses: to answer in song, to sing in response
和.shuowenEn: To answer one another. From 口 (mouth), with 禾 for the sound.
和.story: 和 began in music: one voice or instrument that answers another. It also belonged to the kitchen. A statesman in the Zuo Tradition explains 和 with a cook who makes soup: water, fire, vinegar, salt, and plums are different, and the cook balances them. If all were the same, he says, who could eat it? So 和 is never sameness; it needs difference. In the Laozi, sounds and voices 和 each other (2), the breaths of yin and yang surge into 和 (42), and to know 和 is called the constant (55). In passage 4 it takes an unusual object: light.
和.gap: English “harmony” has become soft and vague, and “peace” is only the absence of conflict. 和 is an active skill: to tune different things so that each can still be heard.

senses: to blame, to hold at fault
无咎: no harm (a verdict in divination)
咎.shuowen: 災也。从人从各。各者，相違也。
咎.shuowenEn: Calamity. From 人 (person) and 各; 各 means to be at odds with each other.

parts.m: a foot that points down (top of 各)
a person (written small at the upper right)

咎.story: A word of the diviners. In the Book of Changes a line is judged 吉, good fortune; 凶, misfortune; or very often 无咎, “no harm”: a result with nothing to regret. The Shuowen reads the graph as a person at cross purposes. The Laozi uses the word twice, and both times the harm is self-made. The rich and proud leave their 咎 to themselves (9). No 咎 is greater than the wish to get (46).
咎.gap: English keeps harm (what happens) apart from blame (who is at fault). 咎 is both at once: a harm that has an owner.

senses: the wailing of the bereaved in the funeral rites
to pity, to feel sorrow for
哀.shuowenEn: To mourn (閔: the mourner at the gate). From 口 (mouth), with 衣 (garment) for the sound.
哀.story: 哀 is the grief of the funeral: a mouth set inside the graph for a robe. The rites gave it a form, with set times for wailing and set clothes of coarse hemp. The Laozi uses the word twice, and both times in war. When many have been killed, weep for them with 哀 and sorrow; observe a victory with the rites of mourning (31). When raised weapons meet, the one who grieves wins (69). From the second line came a later proverb, 哀兵必勝: an army in mourning is sure to win.
哀.gap: “Sorrow” and “compassion” are feelings one may have at a distance. 哀 is ritual mourning, done aloud and in public, as for one’s own dead.

senses: wéi: only; it is just that
唯.shuowenEn: To assent. From 口 (mouth), with 隹 for the sound.
唯.story: The quick “yes” that a junior owed a senior. Passage 20 sets it against 阿, a slacker sound, and asks how far apart they are. As a grammar word it means “only”: 夫唯不爭, “just because one does not contend”.
唯.gap: English has “yes, sir”, “yes”, “yeah”, “uh-huh”. Chinese ritual made a rule of the difference.

senses: to approve, to treat as good
善.shuowen: 吉也。从誩从羊。此與義美同意。
善.shuowenEn: Lucky, auspicious. From 誩 (two “speech”) and 羊 (sheep). This shares one idea with 義 and 美. (The Shuowen enters the word under the older graph 譱.)

parts.m: speech (two of them in the old form)

善.story: The old graph 譱 is a sheep between two words. The modern form keeps the sheep on top and has pressed the two 言 into the strokes below it. The Shuowen ties it to 美 and 義 through the sheep, the animal of offerings and good omens. The word is moral and practical together: good, and good at. The Laozi plays on both. The highest 善 is like water, and then seven lines say what each thing is good at (8). The one who is good at walking leaves no track (27). The sage is good to the good and good to the not-good also (49).
善.gap: English keeps “good” (moral) apart from “good at” (skill). 善 does not. A reader must hear both each time.

senses: sàng: to lose; to be bereft of; to perish
sāng: mourning, a funeral; the rites for the dead
喪.shuowen: 亾也。从哭从亾。會意。亾亦聲。
喪.shuowenEn: To lose. From 哭 (to wail) and 亾 (gone); a joined-meaning graph. 亾 also gives the sound.
喪.story: The Shuowen reads 喪 as wailing for one who is gone. The oracle-bone forms are commonly described as a mulberry tree, borrowed for its sound, with mouths added. The word names both the loss and the rites that answer it. In Laozi 31 a victory in battle is to be received with 喪禮, the rites of mourning; passage 69 warns that to take the enemy lightly is close to 喪, losing, one’s treasures.
喪.gap: English keeps “loss” and “funeral” apart. 喪 is one graph, so to mourn a victory is also to call it a loss.

嗇.def: miserly, thrifty, stingy; stopped up, constipated
senses: to store the harvest; to hold back, to not spend
嗇夫: a farmer; a village granary officer
嗇.shuowen: 愛瀒也。从來从㐭。來者，㐭而藏之。故田夫謂之嗇夫。
嗇.shuowenEn: To be sparing. From 來 (wheat) and 㐭 (granary). The wheat is put into the granary and stored. So men of the fields are called 嗇夫.
嗇.story: Wheat over a granary: a farmer shuts away part of the harvest, and above all the seed. The Laozi uses the word once, in passage 59, and makes it the best rule for ordering people and serving heaven. Han Feizi explains it as not spending one’s spirit; Wang Bi takes it as the farmer who weeds and does not force the crop. It differs from 儉, the plain living of passage 67.
嗇.gap: “Frugality” and “moderation” are mild. “Stingy” is the modern sense and a vice. 嗇 is restraint now for the sake of life later.

senses: a person’s capacity or talent; to value someone’s ability
器.shuowen: 皿也。象器之口，犬所以守之。
器.shuowenEn: A dish. The graph shows the mouths of vessels, and a dog that guards them.
器.story: Four mouths around a dog: the Shuowen sees a row of vessels with a watchdog. Modern scholars debate the middle part, but the four openings are plain. 器 first meant pots, then each made tool, and above all the cast bronzes of ancestral ritual, which were the signs of rank. From there it came to mean a person’s capacity. Confucius said that the noble person is not a 器. The Laozi turns the word several ways: the uncarved block is split to make 器 (28); the world is a spirit 器 and cannot be handled (29); the great 器 is completed late (41); and in passage 11 its use is its hollow.
器.gap: English keeps “vessel”, “tool”, and “talent” apart. 器 joins them, so that each statement about a pot is quietly a statement about a person.

固.shuowenEn: Blocked on four sides. From 囗 (an enclosure), with 古 for the sound.
固.story: A wall on four sides: 固 is what cannot be got into or pulled open. Passage 55 uses it for a newborn’s fist: bones weak, sinews soft, and the grip 固. Passage 59 uses it for the deep root. Later breathing manuals call a fist with the thumb folded inside 握固, “the firm grip”.
固.gap: “Firm” suggests hardness. The passage’s point is that this firmness comes from softness.

senses: a state, a domain with its walled capital
國.shuowenEn: A state. From 囗 (an enclosure) and 或 (an enclosure with a dagger-axe that guards a piece of ground).

parts.m: a town 口, a dagger-axe 戈, and ground 一: a defended place

國.story: A wall around a weapon and a piece of land. In the Warring States a 國 was a territorial state with borders, registers, and an army. The Laozi speaks to its rulers: govern a great state as you cook a small fish (60); a great state is like the low reach of a river (61). The old manuscripts write 邦 in these places; scribes changed it to 國 to avoid the name of the first Han emperor. Passage 80 imagines the state small.
國.gap: “Country” and “nation” suggest a people with a shared identity. A 國 was a ruler’s armed domain; the people in it could be lured away by a rival.

senses: to plan, to map out, to think ahead about
a map, a chart, a picture
圖.shuowen: 畫計難也。从囗从啚。啚，難意也。
圖.shuowenEn: To draw up plans for a difficulty. From 囗 (an enclosure) and 啚; 啚 gives the idea of difficulty.

parts.m: a granary district; hard to get

圖.story: A border drawn round the granaries of a district: a map, and then the act of planning. The Shuowen’s gloss joins 圖 to 難, “difficulty”, and so does passage 63: 圖難於其易, plan for the hard while it is easy. A map was the standard gift of surrender between states, and the famous attempt on the life of the king of Qin was made with a dagger rolled in one.
圖.gap: “Plan” is dry in English. 圖 keeps the drawn line: to plan is to see the thing laid out before it happens.

土.def: soil, earth; items made of earth

在.def: be at, in, on; consist in, rest

senses: all alike; a potter’s wheel (also written 鈞)
均.shuowen: 平徧也。从土从勻，勻亦聲。
均.shuowenEn: Level and reaching everywhere. From 土 (earth) and 勻 (evenly spread), which also gives the sound.
均.story: 均 is ground made level, and by extension any fair division: of land, of tax, of labour. It was a live political word; Confucius says that a ruler should worry less about scarcity than about uneven shares. In Laozi 32 the dew falls and the people, with no one’s order, 自均, become even of themselves.
均.gap: “Harmony” is a feeling. 均 is arithmetic: the same amount to each.

senses: to sit: to kneel on a mat, upright
坐.shuowen: 止也。从土，从畱省。土，所止也。
坐.shuowenEn: To stop, to rest. From 土 (earth) and a short form of 畱 (to stay). Earth is where one stops.
坐.story: The modern form shows two people on the earth. Before chairs, to sit was to kneel on a mat with the body upright. In passage 62 it is better to 坐 and present the Dao than to bring jade and horses. Later Daoists gave the word a full practice: 坐忘, “to sit and forget”, from the Zhuangzi.
坐.gap: “Sit” suggests a chair and ease. 坐 is a formal, grounded posture.

垢.shuowenEn: Turbid. From 土 (earth), with 后 for the sound.

parts.m: sound hòu; by itself: a sovereign, later a queen

垢.story: Dirt that clings: on skin, in water. The Zuo chronicle has an old saying that the ruler of a state “holds dirt in the mouth”, as rivers and marshes take in filth. In the Laozi the word comes once, in the sage’s saying of passage 78: to take on the dirt of the state is to be lord of its altars. A modern collated edition of the Mawangdui silk texts prints 詬, spoken abuse, with the same sound-part.
垢.gap: “Disgrace” and “blame” are social and abstract. 垢 is mud. The link to water, which takes all dirt, depends on the plain sense.

埴.shuowenEn: Sticky earth. From 土 (earth), with 直 for the sound.

parts.m: gives the sound; by itself: straight

埴.story: 埴 is fine clay that holds together when it is wet. With 埏, to knead, it makes the craft phrase 埏埴, “to work clay”, which both the Laozi (11) and the Xunzi use for the potter’s trade. The two books draw opposite lessons from the same act. Xunzi points to the potter’s effort: a vessel does not come from the clay’s nature, and a good person does not come from human nature without training. The Laozi points to the hollow that the potter leaves. China’s oldest pots are many thousands of years older than either book.
埴.gap: “Clay” is close. That which English loses is the phrase: 埏埴 was a set term of a trade, as plain to its first hearers as “throw a pot” is to an English potter.

執.def: hold in hand; keep; carry out
senses: to hold in the hand, to grip
to hold to, to maintain; later (Buddhist): to cling
執.shuowen: 捕罪人也。从丮从幸，幸亦聲。
執.shuowenEn: To arrest a criminal. From 丮 (a kneeling person with hands out) and 幸 (here the old graph 㚔, manacles), which also gives the sound.

parts.m: here: 丮, a kneeling person with both hands held out

執.story: 執 pictures a kneeling person with the hands in a shackle. From “arrest” it widened to any firm hold: to hold a brush, to hold office, to hold a view. The Laozi warns against the grip: “who grips it loses it” (29, 64). Yet it also says to “hold the great image” (35) and “hold the Dao of old” (14); there the hold is of something that cannot be shackled. Buddhist translators later used the word for attachment.
執.gap: English “hold” is gentle. 執 began as handcuffs.

senses: strong (of armor, walls); to make firm
堅.shuowenEn: Hard. From 臤 and 土 (earth).

parts.m: firm, tight; the Shuowen glosses it with 堅 itself

堅.story: Hardness as of packed earth. In the Laozi it is the mark of death and of that which loses. People are soft and weak at birth and 堅 and stiff at death; the hard and strong are followers of death (76). Nothing is better than water at attacking the 堅 (78). The softest gallops over the most 堅 (43).
堅.gap: “Firm” is praise in English. In the Laozi 堅 is a warning.

senses: to repay, to requite, to answer in kind
報.shuowen: 當罪人也。从幸从𠬝。𠬝，服罪也。
報.shuowenEn: To sentence an offender. From 幸 (a sign of fetters) and 𠬝; 𠬝 is to submit to punishment.
報.story: The Shuowen starts from the law court: to give an offender what is due. The wider sense is any paying back, of kindness or of wrong, and the ethics of the time rested on it. Passage 63 keeps the verb and changes the coin: 報怨以德, repay grievance with 德.
報.gap: “Repay” in English is mostly about money. 報 covers gratitude, vengeance, and a judge’s sentence.

塞.def: stop up, block, seal, cork; pass, frontier; fortress

senses: the common world and its affairs
塵.shuowenEn: Deer run and the earth rises. From 麤 (three deer) and 土 (earth).
塵.story: The Shuowen’s form has three deer over earth, and its definition is a scene: a herd runs and dust goes up. The modern graph keeps one deer. Dust in Chinese is thus first a sign of movement and life. In the Laozi it occurs in one phrase, 同其塵, “be one with its dust” (4, 56). Later the word became the usual figure for worldly life: 紅塵, “red dust”, is the busy world; 風塵, “wind and dust”, is hard travel; in Buddhist texts the six 塵 are the objects of the senses. To leave home for a monastery was to leave the dust. The Laozi’s phrase goes the other way.
塵.gap: English “dust” suggests neglect and death (“dust to dust”). 塵 suggests traffic: the world where things are happening.

壁.def: partition wall; walls of a house; 14th lunar mansion, determinative star γ Pegasi (Algenib)

senses: a man of service: knight, officer
a man of learning; an adviser
士.story: The lowest rank of the Zhou nobility, trained in arms and rites. In the Warring States the 士 became a mobile class of experts who sold advice and service to the courts. The Laozi names them in passage 15 (good at being 士), passage 41 (the highest 士 hears the Way and practises it; the lowest laughs), and passage 68 (one good at being a 士 is not warlike).
士.shuowen: 事也。數始於一，終於十。从一从十。孔子曰：「推十合一爲士。」
士.shuowenEn: One who serves. Numbers begin at one and end at ten; the graph is from 一 and 十. Confucius said: “One who can reason from the ten and bring them to one is a 士.”

壯.def: big, large; robust; name of tribe

senses: a birthday (of an elder); to wish long life
壽.shuowenEn: Long-lasting. From a short form of 老 (old); 𠷎 gives the sound.
壽.story: 壽 is long life in the body, the first thing that Zhou bronzes ask of the ancestors and the first of the “five blessings” in the Book of Documents. It became the centre of a whole art of living, and its graph, in a hundred decorative forms, is the commonest emblem on Chinese gifts. The Laozi uses the word once, in the last line of passage 33, and gives it to one who has died and is not lost.
壽.gap: “Immortality” and “eternal life” are about another world. 壽 is years in this one, which is what makes the Laozi’s use of it strange.

senses: to put outside, to leave out of account
外.shuowen: 遠也。卜尚平旦，今夕卜，於事外矣。
外.shuowenEn: Far. Divination values the early morning; now to divine in the evening is to be outside the matter.

parts.m: to divine; a crack in a heated shell

外.story: The Shuowen explains the graph as a divination made at the wrong hour, and so off the point. Modern scholars doubt this and often take one part as the sound. The word is the partner of 內, inside. In the Laozi it is used as a verb: the sage puts the body outside, and the body remains (7). The Zhuangzi makes this a ladder of practice: to put the world outside, then things, then life itself.
外.gap: English cannot say “to outside a thing”. The classical verb means to treat as not one’s concern, with no hostility in it.

senses: to be great; to make great
大.shuowen: 天大，地大，人亦大。故大象人形。
大.shuowenEn: Heaven is great, earth is great, the human too is great. So 大 pictures the human form.

parts.m: a person seen from the front, arms and legs spread

大.story: 大 is a front view of a person with the arms out: the adult who takes up room, used to write “big”. The Shuowen explains the graph with a line from Laozi 25, and in its version the fourth great thing is the human (人), where the received text and, as reported, the excavated copies say the king (王). The figure is the base of 天 (sky, heaven), 夫 (a grown man), and 立 (to stand). In Laozi 25, “great” is the name that the speaker is forced to give the Dao, and it at once turns into “passing on”.
大.gap: English “great” leans toward praise. 大 is first about extent: what reaches everywhere and leaves nothing outside.

senses: to miss, to fail to keep
失.shuowenEn: To let go. From 手 (hand), with 乙 for the sound.
失.story: A thing that leaves the hand. In the Laozi it is the price of grasping: one who grips loses it (29, 64). It is the verb of the great decline: the Way is lost and then comes De, and so on down to ritual (38). And it is a place where a person can settle: the one of loss is at one with loss (23).
失.gap: “Failure” is a verdict on a person. 失 is an event: it slipped.

senses: the peoples of the east (Zhou usage)
夷.shuowen: 平也。从大从弓。東方之人也。
夷.shuowenEn: Level. From 大 (a person) and 弓 (a bow). The people of the east.
夷.story: The Shuowen gives two senses at once: “level”, and the name that the Zhou gave to the peoples east of them, whom it pictures as a person with a bow. The Laozi uses only the first. In passage 14 it is the name of that which the eye cannot see: a surface so even that sight finds no hold. Passage 41 says 夷道若纇, “the level way seems rough”, and passage 53 says 大道甚夷, “the great way is very level”, and people still prefer the side paths.
夷.gap: English versions of passage 14 often say “invisible”. The word does not say that nothing is there. It says there is no feature.

夸.shuowenEn: Extravagance. From 大 (big), with 于 for the sound.

parts.m: big; a person with arms spread

夸.story: 夷 has 大 with a bow; 夸 has 大 with a sound-part below. It is display: spending and talking large. Later the word was written 誇 with a speech sign for “to boast”. In passage 53 it closes the verdict 盜夸. The silk text and the Han Feizi read 竽, a reed pipe, in its place: the lead instrument of a band of thieves.
夸.gap: “Boast” is only talk. 夸 is also lavish living, so 盜夸 is theft worn as a costume.

senses: jī: odd, not paired; a remainder
奇.shuowen: 異也。一曰不耦。从大从可。
奇.shuowenEn: Different. One view: not paired. From 大 (great) and 可 (can).
奇.story: 奇 is what stands out of the row: the odd one, the surprise. Sunzi makes it half of the art of war, the irregular force that wins after the regular force engages. The Laozi gives it to war and to nothing else (57), and sees it grow where it is not wanted: strange things arise, the straight turns into the strange (58). Passage 74 speaks of those who do 奇, and means crime.
奇.gap: English “strange” is mild and “wonderful” is praise. 奇 is neutral and a little dangerous.

parts.m: great; a person with arms out

senses: to hold up with both hands, to offer to a superior
to serve, to wait on; tribute, salary (later 俸)
奉.shuowenEn: To bear up. From 手 (hand) and 廾 (a pair of hands), with 𡴀 for the sound.

parts.m: two hands held up (hidden in the modern form)

奉.story: The gesture of lifting a thing to someone above. In passage 77 the way of people takes from those who lack and 奉 it to those with a surplus: tribute goes up. Then the same verb is turned: who can offer a surplus to all under heaven?
奉.gap: “To give” and “to serve” have no direction. 奉 always goes upward, from the lower to the higher.

senses: a tally: a notched contract split in two halves
to fit together exactly; to be in accord
契.shuowen: 大約也。从大从㓞。《易》曰：“後代聖人易之以書契。”
契.shuowenEn: A major agreement. From 大 (great) and 㓞 (to carve). The Changes says: “The sages of later ages replaced them with writing and tallies.”
契.story: A strip of wood or bamboo, written on, notched, and split; each party kept a half, and the halves were matched when the debt was due. In passage 79 the sage holds the left tally and makes no claim on anyone, and the one with 德 keeps the tally while the one without keeps the tithe. From the object comes the sense “to fit as two halves fit”: 默契, a silent understanding.
契.gap: “Contract” is paper and law courts. A 契 is a thing in the hand, and half of it is in the hand of someone else.

奢.shuowenEn: Stretched out. From 大 (big); 者 gives the sound.

parts.m: big; a person with arms spread

奢.story: 奢 is display that takes more room than it needs. In the classics it is the standing opposite of 儉, thrift; Confucius says that in ritual it is better to be sparing than lavish. In Laozi 29 it is the second of three excesses that the sage puts away, between 甚 (too much pleasure) and 泰 (too much grandeur). Passage 67 names thrift as one of the speaker’s three treasured things.
奢.gap: “Extravagance” sounds like a private vice. 奢 in a ruler meant terraces, taxes, and conscript labour.

senses: the south-west corner of a house: the innermost, honoured place
奧.shuowen: 宛也。室之西南隅。从宀𢍏聲。
奧.shuowenEn: A recess. The south-west corner of the room. From 宀 (roof), with 𢍏 for the sound.
奧.story: In an old house the south-west corner was farthest from the door: the darkest and most sheltered place, where the elder sat and the household offerings were set. The Analects has a proverb about paying court to the 奧 or to the stove. The Laozi says that the Dao is the 奧 of the ten thousand things (62); Wang Bi explains it as a place of shade and cover. The silk texts are reported to read 注, “where things pour”.
奧.gap: “Mystery” and “sanctuary” are church words. 奧 is a corner of an ordinary room.

senses: to take by force, to snatch
(old sense) to lose from one’s grip; to slip away
奪.shuowen: 手持隹失之也。从又从奞。
奪.shuowenEn: A hand holds a bird and loses it. From 又 (a hand) and 奞 (a bird that spreads its wings).

parts.m: a figure with arms out; with 隹 it makes 奞, a bird that rouses itself

奪.story: The dictionary’s first sense is a loss: the bird gets out of the hand. The Qing scholar Duan Yucai noted that this old sense is the word later written 脫, “to slip free”, and that the sense “to seize” at first had its own graph, 敓. In time 奪 took the meaning “to seize” and kept the picture of the loss. In passage 36 the two words stand near each other: that which is to be 奪 must first be given, and the fish must not 脫 from the deep. The short form is 夺.
奪.gap: “Seize” and “take away” have only the winner’s view. The graph shows the moment from the side of the open hand.

如.def: if, supposing; as if; like, as

senses: the first hidden stir of a thing
妙.story: 妙 has no entry of its own in the Shuowen, and the early manuscripts of the Laozi do not write it this way. The Mawangdui silk texts have 眇, with the eye radical: tiny, at the limit of sight. Wang Bi defines the word as 微之極, “the far limit of the minute”, the point where a thing is only starting to be a thing. The later graph is written with 女 and 少, and readers have long liked to see in it a young woman, and so freshness and grace; that is a reading of the modern shape, not a recorded origin. From “fine” the word grew to mean wonderful and skilled: a 妙 hand, a 妙 plan. In Buddhism it translated the Sanskrit sat, “true, excellent”, as in the title of the Lotus Sutra, 妙法蓮華經.
妙.gap: “Mystery” makes it a secret. “Wonder” makes it large. “Subtlety” makes it dry. 妙 is small, early, and delightful together: the thing you only see if you want nothing from it.

senses: 百姓: the hundred clans; the common people
姓.shuowenEn: That from which a person is born.

parts.m: birth, to be born; also the sound

姓.story: A woman and birth: the line of descent that a person is born into. Several of the oldest clan names are themselves written with 女, such as 姬, the clan of the Zhou kings, and 姜. In early Zhou only the nobility had a 姓, and 百姓 meant the great families. By the Warring States the phrase meant the people at large. The Laozi uses 百姓 for those whom a ruler affects: the sage treats them as straw dogs (5); when the work is done, they say “we are so of ourselves” (17); the sage takes their heart as the sage’s own (49).
姓.gap: “The people” is a political abstraction. 百姓 is concrete: a hundred family names, each a line of births.

senses: awe, dread; that which is feared
majesty, the power to overawe and punish
威姑: (Han law) the husband’s mother
威.shuowen: 姑也。从女从戌。漢律曰：“婦告威姑。”
威.shuowenEn: The husband’s mother. From 女 (woman) and 戌. The Han statutes say: “A wife reports to the 威姑.”

parts.m: at first a broad axe; a weapon

威.story: A woman under a weapon. The Shuowen takes the first sense as the mother-in-law, before whom a bride stood in awe; modern scholars read the graph as fear and its cause. In political writing 威 is the ruler’s dread power, the partner of 德, favour, and the main tool of the Legalists. It is the same root as 畏, to fear, and the Mawangdui silk texts are reported to write both with one graph. The Laozi has the word only in passage 72: when the people do not fear 威, the great 威 arrives. The power lasts only as long as the fear does.
威.gap: “Authority” sounds lawful and calm; “terror” sounds criminal. 威 is between them: the weight of a power that can hurt you, felt as awe.

senses: a necklace; to wear at the neck (old sense)
to wind round, to be bound by
嬰.shuowen: 頸飾也。从女、賏。賏，其連也。
嬰.shuowenEn: An ornament for the neck. From 女 (woman) and 賏 (two shells); 賏 is the string of them.
嬰.story: First a string of shells at a woman’s neck. The sense “infant” is commonly explained from the child carried at the neck and breast; some scholars say the graph was only borrowed for the sound. The infant is the Laozi’s picture of whole power. Gather the breath to full softness: can there be an infant? (10). “I alone am still, with no sign yet, like an infant that has not yet smiled” (20). Keep to the hen, and return to the infant (28). The one who holds power in fullness is like a newborn child (55).
嬰.gap: The English infant is helpless and “infantile” is an insult. The Laozi’s infant is the strongest state of a person: soft, whole, with no wasted force.

子.def: offspring, child; fruit, seed of; first earthly branch

senses: a hole, an opening; to pass through
孔.shuowen: 通也。从𠃉从子。𠃉，請子之候鳥也。𠃉至而得子，嘉美之也。古人名嘉字子孔。
孔.shuowenEn: To pass through. From 𠃉 (swallow) and 子 (child). The swallow is the bird of the season at which one prays for children. The swallow comes and a child is got; this is cause for joy and praise. Men of old named 嘉 had the formal name 子孔.
孔.story: For the Shuowen, a child and the swallow of spring; for modern scholars, commonly a child with a mark that shows a small opening. The word means “hole” and, in old texts, “very, great”. Passage 21 opens with 孔德, great De. Wang Bi reads “hollow De”.
孔.gap: English must choose “great” or “hollow”. A reader of Chinese sees an opening, and may think of both.

senses: to bear and nurse young; to rear
a style-name, the public name taken at adulthood; to give one
字.shuowen: 乳也。从子在宀下，子亦聲。
字.shuowenEn: To suckle, to bear young. From a child under a roof; 子 also gives the sound.
字.story: A child under a roof. The first sense is to bear and nurse young. Two great later senses grew from it. A written character is a 字 because, as Xu Shen says in the postface to the Shuowen, compound graphs are “born and nursed” from simple pictures and so multiply. And a person’s public name is a 字 because it is born from the given name (名) at the capping rite. In Laozi 25 the speaker does not know the 名 of the thing that came before heaven and earth and so gives it a 字: Dao.
字.gap: English has “name” and “nickname”, and neither fits. A 字 is a formal second name that others use out of respect, because the first name is too intimate to say.

senses: to survive (opposite of 亡, to perish)
to ask after, to care for (old sense)
存.story: The Shuowen gives the old social sense: to visit and ask how someone is. The common classical sense is “to survive”, the partner of 亡 in 存亡, survival or ruin, the constant question for states and families. The Laozi uses it for a presence that is hard to fix. Dao seems, perhaps, to 存 (4). The valley spirit is fine as floss, as if it were 存 (6). The sage puts the body outside, and the body 存 (7). The middling student hears of Dao: it seems to 存, it seems to be lost (41).
存.gap: “Exist” is a flat, philosophical word. 存 is to be still here, to have come through.

senses: a child’s devotion and service to parents
to mourn a parent; mourning dress
孝.shuowen: 善事父母者。从老省，从子。子承老也。
孝.shuowenEn: One who serves father and mother well. From 老 (old), abbreviated, and 子 (child). The child bears up the old.

parts.m: top of 老: an old person

孝.story: An old person above, a child below, and the child carries. 孝 was the root virtue of the Confucian family and later of imperial law. The Laozi names it twice, each time paired with 慈, a parent’s care. When the six kin are out of tune, there are 孝慈 (18). Drop the slogans of humaneness and duty, and the people return to 孝慈 (19). So the book has no quarrel with the thing. It notes when the word becomes loud.
孝.gap: “Filial piety” is a term from Latin and the church. 孝 is concrete: to feed, to carry, to bury, to remember.

senses: “the orphan”: a ruler’s word for himself
孤.shuowenEn: Without a father. From 子 (child), with 瓜 for the sound.
孤.story: A child, and a melon for the sound. Rulers used it of themselves, at first in times of mourning and disaster, since a lord came to his seat when his father died. With 寡 and 不穀 it makes the three royal names of modesty that the Laozi cites two times (39, 42) as proof that the high rests on the low.
孤.gap: English “orphan” asks for pity. In a king’s mouth 孤 was a formula, as flat as “the Crown”.

senses: of a baby: to laugh, to smile (classical)
孩.shuowenEn: A small child laughs. From 口 (mouth), with 亥 for the sound. (This is the entry for 咳; the Shuowen gives 孩, with 子, as its old-script form.)
孩.story: First a verb: the laugh of an infant. By the old rite a father named his child at three months, when he took its hand and made it laugh. In passage 20 the speaker is “like an infant that has not yet laughed”. In passage 49 the sage treats all the people as children who laugh: 聖人皆孩之. Later the graph with the mouth, 咳, went to “cough”, and 孩 became the noun “child”.
孩.gap: English versions say “not yet smiled” or “not yet a child”. The first is right; the second reads a modern noun into an old verb.

孫.shuowen: 子之子曰孫。从子从系。系，續也。
孫.shuowenEn: The child of a child is called 孫. From 子 (child) and 系 (thread). 系 is to continue.

parts.m: a hanging thread; to tie, to continue

孫.story: A grandchild is the child who continues the thread. Chinese speaks of a family as a line of silk: 繼 is to succeed, 續 to continue, 絕 to cut off. In passage 54, 子孫 are the descendants whose offerings do not stop; the silk texts are reported to use the thread word itself, 不絕, “not cut”. 孫 is also the family name of Sunzi, the strategist, whose book shares a world with the Laozi.
孫.gap: English “grandson” counts a generation. 孫 pictures a continuity: one thread that passes through each child.

senses: a school; a branch of learning
學.shuowen: 覺悟也。从教从冂。冂，尚矇也。臼聲。
學.shuowenEn: To awaken. From 教 (to teach) and 冂. 冂 is “still in the dark”. 臼 gives the sound. (The Shuowen enters the word under the fuller graph 斆.)

parts.m: top: two hands around 爻, and a cover

學.story: Two hands, a cover, and a child beneath. In the age of the Laozi 學 meant training in the rites and the texts, with a career as its goal. The book treats it with reserve: cut off learning, no worry (20); in learning one adds each day, in the Way one takes away (48); the sage “learns to unlearn” (64).
學.gap: “Knowledge” is what one has. 學 is the institution and the effort: school.

senses: to stay at, to hold to
守.shuowenEn: To keep an office. From 宀 (roof) and 寸 (hand, measure).

parts.m: a hand at the wrist; measure, rule

守.story: A hand under a roof: to stay at a post and keep it. The Shuowen explains it as the keeping of an office under a rule. The Laozi turns this official word inward. Its sage keeps things that are low and quiet: keep to the middle (5); keep to stillness (16); know the male and keep to the female, know the white and keep to the black (28); keep to the mother (52); keep to the soft (52). If lords and kings could keep to Dao, things would change of themselves (32, 37).
守.gap: “Guard” sounds like defense against attack. 守 is mostly to stay with a thing and not leave it.

安.shuowenEn: Still. From a woman under a roof.
安.story: A woman under a roof: the peace of a house in order. As a verb it is “to settle”: the Laozi asks who can settle the muddy water until it clears (15), and says that a thing still in its place can be held with ease (64). It is also a small grammar word. In 大道廢，有仁義 the Guodian and Mawangdui texts are reported to add it, 安有仁義, where it means “then, thereupon”. In passage 35, 安平太 can be three kinds of peace, or “and then: even and at great ease”.
安.gap: “Peace” in English comes from a word for a pact. 安 is not the end of a fight. It is the stillness of being at home.

senses: ancestor; the main line of a clan
to honor as head; the head or root of a thing
宗.shuowenEn: The shrine where the ancestors are honored. From 宀 (roof) and 示 (altar).

parts.m: altar; a thing shown to the spirits

宗.story: Under a roof stands an altar: 宗 is the hall where a clan keeps the tablets of its dead and feeds them. From the hall the word moved to the first ancestor, to the senior line of descent, and to the act of looking to someone as head.
