Zhou society was organized by 宗法, the rule of the ancestral line, which decided who inherited rank and who made the offerings. Later the word named religious schools: 禪宗 is the Chan (Zen) school. When the Laozi calls Dao the 宗 of the ten thousand things (4), and says “my words have a 宗” (70), it uses the strongest word for authority and belonging that its world had.
宗.gap: “Source” and “origin” are impersonal. 宗 is family: the ancestor is still present and still owed something.

senses: to settle, to come to rest
定.shuowenEn: To be at rest. From a roof and 正 (straight, correct).

parts.m: straight, correct; a foot that goes to a goal

定.story: 正 under a roof: that which has come home and stopped. The Laozi uses it once, as its last word of the Dao book: all under heaven will 自定, settle of itself (37). The silk texts are reported to read 自正, “come right of itself”. Later the word became the usual Chinese translation for the Buddhist term samādhi, settled concentration.
定.gap: “Stabilize” is a verb of management. 定 is what a pendulum does.

senses: a retainer who lives at a lord’s table
the invading side in war (the opposite of 主, the host)
客.shuowenEn: To lodge. From a roof, with 各 for the sound.

parts.m: a foot that arrives at an opening; also the sound part

客.story: A guest is one who stays under a roof that belongs to another. 各, the lower part, wrote the verb “to arrive” in early inscriptions. In the Warring States the 客 were a social class: men of talent who traveled from court to court and lived as retainers. The Laozi uses the word three times: the cautious masters of old are “grave, like a guest” (15); the passing guest stops for music and cakes (35); and the soldier says “I do not dare to be the host, I would rather be the guest” (69).
客.gap: English “guest” is warm and domestic. 客 is also the stranger, the customer, and the one who will leave.

室.def: room, home, house, chamber; 13th lunar mansion, determinative star α Pegasi (Markab)
senses: wife (the one of the inner room)
室.shuowen: 實也。从宀从至。至，所止也。
室.shuowenEn: “Full, solid” (a gloss by like sound). From 宀 (roof) and 至 (to arrive). To arrive: the place where one stops.
室.story: In an early Chinese house the 堂 was the open front hall and the 室 was the closed room behind it, where the family slept. The Analects has a saying about a student who has “gone up into the hall but not yet entered the 室”: the room is the inner part of learning. The Shuowen explains the word by a pun, 實, “full”: a room is where people and goods come to rest. The Laozi (11) looks at the same room and sees that its use is where it has nothing. The Zhuangzi has a famous phrase in the same spirit: 虛室生白, “the empty room gives birth to light”.
室.gap: “Room” in English also means space (“make room”), which is a lucky fit for passage 11. 室 does not have that second sense; the Chinese reader gets the point from the picture, not from the word.

senses: a bound servant in a great house (first sense)
to rule over, to dispose of
宰.shuowen: 辠人在屋下執事者。从宀从辛。辛，辠也。
宰.shuowenEn: A convict who does service under a roof. From 宀 (roof) and 辛; 辛 means crime.

parts.m: a blade for marking convicts; crime; bitter

宰.story: From house-slave to steward to chancellor: the word climbed as the servants of great houses became the officers of states. The steward carved and shared the sacrificial meat, and so the word also means to butcher. Later 宰相 is the prime minister, and 主宰 is the master who disposes of all. The Laozi uses the word in one phrase, twice: 長而不宰, to raise and be head of a thing and not carve it up as its master (10, 51).
宰.gap: “Rule” and “dominate” miss the knife. 宰 is to have a thing on the block and decide its parts.

害.shuowen: 傷也。从宀从口。宀、口，言从家起也。丯聲。
害.shuowenEn: To wound. From 宀 (a roof) and 口 (a mouth): roof and mouth mean that the words begin at home. 丯 gives the sound.
害.story: The Shuowen sees harm as something that starts with words spoken under one’s own roof. The Laozi pairs the word with 利, benefit. Go toward the great image and meet no harm (35). The sage stands in front, and the people do not find it harmful (66). Of two kinds of courage, one benefits and one harms (73). Heaven’s way benefits and does not harm (81).
害.gap: “Harm” is general. The old graph is specific: a mouth in a house.

senses: to have room for, to tolerate
容.shuowenEn: To contain, as a vessel does. From 宀 (roof) and 谷 (valley).
容.story: A roof over a valley: a sheltered hollow. From “to hold” come both “capacity” and “the face”, which holds and shows what is within. The Laozi uses the word at three key places in a row: a forced likeness of the old masters (15); the room for all that comes from knowledge of the constant (16); and the look of great De, which is only to follow the Way (21).
容.gap: English has “contain”, “tolerate”, and “countenance” as three words. The last still keeps a trace of the link.

senses: to lodge, to stay for a time
to leave in someone’s keeping, to entrust
寄.shuowenEn: To entrust. From 宀 (roof), with 奇 for the sound.
寄.story: To be under another’s roof for a while: a traveller lodges, and a thing is left in keeping. The Shuowen defines 寄 by 託 and 託 by 寄. Poets later used the word for life itself: a person 寄 in the world like a guest. The Laozi uses it once: to the one who honors the body as all under heaven, all under heaven can be 寄 (13). The realm is a thing lodged. It is not a thing possessed.
寄.gap: English says a ruler “holds” or “takes” power. 寄 gives the ruler a guest’s position, or that of a keeper of another’s goods.

富.shuowen: 備也。一曰厚也。从宀畐聲。
富.shuowenEn: Complete, provided for. Another sense: thick, ample. From 宀 (roof), with 畐 for the sound.

parts.m: sound part; commonly explained as a full wine jar

富.story: A roof with fullness under it. The Shuowen’s first gloss is not “much money”. It is “complete”: a house that lacks nothing. With 貴, high rank, it makes 富貴, the standard pair for worldly success. The Laozi redefines the word. Rich and high and proud: ruin (9). The one who knows what is enough is 富 (33). “I have no affairs, and the people 富 of themselves” (57).
富.gap: “Rich” in English measures against others. 富 measures against need: provided for. Passage 33 uses that sense against the common one.

寒.shuowen: 凍也。从人在宀下，以茻薦覆之，下有仌。
寒.shuowenEn: To freeze. A person under a roof, with grass laid as bedding and cover; below there is ice.

parts.m: ice: the two dots at the base

寒.story: The Shuowen reads the graph as a scene: someone in a house, packed in straw, with ice below. From the cold of that house came the sense “poor”: a 寒士 is a scholar without means. The Laozi uses the word once: 躁勝寒, movement overcomes cold (45). 寒 and 熱, cold and heat, are also a basic pair of Chinese medicine.
寒.gap: English “cold” is a temperature. 寒 is the cold that a person suffers; the graph has a person in it.

察.shuowenEn: To go over a thing. From 宀 (roof) and 祭 (sacrifice).
察.story: A close check under the temple roof. For most schools 察 is a virtue of rulers and judges. The Laozi uses it only doubled and only as a warning: the common people are 察察 (20), and where the rule is 察察 the people are chipped (58).
察.gap: “Scrutiny” is neutral in English. Here it is what a watched person feels.

senses: 寡人: “the lonely one”, a ruler’s word for himself
寡.shuowen: 少也。从宀从頒。頒，分賦也，故爲少。
寡.shuowenEn: Few. From 宀 (roof) and 頒. 頒 is to share out, and so there is little.
寡.story: Few, and so alone. Kings called themselves 寡人, and the Laozi notes it twice: lords and kings name themselves “orphaned, lonely, without grain” (39, 42). As a verb it is “to reduce”: 寡欲, fewer wants (19); 小國寡民, a small state with few people (80).
寡.gap: 寡欲 is often turned into “desireless”. It says “few”.

實.shuowen: 富也。从宀从貫。貫，貨貝也。
實.shuowenEn: Wealth. From a roof and 貫; 貫 is strings of cowrie money.
實.story: A house with strings of cowries in it: full. In plants it is the fruit that follows the flower. The Laozi uses it for the belly that the sage fills, 實其腹 (3), and for the fruit in which the full-grown person stays (38). Chinese thought later set 實, the actual, against 名, the name: does the title fit the fact?
實.gap: “Substance” and “reality” are abstract. 實 is something that you can bite.

senses: at rest, peaceful, safe; to bring peace to
寧.shuowenEn: A word of wishing (“would rather”). From 丂, with 寍 for the sound. (For the sense “peace” the Shuowen has the older graph 寍: a roof, with a heart above a bowl.)

parts.m: here from 丂, breath that comes out: the particle

寧.story: Two words in one graph. The peace word is a roof, a heart, and a bowl: the Shuowen says that food vessels are that by which people are at peace. The particle “would rather” added a sign for breath. In passage 39 earth got the One and so is 寧, and heaven is 清; the pair gave names to palaces in Beijing. The short form is 宁.
寧.gap: “Tranquil” is a mood. 寧 is security: the ground does not move and there is food in the house.

senses: a favorite: a minister, a consort; later, a pet
寵.shuowenEn: To dwell in honor. From 宀 (roof), with 龍 for the sound.
寵.story: A dragon under a roof. The word is used only downward: a lord’s regard for someone below. The Han Feizi’s story of Mi Zixia and the peach shows its nature: the same act is charming under favor and criminal after it. The Laozi uses the word in one passage only, and gives it no good sense: 寵 makes one the lower; to get it is a fright and to lose it is a fright (13). In modern Chinese a pet animal is a 寵物, “favor-thing”.
寵.gap: “Favor” and “honor” can sound like things a person has. 寵 stays in the giver’s hands. To have it is to be held.

senses: (of a ruler) the throne, the seal
寶.shuowen: 珍也。从宀从王从貝，缶聲。
寶.shuowenEn: Precious things. From 宀 (roof), 王 (jade), and 貝 (shell), with 缶 (jar) for the sound.

parts.m: an earthenware jar; gives the sound

寶.story: Jade, shells, and a jar under one roof. The Laozi uses the word to move value away from such things. The Dao is the good person’s 寶 (62). The speaker has three 寶 and keeps them: care, plain living, and not daring to be first (67). And there is no greater disaster than to take an enemy lightly, which nearly loses “my 寶” (69).
寶.gap: “Treasure” is close. What English loses is the inventory inside the character: ritual jade, money, and wine.

senses: a wine vessel of the rites

parts.m: a wine jar with vapour or a cover above

尊.story: First a bronze jar for sacrificial wine; the Shuowen lists it in an older form with two hands that raise the jar. To honour is to lift the wine to someone. In the Laozi all creatures 尊 the Way (51), and fine words can buy 尊 (62). The vessel sense later got its own graphs, 樽 and 罇.
尊.gap: “Honour” in English is abstract. 尊 is a gesture: both hands, a full jar, raised.

尤.story: In classical texts 尤 is a fault and the blame or grudge that follows it. The Analects speaks of a man whose words give few occasions for 尤. The Laozi uses it once, as the last word of the water passage: only by not contending is there no 尤 (8). The phrase is near to the “no blame” of the Book of Changes. In later Chinese the common sense is “especially”: what stands out, for good or ill.
尤.gap: English separates the fault (mine) from the blame (yours). 尤 is the whole event: a wrong and the resentment that it draws.

senses: to occupy a position, to claim
居.story: The Shuowen gives the body sense: to get down on the heels and stay. From there the word came to mean to live in a place and to hold a position. The Laozi uses it for both a posture and a claim. When the work is done the sage does not 居 it, and so it does not leave (2). Water is good at 居 on low ground (8). The person of Dao does not 居 where the crowd wants to be (24, 31). To 居 is to settle your weight on a thing. The book asks again and again where a person settles.
居.gap: “Dwell” or “claim” each gives half. 居 is one act of the body: to sit down in a place, or in an achievement.

senses: to run out, to be exhausted (passage 5)
屈.shuowenEn: To be without a tail. From 尾 (tail), with 出 for the sound.

parts.m: what is left of 尾, tail

屈.story: The Shuowen’s first sense is “tailless, cut short”; from it come “curled up, bent”, and then “made to give way”. In passage 5 the bellows is 虛而不屈, empty and not exhausted. In passage 45 great straightness is like 屈. The name of the poet Qu Yuan, the upright minister who was slandered and drowned himself, is written with it.
屈.gap: “Bent” is a shape. 屈 is also what happens to a person who is forced to yield or to bear a wrong.

屬.def: class, category, type; to belong to
senses: to belong to; a kind, a class
zhǔ: to attach; to entrust, to enjoin
屬.shuowenEn: To connect. From 尾 (tail), with 蜀 for the sound.
屬.story: What follows on behind and is joined, as a tail to a body. In passage 19 the bare bans are given “something to belong to”: plain silk and uncarved wood.
屬.gap: English must choose “belong”, “attach”, or “entrust”. The picture is a thing that hangs on to another.

senses: the left hand; the left side
to help, to assist (later written 佐)
the east side (facing south); the side of honour in peace
左.shuowenEn: Hands that help each other. From 𠂇 (the left hand) and 工 (a tool).
左.story: 左 is a left hand with a tool: the hand that steadies the work. Its first meaning was “to assist”, which later took the form 佐. As a side, left ranked above right in Zhou ceremony. Laozi 31 uses the fact: the gentleman honours the left at home and the right in war, since the right is the side of death. In passage 79 the sage “holds the left tally”, and does not press a claim; which party held the left half is disputed, and silk A is reported to say “right”.
左.gap: In English the left is “sinister” and the right is “right”. In Zhou ritual it is the other way: left is life and honour.

巧.shuowenEn: Technique. From 工 (work; a carpenter’s square), with 丂 for the sound.
巧.story: The craftsman’s gift, and the cunning that grows from it. Passage 19 says to cut it off; passage 45 says 大巧若拙, “great skill seems clumsy”; passage 57 says that the more skills people have, the more strange things appear.
巧.gap: “Skill” is praise in English. 巧 has a shadow: too clever by half.

差.def: to differ; different, wrong; nearly, almost; an officer

己.def: self, oneself; personal, private; 6th heavenly stem

senses: to buy, to sell, to trade
市.story: The market-place, and the acts done in it. Passage 62 says that fine words can 市: they can be traded, or can buy honour, according to where the sentence is cut. The same book ends by saying that words which can be trusted are not fine (81).
市.gap: English keeps “market” and “to sell” apart. 市 is the place and the deal in one word.

senses: sparse, thin, far apart (later written 稀)
希.story: The Shuowen has no entry for 希 itself; it has 稀, with the grain sign, defined as “thinly spaced”. In the Laozi, 希 is the word for sound at its thinnest. What the ear cannot hear is named 希 (14); sparse speech is natural (23); the great note has sparse sound (41); few in the world attain the teaching without words (43). The modern sense “to hope” (希望) is later.
希.gap: “Inaudible” says the sound is absent. 希 says it is thin: the notes are far apart, and most of what is there is the interval.

senses: Di, the high god of the Shang
Lord on High (上帝); a deified royal ancestor
帝.story: In the Shang oracle-bone inscriptions, Di is the highest power: Di sends rain or holds it back, and approves or ruins the king’s plans. Dead Shang kings also received the title. The Zhou identified Di with their Heaven, 天, and the two words stand side by side in the early classics. The early shape of the graph is disputed, and we give no picture for it. In 221 BCE the king of Qin joined it to 皇 and made 皇帝, “emperor”, which is why the Shuowen, written under the Han, defines the word as a ruler’s title. The Laozi names Di once, to say that Dao seems to come before it (4).
帝.gap: “God” makes Di the creator of the Bible, which Di was not; Legge chose it for reasons of mission. “Emperor” is too late and too human. Di is a high ancestor-god of a royal house, and nearer to a first ancestor than to a creator.

師.def: teacher, master, specialist; multitude, troops; hexagram ䷆
senses: a host, an army; a division of 2,500 men
a master, a teacher; a model
師.shuowen: 二千五百人爲師。从帀从𠂤。𠂤，四帀，眾意也。
師.shuowenEn: Two thousand five hundred men make a 師. From 帀 (all round) and 𠂤. 𠂤 with “round on four sides” gives the idea of a multitude.

parts.m: a mound; in early writing, an army in the field

師.story: 師 is a crowd before it is a person: the Shuowen defines it as an army unit. The one who commands and trains a host is its master, and from there the word came to mean the master of any skill, and a teacher. The Laozi uses both ends of the word within four passages. In passage 27 the good person is the 師 of the not-good. In passage 30, where a 師 has camped, thorns and brambles grow.
師.gap: “Teacher” in English has no army behind it. 師 keeps a memory of command, which is why the Laozi’s teacher, who owes care to the pupil, is a quiet correction.

senses: a constant: a law or norm
常.shuowenEn: A lower garment, a skirt. From 巾 (cloth), with 尚 for the sound.

parts.m: gives the sound; by itself: still, to esteem

常.story: The Shuowen files 常 as an item of dress, the same word as 裳, the skirt of formal robes. The sense “constant” is a second, borrowed use of the graph that became the main one. In the Laozi the word is everywhere: the constant Way, constant virtue-power, and “to know the constant is called clear sight” (16, 55). But in the oldest manuscripts most of these places read 恆. Han scribes replaced 恆 with 常 to avoid the personal name of Emperor Wen, Liu Heng (劉恆, ruled 180–157 BCE). The word also means plain and ordinary, as in the modern 平常. The Laozi’s constant is not far from its ordinary: that which lasts is that which keeps coming back.
常.gap: “Eternal”, “unchanging”, and “absolute” bring in a timeless realm above this world. 常 is constancy inside time: the regular return of seasons, the habit of water. It can be an adjective, an adverb (“always”), or a noun, and passage 1 uses it in more than one way.

幹.def: trunk of tree or of human body

幾.def: how many? how much?; a few, some
senses: jī: minute; the first faint sign of a thing
jī: on the edge of danger
幾.shuowen: 微也。殆也。从𢆶从戍。戍，兵守也。𢆶而兵守者，危也。
幾.shuowenEn: Minute. Perilous. From 𢆶 (fine threads) and 戍 (to guard); 戍 is a guard with weapons. Fine, and guarded with weapons: that is danger.
幾.story: The Shuowen reads the graph as tiny threads and an armed guard: something very small that still needs watching. The word names the first faint stirring of an event, the point where a change can still be seen and turned; the Book of Changes says that the noble person acts on seeing the 幾. From “the edge of” comes “almost”. In the Laozi: water is 幾 to Dao, at its very edge (8); people at their work often fail when they are 幾 at completion (64); how far apart are yes and a sneer, 相去幾何? (20).
幾.gap: “Almost” in English is a shortfall. 幾 is a place: the fine edge where one thing is about to become another.

senses: the edge of a hall’s platform; a corner, an angle
廉.shuowenEn: A side, an edge. From 广 (a building), with 兼 for the sound.

parts.m: a building open at the front
to hold two together; gives the sound

廉.story: First the sharp border of the platform under a hall; then a person with such an edge, who takes nothing over the line. 廉 became the standard praise for an honest official. Passage 58 gives the craftsman’s warning: 廉而不劌, have the edge and do not wound with it. The same four characters are said of jade in the Record of Rites.
廉.gap: “Incorruptible” is only moral. 廉 keeps the picture of a corner that is exact and can hurt.

廓.def: broad, wide, open, empty; to expand

senses: to fall out of use; to abandon; to abolish
廢.shuowenEn: A house that collapses. From 广 (a building), with 發 for the sound.

parts.m: sound; alone: to shoot, to send out

廢.story: A building that falls in for lack of care. In passage 18 it is what happens to the great Dao; in passage 36 it is paired with 興: “to make a thing fall, first raise it up”.
廢.gap: “Abandoned” needs someone who abandons. 廢 can happen with nobody to blame.

senses: to found, to establish (a state, a house, a rule)
建.shuowenEn: To establish the statutes of the court. From 聿 (a hand with a brush) and 廴 (to go a long way).

parts.m: a hand that holds a brush

建.story: 建 is the verb for founding: 建國, to found a state; 封建, to grant land and set up a lord. The Shuowen sees a writing brush in it and defines it from the court, as the setting up of statutes. In passage 54 it is paired with 拔, “to pull out”, the verb of the war records for a town that falls. Passage 41 has the phrase 建德, “de that is set up firm”, and quotes a lost book called 建言, “Established Sayings”.
建.gap: Translations say “planted”, which gives a garden. The Chinese word belongs to building and to politics.

senses: a pattern, a standard, a model
a rule, a form; a ceremony
式.shuowenEn: A standard. From 工 (the carpenter’s square), with 弋 for the sound.
式.story: The pattern piece from which others are cut. The sage holds the One and is the 式 of the world (22); know the white, keep the black, and be the 式 of the world (28); to know the two models of rule is a standing 式 (65). The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 牧, herdsman, in passage 22.
式.gap: “Model” in English suggests a person to imitate. 式 is nearer to a gauge: it does nothing, and things are checked against it.

senses: a measure of length (in archery and land survey)
弓.shuowen: 以近窮遠。象形。古者揮作弓。
弓.shuowenEn: From near at hand, to reach the far. A picture. In antiquity Hui made the bow.
弓.story: A picture of the bow stave. The war bow of the age was a composite of wood, horn, and sinew that curved forward when unstrung. Many words of tension are written with it: 張 (to string), 引 (to draw), 弛 (to unstring), 弦 (the string), 彊 (strong), and 弱 (weak). In the Laozi the bow appears once, as the image of heaven’s way (77).
弓.gap: For an English reader the bow is sport or legend. For the first readers it was the main weapon of war and the measure of a gentleman’s training.

senses: young (弱冠, the age of twenty)
弱.story: The Shuowen defines weakness as a bend and sees fine hairs in the graph; many modern scholars see two weak bows. The Laozi does not soften the word. “Weakness is the use of the Dao” (40). The sage weakens the ambitions of the people and strengthens their bones (3). The weak overcomes the strong, and everyone knows it, and no one can practice it (78).
弱.gap: Translators write “yielding” or “receptive” to spare the reader. The Chinese word is the plain opposite of strong, and the book praises it on purpose.

parts.m: now the graph for a bow; for the Shuowen, a bent shape
two short strokes; for the Shuowen, fine hair

張.def: stretch, extend, expand; sheet; 26th lunar mansion, determinative star υ¹ Hydrae
senses: to string a bow; to draw it
to stretch, to spread, to open out
to display, to make much of
張.shuowenEn: To put the string on a bow. From 弓 (bow), with 長 for the sound.
張.story: The bow at the left gives the first sense: to load a bow with tension. In passage 36 it is the full stretch that comes before the drawing-in. In passage 77 heaven’s way is like the stringing of a bow: the high part is pressed down and the low part is lifted. The word later became the counter for flat, spread things, a sheet of paper, a table, and one of the most common family names.
張.gap: “Expand” has no bow in it. A strung bow is a thing that waits to be released.

senses: to force; forced, against the grain (qiǎng)
強.shuowenEn: A weevil. From 虫 (insect); 弘 gives the sound.

parts.m: a bow (in the sound part 弘)

強.story: The Shuowen lists 強 as the name of an insect and gives “strong” its own graph, 彊, “the bow has power”. Scribes borrowed the insect for the bow, and 強 became the normal way to write strength. In the Laozi the word is mostly a warning: the stiff and strong are companions of death (76), a thing forced to its prime grows old (30, 55). Read qiǎng, it is the adverb “by force”: the speaker is forced to describe the old masters (15) and forced to name the Dao “great” (25).
強.gap: English “strong” is nearly always praise. 強 in this book is closer to “rigid” or “forcing”, and is usually a sign of something about to break.

senses: full, to fill, to extend over
more and more; 彌 A 彌 B: the more A, the more B
彌.story: 彌 has a bow at its left, and its early sense is commonly given as a bow drawn to the full, and so “full, complete, all over”. As an adverb it means “increasingly”. The paired use is a favourite of early prose. Yan Hui says of his master’s teaching: 仰之彌高，鑽之彌堅, “the more I look up at it, the higher it is; the more I bore into it, the harder” (Analects 9.11). The Laozi uses the pair in passages 47 and 57.
彌.gap: English needs the frame “the more … the more”. Chinese does it with one repeated word.

役.def: service; a servant, laborer; to serve

senses: to go toward, to set out for
往.story: The plain verb for motion away from the speaker and toward a goal; its partner is 來, to come. With 來 it also makes the pair past and future. In passage 35 all under heaven 往 to the one who holds the great image. In passage 80 the people of the small state grow old and die and do not 往來, go and come, to the next village. Both are pictures of a world at peace, and they point in opposite directions.
往.gap: English versions often write “comes” for 天下往 and so stand beside the ruler. The Chinese verb stands on the road with the people.

senses: to put behind; to come after
後.story: The parts are commonly explained as a foot held back by a cord on a road: one who lags. The word covers the rear in space, the later in time, and those who come after, one’s descendants. In the Laozi it is the chosen place. Before and after follow each other (2). The sage puts the body behind (7). Meet Dao and you do not see its head; follow it and you do not see its 後, its back (14). To give up the rear and take the front is death (67).
後.gap: “Last” in English is a defeat. 後 is only the place behind, and in this book it is the safer and the stronger one.

徐.shuowenEn: To walk at ease. From 彳 (a step), with 余 for the sound.
徐.story: Slowness measured by the legs. In passage 15 it is the pace at which mud settles and at which life starts again: 徐清, 徐生. Wang Bi glosses it “careful and attentive”.
徐.gap: “Gradually” is about a rate. 徐 is about a way of moving.

senses: a shortcut; a private or crooked way
徑.shuowenEn: A path for walking. From 彳 (step, road), with 巠 for the sound.
徑.story: A track too narrow for a cart, which cuts across the fields and saves time. It became a figure for the clever private way: an honest man “does not go by the 徑” (Analects 6.14). In passage 53 the great road is level and people love the 徑. Modern 捷徑, “shortcut”, keeps the sense.
徑.gap: “By-way” or “side path” sounds like a pleasant detour. The point of 徑 is that it is quicker.

senses: a kind, a class of people
徒.story: The Shuowen lists the word under an older graph and defines it as “to go on foot”. Those on foot behind the chariots were the infantry and the retinue; so 徒 came to mean followers and then a kind of people. The Laozi speaks of the 徒 of life and the 徒 of death (50, 76): two companies, and each person walks in one.
徒.gap: “Follower” or “disciple” suggests a choice of teacher. 徒 is simply the crowd on foot behind something.

senses: to fit, to be at ease with
得.shuowenEn: To walk and come upon something. From 彳 (a step), with 㝵 for the sound.

parts.m: a hand on a cowrie: to get

得.story: A hand closes on a shell, on the road. The word sounds like 德, inner power, and early writers defined the one by the other: 德 is what one has got. The Laozi plays on the pair in passage 23. It warns against 難得之貨, goods hard to get (3, 12, 64), and says: few, then gain (22).
得.gap: English keeps “get” and “virtue” far apart. In Chinese they are near-homophones, and thinkers used the echo.

senses: to obey, to go along with
從.shuowenEn: To walk after. From 辵 (walking) and 从 (two persons, one behind the other); 从 is also the sound.
從.story: Two people in file on a road. Great De follows only the Way (21); one who 從事, “follows the work” of the Way, becomes one with the Way (23).
從.gap: “Obey” has a command in it. 從 only says who walks in front.

senses: to guide, to steer; to ride (the wind)
御.shuowenEn: To make the horses go. From 彳 (a step, a road) and 卸 (to unharness).

parts.m: a step; half of the crossroads 行
to leave the car and loose the horses

御.story: Driving was one of the six arts of a Zhou gentleman, with rites, music, archery, writing, and reckoning. The driver stands behind two or four horses and holds all the reins; he feels each mouth and cannot use force. Because the king’s driver stood beside the king, 御 later meant “to attend the ruler” and then “imperial”. The word is also written 馭, a horse and a hand. In passage 14 the object is 今之有, what there is now.
御.gap: “Control” and “manage” make an office of it. A driver does not control horses; he keeps contact with them. The word is about feel, timing, and a light hand.

senses: to go and come back; to return
復.shuowenEn: To go and to come. From 彳 (a step), with 复 for the sound.

parts.m: sound and sense: to go back over

復.story: To come back along the road. As a hexagram it is the first light after the winter solstice. In the Laozi it is the direction of all things: it returns to no-thing (14); I watch the return, and each returns to its root (16); return to the infant, to the limitless, to the uncarved wood (28); “turning back is the movement of the Way”, with the near-synonym 反 (40).
復.gap: “Return” in English can sound like retreat or repetition. 復 is the second half of every going-out.

微.shuowenEn: To go in concealment. From 彳 (a step), with 𢼸 for the sound.
微.story: The first sense is movement that no one notices: to travel in disguise. From it come “hidden” and “minute”. The Laozi uses the word for the grain of things below the level of the senses. Wang Bi explains 妙 in passage 1 as “the far limit of 微”. In passage 14 it names that which the hand cannot get; passage 15 opens its portrait of the old masters with it; passage 36 has 微明, “the fine light”; and passage 64 says a thing is easy to scatter while it is still 微.
微.gap: “Subtle” is close, but in English it praises a mind. 微 describes the thing: small, and on the move, and not seen.

senses: de: the power proper to a thing or person
the quality of a ruler that draws people with no force
favor, kindness received; to be grateful
德.shuowenEn: To rise. From 彳 (a step), with 㥁 for the sound.

parts.m: right part: commonly explained as a straight eye over a heart

德.story: The second word of the book’s title. In Zhou bronze inscriptions it is the quality that a king receives from Heaven and the ancestors and by which he holds the realm; Confucians made it moral virtue. Early writers explain it by a near-homophone: 德 is 得, what one has got. In the Laozi it is what each thing has from Dao: its own power to be what it is. The highest 德 does not act as 德, and so has it (38). Dao gives life, and 德 rears (51). To give life and not own is the dark 德 (10, 51). One who holds 德 in fullness is like an infant (55).
德.gap: “Virtue” now means moral goodness, and “power” suggests force. 德 is the working strength of a thing’s own nature, which acts on others with no push.

senses: to go right through, to penetrate
the land tax of the Zhou, about one part in ten
徹.shuowenEn: To pass through. From 彳 (a step), 攴 (a hand with a stick), and 育.

parts.m: a step, movement on a road
the middle part in the modern form
a hand with a stick: to act on

徹.story: Mencius gives 徹 as the name of the Zhou tax on a hundred mu of land. In passage 79 the one without 德 “keeps the 徹”: on the usual reading, runs the tithe and takes a fixed share. Wang Bi reads the word as watching for people’s faults; others read it as 轍, wheel-tracks.
徹.gap: No English word joins “thorough” and “tithe”. The link is the idea of taking a clean cut through the whole.

senses: edge, outer limit; the end to which a thing returns (Wang Bi)
徼.shuowenEn: To go along, to patrol. From 彳 (a step), with 敫 for the sound.

parts.m: a step; movement on a road

徼.story: 徼 is a word from border service: the rounds that guards walk, and so the frontier line itself. Han texts speak of 徼外, “beyond the frontier”. In the Laozi it occurs once, in passage 1, as that which the wanting mind sees. Wang Bi explains it as 歸終, the return and the end: the place where a thing arrives when it is complete. Other readers have proposed that the graph stands for 皦, “bright”, or 竅, “opening”, and the Mawangdui silk texts read 其所噭, also disputed. The patrol sense is the oldest attested gloss, and it fits the passage: names and desires walk the borders of things.
徼.gap: No single English word covers border, outcome, and outline together. “Manifestations”, a common choice, has no basis in the old glosses.

心.def: heart; mind, intelligence; soul; 5th lunar mansion, determinative star α Scorpii (Antares)
senses: the seat of thought and feeling; mind
心.story: A picture of the heart. Early Chinese thought gave thinking, feeling, and wanting to this one organ: Mencius says that its office is to think. So there is no “head against heart” in these texts. In the Laozi the 心 is a thing to quiet and to empty: empty the heart (3); the heart is good when it is deep like a pool (8); the hunt makes the heart go wild (12); the sage has no fixed 心 and takes the people’s 心 as the sage’s own (49).
心.gap: “Mind” cuts off feeling and the body. “Heart” cuts off thought. Translators write “heart-mind”, which is exact and is not English.
心.shuowen: 人心，土藏，在身之中。象形。
心.shuowenEn: The human heart, the organ of earth, in the middle of the body. A picture.

忒.def: excessive; too; very-usually of objectionable things; to err; to mistake; changeable

志.shuowenEn: Intention. From 心 (heart), with 之 for the sound.

parts.m: top part as now written; the Shuowen takes it as 之, to go

志.story: A heart with a direction. For Confucius 志 is where a life starts: at fifteen he set his 志 on learning. The Warring States praised the man of 志. The Laozi is cool toward it. The sage weakens the 志 (3). To act with force is to have 志 (33). The one who wants to rule the world by killing cannot get his 志 in the world (31). Wang Bi’s reason: the will breeds affairs, and affairs breed disorder.
志.gap: “Will” in the West is a faculty and a virtue: willpower, free will. 志 is simpler: where the heart is headed. To weaken it is to loosen an aim. It is not to break a person.

senses: loyal; to do one’s utmost for another
忠.shuowenEn: Reverent care. From 心 (heart), with 中 (centre) for the sound.
忠.story: A heart at its centre. In early use it is whole-heartedness toward anyone; the empire narrowed it to loyalty to the ruler. The Laozi has it twice: loyal ministers appear when the state is dark (18), and ritual is “the thin edge of 忠 and trust” (38).
忠.gap: “Loyalty” is owed to someone. 忠 is first a state of the heart: undivided.

senses: to be angry; to rouse to fury
vigorous, bursting (of growth, of a wave)
怒.shuowenEn: To be angry. From 心 (heart), with 奴 for the sound.
怒.story: A heart under the graph for a slave. The Shuowen says that 奴 is here for the sound, but readers have long taken the picture as a comment: in anger the heart is not free. Early writers also use 怒 for any bursting energy, such as a bird that rises or a plant that shoots up. The strategists treated anger as a danger in a commander and a weakness to use in an enemy. The Laozi has the word once: 善戰者不怒, one good at fighting is not angry (68).
怒.gap: English “anger” can be righteous, and modern culture often praises it as energy. In the military texts 怒 is simply a loss of command over oneself.

怨.shuowenEn: Anger, rancour. From 心 (heart), with 夗 for the sound.

parts.m: to turn in sleep; gives the sound

怨.story: The bitterness of one who has been wronged. In early China it was a public fact: grievances between houses called for repayment. The Laozi says to answer 怨 with 德 (63), a saying that Confucius is on record as refusing, and adds that when a great 怨 is settled, some of it is sure to remain (79).
怨.gap: “Injury” names the act and “hatred” is too hot. 怨 is the cold residue that stays in the wronged party.

恃.def: rely on, presume on, trust to
senses: to lean on, to rely on
恃.shuowenEn: To depend on. From 心 (heart), with 寺 for the sound.

parts.m: sound part; a court office, later a temple

恃.story: To 恃 is to put your weight on a thing: walls, allies, a ruler’s favor, your own past success. Military writers warn against it: do not 恃 that the enemy will not come. The Laozi uses the word in one fixed phrase, 為而不恃, “to act and not lean on it”. The phrase stands in passages 2, 10, 51, and 77. Passage 34 turns it round: the ten thousand things lean on Dao for life, and Dao does not refuse them.
恃.gap: Translations often make this a word about hope for a return. Hope looks ahead. 恃 looks back and down: it is weight placed on a thing you have or did.

恢.shuowenEn: Great. From 心 (heart), with 灰 (ash) for the sound.
恢.story: The heart at the left suggests that the word first described a large mind. Doubled, 恢恢 gives the feel of roominess: the Zhuangzi uses it for the space in an ox’s joints where the cook’s blade can play. In passage 73 it describes heaven’s net.
恢.gap: “Vast” is only size. 恢恢 is room to move in.

息.def: rest, put stop to, end, cease

悠.shuowenEn: Care, sorrow. From 心 (heart), with 攸 for the sound.

parts.m: sound part; alone: to flow on

悠.story: In the old songs 悠悠 is the far sky and the long road, and the long thoughts of one who looks at them. In the received text of passage 17 it describes the best ruler: far off, unhurried. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 猶, “watchful”.
悠.gap: “Remote” is cold. 悠 has distance and ease, and a little sadness.

患.shuowen: 憂也。从心上貫吅，吅亦聲。
患.shuowenEn: Worry. From 心 (heart), with 吅 strung through above it; 吅 also gives the sound.

parts.m: two things strung on one line

患.story: A heart with something run through it. One word serves for the outer disaster and for the inner distress. Confucius uses it often for what should and should not worry a person: do not 患 that others do not know you. The Laozi uses it in one passage: great 患 comes from having a body, and with no body, what 患 would there be? (13). A modern patient is a 患者, “one who has a 患”.
患.gap: English divides the event (“disaster”) from the feeling (“worry”). 患 does not, and the passage depends on that: the trouble and the one who can be troubled arrive together.

悶.shuowenEn: Stifled, pent up. From 心 (heart), with 門 (gate) for the sound.
悶.story: A heart behind a gate. The Laozi takes this unflattering word as a badge. In passage 20 the speaker says: the common people are sharp-eyed, I alone am 悶悶. In passage 58 the same doubled word describes the best government, under which the people are whole.
悶.gap: English has no praise-word for dullness. “Unobtrusive” is too polite; 悶悶 really does mean dull.

senses: è: ugly, foul, bad in quality
wù: to hate, to find repulsive
惡.shuowenEn: A fault, a going too far. From 心 (heart), with 亞 for the sound.
惡.story: One graph holds a quality and a feeling. Read è, it is the opposite of 美: the ugly and the bad. Read wù, it is what the heart does to such things: to hate. The Laozi uses both. The ugly appears when beauty is known (2). Water stays in the place that the crowd hates, 眾人之所惡 (8). Weapons are things that people hate (31). Passage 20 asks how far apart 善 and 惡 really are. The character has a heart in it: the bad is first what a heart turns from.
惡.gap: “Evil” is too heavy. It brings sin and a cosmic enemy. 惡 is the foul, the coarse, the disliked. The Chinese also does not divide “bad” from “hated”, as English does.

senses: to heal, to recover (also written 癒)
愈.story: A word of increase. It comes in two places in the Laozi, and they answer each other. The space between heaven and earth is like a bellows: the more it moves, the more comes out (5). The sage, having already worked for others, has more and more (81).
愈.gap: English needs a paired form, “the more… the more”. 愈 stands alone and can mark an increase with no stated cause.

愚.shuowen: 戇也。从心从禺。禺，猴屬，獸之愚者。
愚.shuowenEn: Simple, thick. From 心 (heart) and 禺. 禺 is of the monkey kind, the simple one among beasts.
愚.story: A monkey’s heart: it does not calculate. The speaker of passage 20 claims it: “mine is the heart of a fool”. Passage 38 calls foreknowledge “the flower of the Way and the beginning of 愚”. Passage 65 says the rulers of old did not make the people sharp but kept them 愚, a line that later autocrats used for their own ends.
愚.gap: “Stupid” is an insult about ability. 愚 in passage 20 is a mind that has stopped sorting things into better and worse.

senses: to be sparing with, to grudge
to care for (愛民, 愛其身)
愛.shuowenEn: The look of walking. From 夊 (slow steps), with 㤅 for the sound.

parts.m: a foot that drags, at the base

愛.story: The Shuowen gives the love-word a different graph, 㤅, glossed 惠也, “kindness”, and defines 愛 itself as a way of walking. Usage joined the two long ago. In early texts 愛 often means to begrudge: the king in Mencius 1A7 is thought 愛, stingy, over an ox. The Laozi uses the word with care: 愛民 (10), 自愛不自貴 (72), and the warning of passage 44 that extreme 愛 costs dear.
愛.gap: English “love” has no shadow of “hoard”. 愛 has: to hold dear and to hold back are one verb.

慈.shuowenEn: To love, to cherish. From 心 (heart), with 兹 for the sound.
慈.story: Care that goes down, from the older to the younger. Paired with 孝 in passages 18 and 19. In passage 67 it stands alone as the first of three things to treasure: “with 慈, one can be brave”, and heaven guards with 慈 those whom it would save. Buddhism later used it for the kindness of a bodhisattva (慈悲).
慈.gap: “Compassion” in English suffers with another. 慈 is the strong tenderness of a mother toward a child.

慜.def: name of a monk in Tang dynasty

慝.def: do evil in secret; evil, vice

senses: the bosom; the fold of the robe at the chest
to hold in the bosom, to carry against the body
to cherish; to long for, to think of
懷.shuowenEn: To think of with longing. From 心 (heart), with 褱 for the sound.

parts.m: to hold against the body: a robe (衣) around a weeping eye; also the sound

懷.story: The right side is a robe opened around an eye with drops beneath it, commonly explained as tears held inside the clothes; the heart was added at the left. The first, physical sense is the pouch that a belted robe forms at the chest, where people carried what they valued. From it come cherishing, longing, and pregnancy. The Laozi uses the word once, in the last line of passage 70: the sage wears coarse cloth and 懷玉, holds jade in the bosom. Wang Bi reads it as treasuring what is genuine.
懷.gap: “Cherish” is all feeling and “carry” is all body. 懷 is both at once: a thing kept warm against the chest, where no one else can see it.

senses: to be afraid, to take fright
懼.shuowenEn: To fear. From 心 (heart), with 瞿 for the sound.

parts.m: sound; by itself, the stare of a hawk: two eyes 䀠 over a bird 隹

懼.story: 懼 is fright: the start of a creature that sees danger. The same graph serves for “to be afraid” and “to make afraid”. In passage 74 a ruler wishes to 懼 the people with death, and the text answers that they no longer hold death in awe (畏).
懼.gap: English needs two verbs, “fear” and “frighten”. The Chinese has one, and the reader decides who does it to whom.

senses: the peoples of the western frontier

parts.m: explained as what is left of 甲, armour

戎.story: The Shuowen records the word under an older graph and explains it as dagger-axe with armour: the full kit of a fighter. The same word named the non-Zhou peoples of the west, whom the Zhou both fought and married. 戎馬 are war horses (46). The Zuo zhuan says that the great affairs of a state are sacrifice and 戎.
戎.gap: “Military” is an abstract adjective. 戎 is the weapon and the armour themselves.

我.def: our, us, i, me, my, we

戰.shuowenEn: To fight. From 戈 (dagger-axe), with 單 for the sound.
戰.story: 戰 gave its name to the age in which the Laozi took form: 戰國, the Warring States. The word means a pitched battle, and it is also used for the shaking of a body in fear or cold. The Laozi does not avoid it. Victory in battle is to be observed with the rites of mourning (31). Tenderness, in battle, wins (67). One good at battle is not angry (68). Those who are good at keeping alive, it is said, are not touched by weapons when they go among armies (50).
戰.gap: “War” in English is often abstract: a policy or a cause. 戰 is the day of battle itself, with the dagger-axe in the graph and trembling in the word.

senses: a household, a family as a unit of count
戶.shuowenEn: That which protects. Half a 門 (gate) is called 戶. A picture.
戶.story: 戶 is one leaf of a door on its post, half of the two-leaved gate 門. From the door came the family behind it: states of the Warring States period registered their people by 戶 for tax and service. In the Laozi the door is cut to make a room (11), and the one who does not go out of it knows the world (47). The Han Feizi reads the body’s openings as the 戶 and 牖 of the spirit.
戶.gap: English “door” is the thing that swings. 戶 is also the opening and the household, so “not going out of the door” is also “staying with one’s own house”.

senses: a place, a location; one’s proper place
所.shuowen: 伐木聲也。从斤戶聲。《詩》曰：“伐木所所。”
所.shuowenEn: The sound of wood being felled. From 斤 (axe); 戶 gives the sound. The Odes say: “They fell the trees, suo, suo.”
所.story: The Shuowen records 所 as the noise of an axe, and the graph was borrowed for the word “place” and for the particle “that which”. As a noun it is where a thing is or belongs. Laozi 33 says that one who does not lose 其所, the place that is one’s own, lasts. The text does not say what the place is; readers have taken it as one’s role, one’s measure, or the centre of the body.
所.gap: English “position” suggests rank among competitors. 所 is only where a thing belongs.

senses: plain, artless (as praise in the arts)
a humble word for one’s own work (拙作)
拙.shuowenEn: Not skilful. From 手 (hand), with 出 for the sound.

parts.m: to go out; gives the sound

拙.story: 拙 occurs once in the Laozi, in 大巧若拙 (45), and that one line changed the word. The Zhuangzi quotes it against the craftsman’s compass and square. Tao Yuanming made 守拙, “to keep to clumsiness”, the motto of his return to the farm. Calligraphers and painters came to rank the awkward, honest line above the clever one; Fu Shan’s rule was 寧拙毋巧, “better clumsy than clever”.
拙.gap: English “clumsy” is only a fault. After the Laozi, 拙 is also a virtue: the absence of display.

拱.def: fold hands on breast; bow, salute

senses: to hold in the hand, to grasp
持.shuowenEn: To grip. From 手 (hand), with 寺 for the sound.
持.story: To hold a thing in the hand and keep holding it. From the grip the word came to mean to maintain a state of affairs, and 持盈, “to hold what is full”, became a set phrase in later Chinese for the hard art of keeping success. The Laozi uses the word three times. Hold it and fill it: better to have stopped (9). A thing that is still quiet is simple to 持 (64). “I have three things that I 持 and keep safe” (67).
持.gap: “Hold” is neutral in English. 持 has effort in it: the hand stays closed.

按.def: put hand on, press down with hand

捨.def: discard, give up willingly; give alms

senses: to push forward, to promote, to acclaim
to infer, to extend (a line of thought)
推.shuowenEn: To push along, to push aside. From 手 (hand), with 隹 for the sound.
推.story: A hand that pushes. From the plain act came the sense “to put a person forward” for office or honour, and later “to reason from one thing to the next”. In the Laozi the word comes once, in passage 66: the world is glad to 推 the sage and does not tire. It is the people’s side of the king pun: a king is the one to whom all go, and the one whom all push to the front. Mencius describes Shun’s rise in this way: the lords, the litigants, and the singers went to him of themselves.
推.gap: “Elect” brings a procedure; “exalt” brings a throne. 推 is hands on a back: support that is physical and can stop at any time.

握.def: grasp, hold fast, take by hand

senses: to lessen, to reduce, to take away
hexagram 41 of the Book of Changes
損.shuowenEn: To reduce. From the hand, with 員 for the sound.
損.story: A hand takes something away. In most books this is a misfortune. In the Laozi it is the practice: for the Dao, lessen each day; lessen and lessen again, until there is no forcing (48). A thing may be lessened and so grow (42). Heaven’s way takes from what has too much; the human way takes from those who have too little (77).
損.gap: “Decrease” and “loss” are bad news in English. The Laozi uses 損 as a discipline, like pruning.

據.def: to occupy, take possession of; a base

攝.def: take in, absorb; act as deputy; administer, assist
senses: to draw in and hold; to gather up
to hold an office for another; to assist
攝.shuowenEn: To draw in and hold. From 手 (hand), with 聶 for the sound.

parts.m: three ears: to whisper; gives the sound

攝.story: 攝 is the gesture of gathering: the skirts of a robe, the reins, a post held in trust. 攝生, to hold life, appears in passage 50 and became a standing term for the care of health in later China, beside 養生, to nourish life. The Laozi’s sense is to keep life collected, as against feeding it thick.
攝.gap: English “preserve” or “manage” life sounds like storage or control. 攝 is a light, gathering hold.

senses: to come to the aid of, to relieve, to rescue
救.shuowenEn: To stop. From 攴 (a hand with a stick); 求 gives the sound.

parts.m: sound part; by itself: to seek
a hand with a stick: action

救.story: To 救 is to halt a disaster in progress: a fire, a famine, a siege. States sent armies to 救 their allies. In Laozi 27 the sage is “always good at 救-ing people”, and the proof is that no one is thrown away. Passage 52 uses the word in the negative: one who opens the gates and adds to affairs is “to the end of life not to be rescued”, and passage 67 says that heaven guards with care those whom it would 救.
救.gap: English “save” brings salvation of the soul. 救 is first aid: it stops a present harm in this world.

senses: to ruin, to spoil, to wreck
敗.shuowen: 毀也。从攴、貝。敗、賊皆从貝，會意。
敗.shuowenEn: To wreck. From 攴 (a hand with a stick) and 貝 (shell). 敗 and 賊 (robber) both have the shell; a joined-meaning graph.

parts.m: a cowrie shell: something of value
a hand with a stick: to strike

敗.story: A valued thing struck with a stick. The word covers a pot that is broken, food that has gone off, a plan that fails, and an army that is beaten. The Laozi uses it for what deliberate doing brings about: “who works on it ruins it” (29, 64), and people “always ruin their affairs when they are close to done” (64).
敗.gap: English separates “to spoil” from “to be defeated”. In 敗 the one who spoils the work and the one who loses are the same person.

senses: to cause, to let (jiào; also jiāo in verse)
教.shuowen: 上所施下所效也。从攴从孝。
教.shuowenEn: What those above give out and those below copy. From 攴 (a hand with a rod) and 孝.

parts.m: left part as now written; early forms are commonly explained as 爻 over 子, a child
a hand that holds a rod

教.story: The character has a child and a hand with a rod. It has no mouth and no word in it. The Shuowen’s definition also leaves speech out: teaching is what the high give out and the low copy. The rod-hand, 攴, stands in 牧 (to herd), 政 (to govern), and 攻 (to attack). The Laozi asks for 不言之教, a teaching without words (2, 43). Much later, 教 became the word for a whole tradition: 道教, the Daoist religion; 佛教, Buddhism; 儒教, the Confucian teaching.
教.gap: “Teach” in English suggests a speaker and a subject. 教 is first a model set from above and copied below. It reaches from a parent’s example to a state’s moral policy.

senses: to presume (in polite speech: 不敢, “I would not presume”)
敢.story: 敢 is the verb of the step past a limit. In court speech 不敢 was a formula of respect. The Laozi makes it a method: the sage does not dare to act on the ten thousand things (64), does not dare to go ahead of all under heaven (67), and does not dare to be the host in war (69). Passage 73 calls this restraint a form of courage. The early forms of the graph are disputed, so we give no picture for it.
敢.gap: “Not daring” sounds like fear in English. 不敢 in the Laozi is the choice of a person who could act and holds back.

senses: to oppose, to be a match for
敵.shuowenEn: A counterpart, a foe. From 攴 (to strike), with 啻 for the sound.

parts.m: a hand with a stick; to strike

敵.story: 敵 is the one who stands opposite and is equal to you: an enemy, and also a match. 無敵, “without a match”, is the old boast of the strongest. The Laozi uses the word in its two military passages. One good at beating an enemy does not engage (68). In passage 69 the received text warns against 輕敵, taking the enemy lightly; the Mawangdui silk texts are reported to have 無敵, as Wang Bi’s own comment has: no disaster is greater than to have no match. The silk texts are reported to write the word with the graph 適.
敵.gap: “Enemy” in English is a person one hates. 敵 is about balance: the party of equal weight on the other side. To have no 敵 is to have no counterweight.

senses: crossed lines; a pattern; a tattoo
a written graph; writing; a text
文.shuowenEn: Crossed strokes. It pictures a crossing pattern.
文.story: First a pattern of lines, on cloth, on bronze, or on skin; the early graph is commonly explained as a person with a mark on the chest. Then all that is patterned in human life: writing, literature, manners, culture. For Confucians it was the precious inheritance of Zhou. The Laozi uses it rarely and coolly: the three bans, “as 文”, are not enough (19); those who wear 文 and coloured silks while the fields are bare are robbers (53).
文.gap: English splits it into “pattern”, “text”, “culture”, and “civil”. In Chinese the weave of a cloth and the classics of a people are one word.

斯.def: this, thus, such; to lop off; emphatic particle

senses: (first sense) to cut firewood: later 薪
新.shuowenEn: To get wood. From 斤 (axe), with the left part for the sound.

parts.m: left part: sound (a tree with 辛)

新.story: At first the word for felling and splitting wood. The sense “new” took over the graph, and firewood was given a grass top: 薪. The Laozi pairs it with 敝, worn out: worn, then new (22).
新.gap: “New” in English is abstract. The graph still has the axe and the white of fresh-cut wood.

senses: to hew, to chop into shape with an axe or adze
to carve away; to damage by cutting
斲.shuowenEn: To chop. From 斤 (an axe) and 𠁁.
斲.story: The verb of the carpenter’s heavy work: to square a log with blows. The axe stands at the right of the graph. The Zhuangzi uses the word for the wheelwright who cannot teach his son the feel of the chisel, and for Carpenter Shi’s stroke at the plaster on a nose. In the Laozi it comes only in passage 74.
斲.gap: “Carve” is too light. 斲 is done with the whole arm, toward one’s own body.

方.def: a square, rectangle; a region; local

parts.m: the left side in the old form: a vessel of food
the right side: a figure that turns its head away

既.story: The mark of a completed act. The early forms are commonly explained as a person who turns away from a food vessel: the meal is over. In the Laozi: use Dao and it cannot be used up, 用之不足既 (35); having found the mother, know the child (52); having already worked for others, the sage has still more (81).
既.gap: English tense is in the verb. 既 is a separate word that says “this is done”, and translators often leave it out.

明.story: The common graph joins sun and moon. The Shuowen’s main entry is the variant 朙, a moon beside a latticed window: moonlight coming into a room. In the Laozi 明 is the name for the highest kind of seeing, and it is usually quiet: to know the constant is 明 (16, 55); to see the small is 明 (52); one who knows the self is 明 (33); one who shows the self is not (24). Passage 41 says that the bright Dao seems dark.
明.gap: “Enlightenment” carries the European eighteenth century or a Buddhist awakening. 明 is plainer: the ability to see in the light that there is.

senses: to change, to exchange, to trade
易.shuowenEn: The lizard, the gecko, the “palace guard”. A picture.

parts.m: here: legs and tail, or the moon

易.story: The Shuowen gives two origins: a house lizard, and the sun and moon that take turns. The word means both “change” and “easy”, and the Laozi lets the two senses lean on each other. The hard and the easy complete each other (2). Plan for the hard at its easy stage; much “easy” brings much hard (63). A thing that lies still is simple to keep hold of (64). My words are very easy to understand, and nobody can (70).
易.gap: English keeps “easy” and “change” far apart. In Chinese the easy is what can still be changed.

senses: ignorant, to be blind to; to hide
昧.shuowen: 爽，旦明也。从日未聲。一曰闇也。
昧.shuowenEn: (In 昧爽:) the light at daybreak. From 日 (sun), with 未 for the sound. Some say: dark.
昧.story: The sun and “not yet”: the grey before sunrise. The Shuowen takes 未 as sound only, but the parts tell the time of day well. In passage 14 the underside of the One is “not 昧”, not dark. In passage 41 the bright way seems 昧.
昧.gap: “Dark” is too black and “obscure” is too learned. 昧 is half-light.

是.def: indeed, yes, right; to be; demonstrative pronoun, this, that

senses: at times; to wait for the moment
時.shuowenEn: The four seasons. From 日 (sun), with 寺 for the sound.

parts.m: sound part; an office, later a temple

時.story: Time in early China is first the season: the sun’s place in the year and the work that is due. From it comes the idea of the right moment, prized by every school. Mencius called Confucius “the timely sage”; military writers and farmers’ calendars taught the same. The Laozi names it once, in the list of what is good: in movement, the good is 時 (8). The idea is in many other lines: act on a thing before it exists (64); a storm does not last the morning (23).
時.gap: English “time” is a neutral line that a clock measures. 時 has quality: this is the time for something, or it is not.

晚.shuowenEn: Dusk. From 日 (sun), with 免 for the sound.

parts.m: to escape, to be spared; the sound part

晚.story: The sun, with a sound part that means “to get away”. The word occurs once in the Laozi, in a line that became a proverb: 大器晚成, the great vessel is completed late (41). The Mawangdui silk text is reported to have only 免 there: the great vessel is spared completion. The difference is the sun radical.
晚.gap: None in the word. The proverb’s comfort, that slow people succeed in the end, may rest on one added part of a character.

senses: a corner; a part; a secluded place
曲.shuowen: 象器曲受物之形。或說曲，蠶薄也。
曲.shuowenEn: It shows the form of a vessel, curved, that receives things. Some say 曲 is a silkworm tray.
曲.story: A single picture: a curved container. From “bent” come a river’s turn, a corner, a twisted meaning, and a melody. The Laozi opens passage 22 with an old proverb, 曲則全, “bent, then whole”, and closes by asking whether the ancients spoke empty words. Passage 45 has the partner line: 大直若屈, “great straightness seems bent”.
曲.gap: “Yield” in English is a decision. 曲 is a shape. Legge’s “partial” takes another real sense of the word, a corner or fragment, and loses the curve.

更.def: more, still further, much more; to change, alter

會.def: to assemble, meet together; a meeting; an organization

有.shuowen: 不宜有也。《春秋傳》曰：「日月有食之。」从月又聲。
有.shuowenEn: That which ought not to be there. The Spring and Autumn Tradition says: “the sun, the moon: there was an eclipse of it.” From 月 (moon), with 又 for the sound.

parts.m: moon, as the Shuowen says; many scholars see 肉, meat

有.story: The Shuowen ties 有 to the moon and to eclipses, a thing that appears when it should not. Many modern scholars read the early forms as a hand that holds a piece of meat: to have is to have food in the hand. Both explanations are on record, and we do not decide between them. The word covers possession and existence with one verb. In the Laozi it is the visible half of each pair: 有名, the named; 有欲, with wanting; and plain 有, that which is there, the clay of the pot and the wall of the room.
有.gap: Western philosophy turned 有 into “Being”. But 有 always suggests a holder and a thing held. “There is a cup” and “has a cup” are one sentence in Chinese.

senses: to take on (a task, a yoke); to take (medicine)
a horse of the chariot team
服.shuowen: 用也。一曰車右騑，所以舟旋。
服.shuowenEn: To use. Another sense: the right outside horse of a chariot, by which it is turned.
服.story: A word of many uses: to wear, to yield, to take on. In passage 59, 早服 is read as “to submit early” (to the Dao), as “to take on the task early”, or, with the graph 備 first read on the Guodian slips, as “to be ready early”. Passage 53 uses it of rulers who 服 patterned silks while the fields are bare.
服.gap: No one English verb covers wearing, yielding, and yoking.

望.def: to look at, look forward; to hope, expect
senses: to look toward with hope; to expect
the full moon, the fifteenth day
望.shuowen: 出亡在外，望其還也。从亡，朢省聲。
望.shuowenEn: Someone has gone away and is abroad; one looks for their return. From 亡 (to be gone), with a reduced 朢 for the sound.

parts.m: in the old form, a person who stands on the ground

望.story: A long look with longing in it. The early forms are commonly explained as a person who stands on tiptoe with a large eye; the moon was added for the day when the full moon faces the sun. In passage 80 neighbouring states gaze toward each other and do not visit.
望.gap: “See” and “look” are neutral. 望 is to look toward something that is far and matters.

senses: the tip of a branch; a treetop
the minor thing (against 本, the root)
末.shuowen: 木上曰末。从木，一在其上。
末.shuowenEn: The top of a tree is called 末. From 木 (tree), with one stroke above it.

parts.m: a mark that points at the top

末.story: 末 is a tree with a mark at its top: the tip. Its partner is 本, the same tree with a mark at its foot: the root. The pair 本末, root and tip, became a common term for the main thing and the minor thing; “to give up the root and chase the tip” is an old Chinese rebuke. The Laozi uses 末 once, in passage 64, and turns the ranking over: the tree that fills the arms is born from 毫末, the tip of a fine hair. Do not confuse 末 with 未, “not yet”: in 末 the upper line is the long one.
末.gap: English “end” has a sense of purpose or finish. 末 is only position: the outermost, smallest part. It can be the least important thing or, as in passage 64, the place where growth begins.

枉.shuowenEn: Slanting and bent. From 木 (wood), with 㞷 for the sound.
枉.story: A carpenter’s word for a board that is not true, and then a judge’s word for a crooked verdict and its victim. The proverb in passage 22 says: crooked, then straight. A saying of the diplomats, which Mencius rejected, promised more: bend a foot and straighten eight.
枉.gap: English “crooked” blames; “wronged” pities. 枉 is both the bent thing and the one bent.

senses: a result, an outcome; to bring to a result
果.shuowen: 木實也。从木，象果形在木之上。
果.shuowenEn: The fruit of a tree. From 木 (tree); it shows the shape of fruit on top of the tree.

parts.m: here: a round fruit (not a field)

果.story: A fruit drawn on a tree. Every later sense is a ripening of the first: a result is what an action bears, a resolute person carries a matter through to its fruit, and Buddhists paired the word with 因, cause, to name the law of acts and their consequences. In Laozi 30 it is said six times of the good commander: get the fruit and stop; fruit and no pride, no boast, no arrogance, no forcing.
果.gap: “Result” and “success” are abstract. 果 hangs on a branch, and a tree does not go on bearing after harvest.

senses: dry (of a well, a river, bones)
枯.shuowenEn: Withered. From 木 (tree), with 古 (old) for the sound.

parts.m: sound gǔ; by itself, old, ancient

枯.story: Wood from which the water has gone. With 槁 it makes the pair 枯槁, the state of dead grasses and trees in passage 76. The Zhuangzi uses “withered wood” for the body of a person in deep stillness.
枯.gap: English says “dead wood” for what is useless. 枯 is only dry: the life went out with the water.

senses: pliant: wood that bends and straightens
to soften, to win over by gentleness
柔.shuowenEn: Wood that can be bent and straightened. From 木 (tree), with 矛 for the sound.
柔.story: The softness of green wood, which bends and comes back. It is a central value of the Laozi and nearly always wins. Gather the breath to full 柔 (10). The 柔 and weak overcome the hard and strong (36). The softest thing under heaven rides over the hardest (43). To keep to the 柔 is called strength (52). The living are 柔 and the dead are stiff (76). Nothing is more 柔 than water, and nothing is better against the hard (78). Later strategists and martial arts took 以柔克剛, “overcome the hard with the soft”, from these lines.
柔.gap: “Soft” and “weak” are faults in English. 柔 is the suppleness of a living thing. Its opposite is the rigidity of a dead one.

柢.shuowenEn: The root of a tree. From 木 (tree), with 氐 for the sound.

parts.m: to reach the ground; bottom; gives the sound

柢.story: The root that goes straight down. Han Feizi sets it apart from the spreading roots: the 柢 is that by which a tree sets up its life. The Laozi uses it once, in 深根固柢 (59), which became the idiom 根深柢固, “deep-rooted”. Its sound-part 氐 is in 低 (low), 底 (bottom), and 抵 (to reach, to resist).
柢.gap: English has one word, “root”. Chinese here has two, for the root that feeds and the root that anchors.

senses: a root; the base of a tree
根.shuowenEn: The base of a tree. From 木 (tree), with 艮 for the sound.

parts.m: sound part; still, stubborn; the trigram of the mountain

根.story: The root is the part that does not show and does not move, and that feeds the rest. The Laozi comes back to it often. The gate of the dark female is the root of heaven and earth (6). All things flourish, and each returns to its root; to return to the root is called stillness (16). The heavy is the root of the light (26). Deep roots and a firm base are the way of long life (59). In later Chinese, 根本 means “fundamental”, and Buddhists used 根 for the sense faculties.
根.gap: “Source” and “origin” point backward to a start. A root is present and below. The difference is between a past cause and a living support.

棄.shuowen: 捐也。从廾推𠦒棄之，从𠫓。𠫓，逆子也。
棄.shuowenEn: To cast off. From two hands (廾) that push a winnowing basket (𠦒) to throw a thing out, and from 𠫓. 𠫓 is a child reversed.

parts.m: a child, head down: a new-born

棄.story: The graph shows a new-born carried out in a basket. The ancestor of the Zhou house, Lord Millet, was named 棄 because his mother exposed him three times. In the Laozi the word is used with force: throw away cleverness, right conduct, profit (19). And with tenderness: the sage is good at saving people, so no person is 棄; good at saving things, so no thing is 棄 (27).
棄.gap: “Discard” is light. 棄 is what one does to a thing that was one’s own.

senses: the wild jujube, a low thorn bush
棘.shuowenEn: The small jujube that grows in clumps. From two 朿 (thorns) side by side.

parts.m: a thorn; a tree with spikes

棘.story: 棘 writes a thicket by setting one thorn tree beside another; the same sign stacked, 棗, is the tall jujube. The shrub colonises neglected ground and makes a hedge that people and animals avoid. Laozi 30 names it with 荊 as what grows where an army has camped. The pair 荊棘 is still the common word for difficulties in one’s path.
棘.gap: English “brambles” suggests a country lane. 棘 in this text is farmland that has gone out of use.

楗.def: bar of door, bolt of lock

senses: the highest point, the farthest limit, the end
a pole (of the sky or earth)
極.shuowenEn: The ridgepole. From 木 (wood), with 亟 for the sound.
極.story: The top beam of a house, where the two slopes of the roof meet; then any utmost point. The Laozi asks who knows the 極 of disaster and fortune (58), and says that nobody knows the 極 of one who stores up 德 (59). Passage 28 speaks of a return to 無極, “that which has no ridge”, a term with a long later life in philosophy.
極.gap: “Limit” and “end” are flat. 極 is the ridge-line where one side becomes the other.

senses: lè: joy; glad; to delight in
yào: to be fond of (old reading)
樂.shuowen: 五聲八音緫名。象鼓鞞。木，虡也。
樂.shuowenEn: The general name for the five notes and the eight kinds of instrument. It pictures drums; 木 is the stand.
樂.story: Drums on a wooden frame; then music, and the gladness that music is. In the received text of passage 23 the Way is “glad to get” those who are at one with it; the Mawangdui silk texts are reported to lack the word. Passage 35 says that music and fine food make the passing guest stop, while the Way has no taste. Passage 66 says the world is glad to push the sage forward and does not tire of it.
樂.gap: English keeps “music” and “joy” apart. One graph, two readings.

parts.m: small drums or strings at the sides

樓.def: building of two or more stories

senses: wood not yet carved; a log, a block
樸.shuowenEn: Wood in its plain state. From 木 (tree), with 菐 for the sound.
樸.story: A block that no tool has shaped. It is one of the book’s chief images: the masters are solid like 樸 (15); embrace the 樸 (19); return to the 樸, and when it is split it becomes vessels (28); the Way is a nameless 樸 (32, 37); “I have no desires and the people are 樸 of themselves” (57). The short form 朴 is now standard on the mainland.
樸.gap: “Simplicity” is a quality. 樸 is a thing: wood with all its possible shapes still in it.

橐.def: a sack, a bag opening at both ends
senses: a sack, a bag open at both ends
the leather bag of a bellows
橐.story: A leather sack. With 籥, a pipe, it names the bag-bellows of the early foundry: the bag is pressed, and the pipe carries the blast to the fire. Chinese smiths were casting iron by about the fifth century BCE, and that needed a strong, steady blast; the bellows was among the important machines of the age. The Laozi uses it once, for the space between heaven and earth: empty, and more comes out the more it moves (5). Wang Bi explains 橐 as the bellows and 籥 as a musical pipe, and says that both are hollow.
橐.gap: “Bellows” is right for the tool. English loses the plain word inside it: a bag. The image is a common sack that works because nothing is in it.

senses: to be about to; to wish to (before a verb)
欲.shuowenEn: Greedy wanting. From 欠 (an open mouth that breathes out), with 谷 for the sound.

parts.m: valley; here it gives the sound
an open mouth, a yawn, breath going out

欲.story: 欲 is desire as the body has it: hunger, thirst, lust, the pull toward gain. The Guodian bamboo slips often write the word simply as 谷, the valley graph, without the open mouth. The Laozi is sometimes read as an enemy of desire, and it does praise 無欲, “without wanting”, and 寡欲, “few wants” (19). But it also says the sage 欲不欲, “wants not-wanting” (64), and passage 1 gives 有欲 its own kind of sight. The same graph is a plain helper word, “to wish to, to be about to”, and this makes some lines open to two readings.
欲.gap: “Desire” in English leans toward sex and romance, and “expectation” moves the word into the head. 欲 is wider and lower: appetite of every kind, felt in the belly and the breath.

歙.def: to suck; a county's name in anhui
senses: (xī) to draw in breath; to shrink, to fold in, to close
歙.shuowenEn: To draw in through the nose. From 欠 (an open mouth), with 翕 for the sound.

parts.m: wings that fold: 合 (to close) over 羽 (feathers); also the sound part
a person with open mouth: breath

歙.story: A breath word. The silk texts are reported to write the simpler 翕, a bird that folds its wings. In passage 36 it is the first of four verbs of decrease, set against 張, to string a bow. In passage 49 the sage in the world is 歙歙, drawn in, and keeps the heart-mind undivided. The county of She in Anhui, written with this graph, gives its name to a famous inkstone.
歙.gap: “Shrink” and “contract” are words of physics. 歙 happens in a nose and a chest.

正.shuowenEn: Right. From 止 (a foot, to stop), with 一 as the place to stop.
正.story: A foot and a line: to go straight to the mark and stop there. Early forms are commonly explained as a foot that marches toward a walled town, the first way of writing 征, to go on campaign. The word was used for 政, government, and Confucius joined the two: to govern is to set straight. The Laozi both uses and unsettles it. In rule, the good is order (8). Stillness is the 正 of the world (45). Govern a state by 正; use an army by surprise (57). The 正 turns again into the odd (58). Straight words seem to say the opposite (78).
正.gap: “Correct” and “righteous” are moral in English. 正 is first a direction: straight, on the mark.

此.def: this, these; in this case, then
此.shuowenEn: To stop. From 止 (a foot at rest) and 匕.
此.story: The Shuowen explains “this” as the place where the foot has stopped. Its partner 彼, “that”, has the road sign and is glossed “to go toward”. So the two pointing words are a foot at rest and a road. The Laozi uses the pair as a formula of choice, three times: leave that, take 此 (12, 38, 72). It also uses 以此, “by this”, as a full answer: “By what do I know that it is so? By 此.” (21, 54, 57).
此.gap: “This” in English is only a pointer. 此 has a body in it: here, where I stand.

senses: Wu: a royal title (King Wu of Zhou)
武.shuowen: 楚莊王曰：“夫武，定功戢兵。故止戈爲武。”
武.shuowenEn: King Zhuang of Chu said: “The martial settles the victory and puts weapons away. So 止 (to stop) and 戈 (dagger-axe) make 武.”
武.story: The Shuowen gives no definition of its own and quotes a king of Chu from the Zuozhuan: to stop the dagger-axe is 武. Xu Shen uses the graph as a model of the joined-meaning class. Modern scholars commonly read the early form as a foot beside a weapon: a man marching to war. The partner word is 文, pattern and civil culture, and Zhou’s two founders are King Wen and King Wu. The Laozi uses 武 once: 善為士者不武, one good at being an officer is not martial (68). The line agrees with the king of Chu: the height of the art is that no weapon moves.
武.gap: “Martial” and “military” describe a trade. 武 is also a bearing, the look and manner of force, and that is what passage 68 denies to the good officer.

senses: to go home; to go where one belongs
of a bride: to go to her husband’s house
to give back; to come together at
歸.shuowenEn: A woman goes to be married. From 止 (foot) and an abbreviated 婦 (wife), with 𠂤 for the sound.
歸.story: The Shuowen’s first sense is the bride’s journey to the house that is hers from then on. So 歸 is arrival where one belongs. In the Laozi all things 歸 to the root (16), the weary one seems to have nowhere to 歸 (20), the whole is 歸 to the one who bends (22), and the ten thousand things 歸 to the Way, which does not play the lord over them (34).
歸.gap: “Go back” looks behind. 歸 looks ahead, to home.

死.shuowen: 澌也，人所離也。从歺从人。
死.shuowenEn: To run dry; that from which people part. From 歺 (bare bones) and 人 (person).

parts.m: form of 歺: bones with the flesh gone
form of 人, a person (here bent or kneeling)

死.story: A person beside bones. The Shuowen glosses death with a near-homophone that means water that runs out. The Laozi speaks of death without fear and without a heaven. The valley spirit does not die (6). To die and not be lost is long life (33). People come out into life and go into death, and three in ten walk toward death by how they live (50). The living are soft and the dead are hard (76). When the people do not fear death, it is useless to threaten them with it (74).
死.gap: “Immortal” for 不死 brings gods and souls. The Chinese says only “does not die”, and it says it of an empty valley.

殺.def: kill, slaughter, murder; hurt; to pare off, reduce, clip
senses: to kill, to put to death
to be killed (no passive form is marked)
to reduce, to pare down (read shài)
殺.shuowenEn: To slay. From 殳 (a striking weapon), with 杀 for the sound.

parts.m: the sound-part; now the simplified form of the whole word
a hand with a striking weapon

殺.story: The plain word for killing. The Laozi does not hide it. Those who delight in killing people cannot have their will in the world, and a victory in war is to be met with the rites of mourning (31). Courage in daring ends in 殺 (73). Passage 74 says the word five times and asks who has the office of killing.
殺.gap: English separates “kill”, “execute”, and “murder” by law and motive. 殺 is all three; the text does not let the state’s killing have a softer name.

senses: the source from which a thing is born and to which it can return
母.shuowen: 牧也。从女，象褱子形。一曰象乳子也。
母.shuowenEn: One who tends (as a herdsman tends). From 女 (woman); it shows her holding a child. Another view: it shows her suckling a child.

parts.m: two dots: commonly explained as the breasts

母.story: A woman with two dots. The Laozi gives the word to the Way: the mother of the ten thousand things (1), the mother on whom the speaker feeds (20), the mother of the world (25, 52), the mother of the state (59). Passage 52 builds a practice on it: get the mother, know the child, go back and keep to the mother. The same form with the dots joined is 毋, “do not”.
母.gap: In English a cosmic “Mother” sounds like a goddess or a metaphor. 母 is plainer and closer: the one you came from, who is still there.

senses: passage 51: to bring to full strength, to ripen
毒.story: Usually “poison”. In passage 51 it stands in a list of nurturing verbs, 亭之毒之. Some read it by sound as 熟, to ripen (the Heshang Gong text writes 成之孰之); others keep the sense “thick, strong”, which is the Shuowen’s first gloss. The pair 亭毒 later became a literary word for heaven’s care of creatures. Other editions of passage 55 use the plain sense: poisonous insects do not sting the infant.
毒.gap: A reader of English, or of modern Chinese, sees “poisons them” in a list of acts of care. The classical word could also mean to make strong.
毒.shuowen: 厚也。害人之艸，往往而生。从屮从毐。
毒.shuowenEn: Thick. A plant that harms people, growing here and there. From 屮 (a sprout) and 毐.

比.def: to compare, liken; comparison; than; hexagram ䷇

民.shuowenEn: The multitude of sprouts. It follows the shape of the ancient graph.

parts.m: disputed: the Shuowen reads it through the word for sprouts; some modern scholars see a pierced eye

民.story: 民 are those who are ruled: the farmers and workers with no office. The Shuowen explains the word by a near-homophone, 萌, a sprout: the people are the many shoots. The oldest forms are debated. In the Laozi the people are mostly what bad government harms: they starve because those above eat too much tax (75), and they order themselves when left alone (32, 57).
民.gap: “The people” in English can be sovereign, as in a constitution. 民 never rule; they are always the ones below.

senses: the fine stuff of life and of all things
氣.shuowenEn: Fodder and rice presented to guests. From 米 (rice), with 气 for the sound.

parts.m: vapor, breath: layers of rising mist

氣.story: The simple graph 气 is commonly explained as thin lines of vapor. The Shuowen says that the fuller graph with 米 was first a word for provisions; it later took over the sense of breath. From breath the word grew to cover weather, vitality, and the stuff of which everything is made. The Laozi names it three times. Gather the 氣 to full softness (10). The ten thousand things carry yin and hold yang, and the surging 氣 makes their harmony (42). When the heart drives the 氣, that is called forcing (55).
