氣.gap: “Energy” is physics and “spirit” is religion. 氣 is neither: it is material, it moves, and it can be felt as breath.

senses: a river, a body of water; a flood
one of the five phases (north, winter, black)
水.shuowen: 凖也。北方之行。象眾水並流，中有微陽之气也。
水.shuowenEn: The level. The phase of the north. It shows many waters running side by side, with a faint yang breath in the middle.
水.story: A picture of a current. The Shuowen’s first word for it is “the level”: water is the thing that makes itself even, and builders found the horizontal with it. In the Laozi, water is the nearest visible thing to Dao. The highest good is like water: it benefits all things, does not contend, and stays in the low place that people hate (8). Nothing under heaven is softer or weaker than water, and nothing is better at attacking the hard and strong (78). The words written with water carry much of the book’s thought: 沖, 淵, 湛, 治, 江海, the rivers and seas that are kings of the valleys (66).
水.gap: For English, water is a substance, H2O. In this book it is a way of acting: to go down, to give, to take any shape, to wear away stone.

senses: to flood, to overflow the banks
to float, to drift (also written 泛)
氾.shuowenEn: To overflow. From water, with 㔾 for the sound.
氾.story: The word for a river that has left its bed, as in the compound 氾濫. Mencius uses it for the chaos that the sage-king Yu ended when he cut channels. The Laozi uses it once, for the great Dao itself: 大道氾兮, the great Dao floods and can go left and right. The same sound and a like graph, 泛, mean “to float, to drift”, so the line also suggests a boat with no mooring.
氾.gap: “All-pervading” and “reaches everywhere” keep the idea and remove the water. A flood is not a calm presence. It moves and it does not ask.

senses: 江海: the River and the sea; the great waters
江.shuowen: 水。出蜀湔氐徼外崏山，入海。从水工聲。
江.shuowenEn: A river. It comes out of the Min mountains beyond the border of Jiandi in Shu, and enters the sea. From 水 (water), with 工 for the sound.
江.story: In early texts 江 is a name: the great river of the south, as 河 is the Yellow River. Xu Shen uses 江 and 河 as his examples of the form-and-sound class of characters. The Laozi names the 江 twice, both times with the sea. In passage 32 the Dao is to the world as 江海 are to the streams and valleys. In passage 66 the 江海 are kings of the hundred valleys because they lie below them. The south was the country of Chu, wide and wet, where tradition places the book’s origin.
江.gap: “Rivers” in the plural hides a proper name. A reader of the time saw one river, far to the south, into which half the known world drained.

沒.def: not, have not, none; to drown, sink

沖.shuowenEn: To well up and rock. From 水 (water) and 中 (middle). Read like 動.
沖.story: Two words meet in this graph. One is the Shuowen’s: water that wells up and rocks. The other is “hollow”, properly written 盅, a dish with 中 above it; the Shuowen defines 盅 as “the emptiness of a vessel” and quotes Laozi 4 as its example. Scribes used 沖 for both. The Laozi uses the word three times: Dao is 沖 and use does not fill it (4); the breaths 沖 and make harmony (42); great fullness seems 沖 (45). In later Chinese the word means mild and modest, as in 沖和 and 謙沖, and also to dash against. So the character holds a waiting bowl and moving water together.
沖.gap: English “empty” is a lack, and often a sad one: an empty house, an empty life. 沖 is emptiness as capacity, with a hint of movement in it. No English adjective does both.

senses: to put in order, to govern
治.shuowen: 水。出東萊曲城陽丘山，南入海。从水台聲。
治.shuowenEn: A river. It rises at Mount Yangqiu in Qucheng, Donglai, and runs south to the sea. From 水 (water), with 台 for the sound.
治.story: The Shuowen lists only a river of this name. The sense “to govern” is commonly explained from flood work: Yu the Great ordered the waters by giving them channels, and that became the model of rule. The same verb is used for healing. In the Laozi, 治 is the aim of the sage’s rule and also a thing done lightly: act by not-forcing and nothing is left unordered (3); govern a large state as you cook a small fish (60); order a thing before it is in disorder (64).
治.gap: “Govern”, “rule”, and “manage” all put a hand on a thing. 治 keeps the picture of water: order as flow that has its channel.

法.def: law, rule, regulation, statute; France, French
senses: a standard, a model, a method
法.story: The old full graph is 灋: water, the one-horned beast 廌 that butts the guilty, and 去, to remove. The Shuowen explains it as punishment that is level like water. The short form 法 dropped the beast. In the Warring States period 法 became the keyword of the Legalists: written statute enforced by reward and punishment. Laozi 25 uses it as a verb of learning: a person takes the earth as model, earth takes heaven, heaven takes Dao, and Dao takes what is so of itself. Chinese Buddhists later chose 法 to translate dharma.
法.gap: “Law” implies a lawgiver and a penalty. 法 in Laozi 25 has neither; it is the pattern that a learner copies from a master.

泣.shuowen: 無聲出涕曰泣。从水立聲。
泣.shuowenEn: To shed tears without sound is called 泣. From 水 (water); 立 gives the sound.

parts.m: sound part; by itself: to stand

泣.story: Chinese separates weeping by sound: 哭 is the loud wail of the mourning rite, and 泣 is quiet tears. Laozi 31 says that when many people have been killed one should 泣 for them with grief and sorrow. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to have a graph read as 莅, “to attend, to stand over”, in this place, and many scholars think that it is the older word.
泣.gap: English “weep” does not say whether there is sound. 泣 says that there is none.

泮.def: Zhou dynasty school; disperse; fall apart
senses: (of ice) to break up, to melt apart
to split, to come apart (loan for 判)
the half-moon pool of a lords’ school; the school itself
泮.shuowen: 諸矦鄉射之宮，西南爲水，東北爲牆。从水从半，半亦聲。
泮.shuowenEn: The hall of the lords for the district archery rite; water on the south-west side, a wall on the north-east. From 水 (water) and 半 (half); 半 also gives the sound.
泮.story: The Shuowen knows 泮 as a building: the school and archery hall of a feudal lord, with a pool around half of it. The Book of Songs also uses the graph for a word of the same sound: river ice that breaks up in spring. Passage 64 has that second word: the brittle is easy to 泮. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 判, “to split”, and both graphs hold 半, “half”. So the image may be thin ice, which a small force parts while it is thin.
泮.gap: English must choose “melt”, “break”, or “split”. The word covers the way ice goes: it weakens, cracks, and separates in one event.

senses: great, grand; at ease, at peace
泰.shuowenEn: Slippery. From 廾 (two hands) and 水 (water); 大 gives the sound.
泰.story: Two hands and water under “big”: the Shuowen’s sense is smoothness, as of water slipping through the hands. The word came to mean ease and greatness (it is the name of hexagram 11, Peace, and of Mount Tai), and then ease that has turned to pride. In Laozi 29 it is the third excess that the sage removes. In passage 35 it is still a good word: those who go to the one who holds the great image find “safety, evenness, peace”.
泰.gap: English has no one word that is good at one strength and bad at a stronger one. 泰 is “great” until it is “too great”.

senses: to keep alive, to save a life
活.shuowenEn: The sound of water that flows. From 水 (water), with 𠯑 for the sound.

parts.m: now written like “tongue”; in the old form a different sound-part

活.story: The usual word for life in the Laozi is 生, to be born and grow. 活 appears only in passage 73, as the opposite of 殺, to kill. The Shuowen defines it by a sound: water that runs. To live, in this word, is to keep moving like a stream. A modern collated edition of the Mawangdui silk texts prints the word with a tree, 栝, a loan by sound.
活.gap: English “live” has no picture in it. 活 has running water.

洽.def: to blend with, be in harmony; to penetrate; to cover; a river in Shenxi

senses: a reach or course of a river
to drift, to spread; a class or school

parts.m: commonly explained as a child born head down, with fluid

流.story: Water that moves. 下流 is the lower course of a river, where all the streams of a basin arrive. Confucius’s school used the phrase for a place of disgrace; the Laozi makes it the definition of a great state (61). Later 流 also meant a school of thought: the “nine currents” of the old philosophers.
流.gap: English “downstream” is only a direction. 下流 is a place, and it has both the filth and the fullness.

海.shuowen: 天池也。以納百川者。从水每聲。
海.shuowenEn: The pool of heaven: that which takes in the hundred rivers. From 水 (water); 每 gives the sound.
海.story: For a people of the inland plain the sea was the far edge of the world and the place where all rivers end. The Shuowen calls it heaven’s pool and defines it by what it receives. The Laozi uses it as the image of the low thing that gathers all: the Dao in the world is like streams and valleys running to River and sea (32), and these are kings of the hundred valleys because they lie below them (66).
海.gap: The English sea is for crossing. 海 in this book does not move and is not crossed; it receives.

senses: to experience; to be involved in
涉.shuowenEn: To cross water on foot. From doubled water and 步 (a step). (The Shuowen enters the word under the fuller graph 𣻣.)
涉.story: Water and two feet. To wade is to cross with no boat and no bridge, with the body in the river. The Book of Changes uses 涉大川, “to cross the great river”, again and again as its phrase for a serious undertaking. Passage 15 chooses the hardest case: 冬涉川, a river in winter.
涉.gap: “Cross” is dry. 涉 is wet to the knee or the chest.

淡.shuowenEn: Thin flavour. From 水 (water); 炎 gives the sound.
淡.story: 淡 is what soup is when it is mostly water. Chinese taste and painting later made it a high value: the pale ink wash, the plain dish that lets the ingredient speak. The Laozi began that: the Dao in words is “thin, with no flavour” (35). In passage 31, if weapons must be used, 恬淡, calm and plain, is best: no relish in the act.
淡.gap: English “bland” and “insipid” are complaints. 淡 is often praise.

淳.def: honest, simple, unsophisticated; cyanogen; ethane dinitrile

senses: a deep pool in a river
淵.shuowen: 回水也。从水，象形。左右，岸也。中象水皃。
淵.shuowenEn: Water that turns back on itself. From 水; a picture. Left and right are the banks; the middle shows the look of water.

parts.m: the old picture: water between two banks

淵.story: A 淵 is the deep, slow place in a river where the water circles and the largest fish stay. It is the home of dragons in early stories. The Laozi likes the word: Dao is a 淵 (4); the heart of the good is 淵 (8); fish must not leave it (36). The Zhuangzi lists nine kinds of 淵 in a story about a shaman who cannot read a master’s face. Confucius’s favorite student was called Yan Yuan, 顏淵. Under the Tang, writers had to avoid the graph, because it was the personal name of the dynasty’s founder, Li Yuan, and many copies wrote 泉 or 深 in its place.
淵.gap: “Abyss” brings in dread and the bottomless pit of Western scripture. 淵 is deep but friendly: depth that shelters and feeds.

混.def: to mix, blend, mingle; to bumble along
混.shuowenEn: An abundant flow. From 水 (water), with 昆 for the sound.
混.story: A water word: streams that run into one flow. The Laozi uses it for the state before things are told apart. The three that the senses cannot reach “blend and are one” (14); the old masters are “blended, like muddy water” (15); and the origin is “a thing blended and complete”, born before heaven and earth (25). Later cosmology called that first state 混沌.
混.gap: “Confused” and “chaos” hear disorder. 混 is not disorder. It is the whole before it is sorted.

游.def: to swim; float, drift; wander, roam

渾.shuowen: 混流聲也。从水軍聲。一曰洿下皃。
渾.shuowenEn: The sound of a mingled current. From 水 (water), with 軍 for the sound. Another sense: the look of low, pooled water.
渾.story: 渾 is water in which nothing has settled out, and so anything not yet divided. The old masters are 渾, like muddy water (15); the sage muddies the heart for the world’s sake (49). The Zhuangzi’s Hundun, 渾沌, is the same word as a person: the one with no openings, who dies when he is given them.
渾.gap: “Muddled” is an insult in English. 渾 is the wholeness before sorting, and the book treats it as a strength.

senses: still and clear, as deep water
湛.shuowen: 沒也。从水甚聲。一曰湛水，豫章浸。
湛.shuowenEn: Submerged. From 水 (water), with 甚 for the sound. Some say it is the Zhan river, a water of Yuzhang.

parts.m: gives the sound; by itself: very, extreme

湛.story: The root sense is “under water”. From it come deep, soaked, and then the quiet clearness of deep water that nothing stirs. The Book of Odes uses it for heavy dew: 湛湛露斯, “soaked, soaked is the dew”. In the Laozi it occurs once (4), for Dao that “seems, perhaps, to be there”, like a thing seen at the bottom of a pool. Later writers used it for a settled mind: 湛然, “limpid and still”, is a common phrase in Daoist and Buddhist writing on meditation.
湛.gap: English must choose among “deep”, “still”, and “clear”. 湛 is one quality: the calm of water so deep that the surface does not disturb it.

senses: to fill; to reach the full term
滿.shuowenEn: Full and running over. From 水 (water), with 㒼 for the sound.
滿.story: Water at the rim and over it. The Shuowen defines it by 盈 and adds 溢, to spill. The proverb 滿招損，謙受益, “fullness invites loss, modesty receives gain”, comes from the Book of Documents. In the Laozi the received text has 滿 once: gold and jade fill the hall (9). The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 盈 there. 滿 is commonly explained as a Han replacement, made to avoid the personal name of Emperor Hui, Liu Ying.
滿.gap: “Full” is the end of a process in English. 滿 already includes the next moment: the spill.

濁.shuowen: 水。出齊郡厲嬀山，東北入鉅定。从水蜀聲。
濁.shuowenEn: A river. It rises at Mount Ligui in Qi commandery and flows north-east into Juding. From 水 (water), with 蜀 for the sound.
濁.story: The opposite of 清, clear. In the moral language of the time, 清 was the pure man and 濁 the foul age. Passage 15 turns this around: the masters look like muddy water, and the mud, left still, clears by itself.
濁.gap: “Dull” or “murky” hears a fault. Here it is water and earth not yet separated.

濟.def: to help, aid, relieve; to ferry, cross

senses: to do, to make, to work upon
to act as, to serve as; to govern
為.story: The commonest verb of the Laozi and the centre of its teaching. The Shuowen, writing 爲, explains it as a female monkey; inscriptions found later are commonly read as a hand that leads an elephant. 為 is purposeful work upon things. 無為, without that, is the book’s name for how the Way and the sage act (2, 3, 37, 43, 48, 57, 63). Passage 48 uses the verb six times in a few lines. With a person at the side it is 偽, the artificial.
為.gap: English spreads this verb over “do”, “make”, “act”, “govern”, and “be”. Then “non-action” sounds like stillness; 無為 is the absence of forcing, not of movement.

烹.def: boil, cook; quick fry, stir fry
senses: to cook in a pot, to boil
to boil a person alive (a punishment)

parts.m: from the old graph for an offering of cooked food

烹.story: Fire under 亨. The Shuowen has only the older graph 亯, an offering of cooked food to the spirits; from it came 享 (to offer, to enjoy), 亨 (to go through, success), and 烹. Cooking was an image of rule: the cauldron was the emblem of a dynasty, and a great minister “blended the cauldron”. Passage 60 picks the most delicate dish: a small fish.
烹.gap: “Cook” is homely in English. 烹 has the altar and the execution ground behind it.

無.def: negative, no, not; lack, have no
senses: to not have, to be without
not-having; the part that is not there
do not (as a prohibition, like 毋)
無.shuowenEn: To be without. From 亡 (to be gone), with 無 for the sound.
無.story: The early graph is widely explained as a dancer with tassels or plumes in the hands; it was the first way to write “dance”, now 舞. It was borrowed for a word of like sound, “to not have”. The oldest Laozi manuscripts mostly write that word as 亡, “gone, lost”, or as 无, a short form that the Shuowen lists as a 奇字, a variant graph of the ancient script. In the Laozi, 無 is the partner of 有. The two give birth to each other (2); the uses of a wheel, a pot, and a room are at their 無 (11); things are born from 有 and 有 from 無 (40). It is also the first half of 無為, not-forcing, and 無名, nameless.
無.gap: “Nothingness” and “Non-being” make it an abstract noun, and the Western tradition tends to hear a void to fear. 無 is first a verb, “have not”. In passage 11 it has an owner: 其無, “its nothing”.

senses: a suffix: “-ly”, in the manner of
然.shuowenEn: To burn. From 火 (fire), with 肰 (dog meat) for the sound.

parts.m: dog meat: 肉 meat and 犬 dog

然.story: Dog meat over a fire: the graph wrote “to burn, to roast”. It was borrowed for the spoken word “so”, and the first sense was later written 燃, with a second fire. In the Laozi it is half of 自然, “so of itself”: the people say “we are so of ourselves” (17); sparse words are so of themselves (23); the Way models itself on what is so of itself (25); no one commands it, it is always so of itself (51); the sage helps the self-so of the ten thousand things and does not dare to act (64).
然.gap: English needs “so”, “thus”, “yes”, “natural”, and “-ly” for the uses of this one word.

senses: yàn: at ease, at rest; to feast (loan for 宴)
Yān: the northern state of Yan
燕.shuowen: 玄鳥也。籋口，布翄，枝尾。象形。
燕.shuowenEn: The dark bird. A mouth like pincers, spread wings, a forked tail. A picture.
燕.story: 燕 is a whole swallow, drawn from above: beak, body, wings, tail. The Shuowen calls it the dark bird, the bird that in an old ode brings the Shang royal house into being. The graph was borrowed for a word of ease and private leisure, so 燕居 and 燕處 mean “to be at home, off duty”. It is also the name of the state of Yan, in the far north-east of the Warring States world. In Laozi 26 the traveller 燕處: rests at ease, with splendid towers close by.
燕.gap: “At ease” loses the bird, and “swallow” loses the sense. The Chinese reader sees one while reading the other.

senses: to pull at one thing from two sides
to contend, to compete, to fight for

parts.m: a second hand (the form of 又), with the pulled thing as the hooked vertical

爭.story: Two hands and one object: the Shuowen defines the word as pulling. It is the Laozi’s word for what goes wrong among people, and 不爭, “not contending”, is close to a summary of the book. Do not exalt the worthy, and the people do not 爭 (3). Water benefits all things and does not 爭 (8). The sage does not 爭, and so no one under heaven can 爭 with the sage (22, 66). The good fighter is not angry; this is the power of not 爭 (68). The way of heaven wins and does not 爭 (73). The last words of the book: the way of the sage is to act and not 爭 (81).
爭.gap: “Compete” is a virtue in modern English and “strive” is noble. 爭 has no good sense in this book. It is the tug itself.

senses: the head or origin of something
父.shuowen: 矩也。家長率教者。从又舉杖。
父.shuowenEn: The rule. The head of the house, who leads and teaches. From a hand that raises a rod.
父.story: A hand with a rod or a stone axe: authority in the house. The Laozi, a book of mothers, uses the word in two places. The Dao is the 眾父 of passage 21 in some editions, “the father of the many”. And in passage 42 a proverb is taken as 教父, father of the teaching.
父.gap: None in the word. The surprise is in the book: the origin is elsewhere a mother.

senses: to err, to miss, to go wrong
爽.shuowenEn: Bright. From 㸚 and 大.
爽.story: A word with two opposite faces. The usual sense is brightness and freshness: 爽 is the clear morning and the cool wind, and in modern speech it is anything that feels great. The other sense is to miss the mark: 爽約 is to break an appointment. The Laozi uses the second: the five flavors make a person’s mouth 爽 (12). Wang Bi glosses it as “to go wrong, to lose the mouth’s function”. The Zhuangzi and the Songs of Chu use it in the same way for a spoiled palate.
爽.gap: No English word means both “fresh” and “ruined”. The line plays on the instant in which a reader hears the first sense before the second.

senses: window cut in a wall, with a lattice
to open, to give light to (the mind)
牖.shuowenEn: Pierce the wall and set crossed wood in it as a window.

parts.m: a split piece of wood, a slat
the third part named by the Shuowen

牖.story: Early Chinese kept two kinds of window apart. An opening in the roof, for smoke and light, was a 囱 (later 窗). An opening in a wall was a 牖, with a lattice of wood. The Analects tells that Confucius came to see a student who was very sick, did not go in, and held the man’s hand through the 牖. The Laozi names it twice: you chisel door and 牖 to make a room (11), and without a look out of the 牖 one may see heaven’s way (47). The Book of Odes uses it as a verb: Heaven 牖 the people, opens and leads them.
牖.gap: “Window” suggests glass and a view. A 牖 was a cut in a thick earth wall: light, air, and a hand could go through it.

senses: the female of an animal: cow, mare, ewe
牝.shuowen: 畜母也。从牛匕聲。易曰：“畜牝牛，吉。”
牝.shuowenEn: The mother among farm animals. From 牛 (ox), with 匕 for the sound. The Changes says: “To keep cows: good fortune.”

parts.m: side form of 牛, an ox
sound part (Shuowen); some scholars take it as an old sign for “female”

牝.story: A word of the herd. Its partner is 牡, the male animal. The Book of Changes speaks of the constancy of the mare, 牝馬之貞, under its second hexagram, Earth. The Laozi uses 牝 three times. The valley spirit is the dark 牝, and her gate is the root of heaven and earth (6). The infant does not know the union of 牝 and 牡 (55). The 牝 always overcomes the 牡 by stillness, and by stillness takes the lower place (61). The book also has a word for the female bird, 雌 (10, 28).
牝.gap: “The Feminine” is an abstraction with a capital letter. 牝 is a cow or a mare. The Chinese grounds the first principle in the farmyard.

牡.def: male of animals; bolt of door
牡.shuowenEn: The father among livestock. From 牛 (ox), with 土 for the sound.
牡.story: Bull, stallion, ram: the partner of 牝. The Laozi names it twice. The infant does not yet know the joining of 牝 and 牡 (55). The female always overcomes the 牡 by stillness (61). In both places the book speaks of sex in the plain words of the stable.
牡.gap: “The masculine” is a theory. 牡 is an animal.

senses: a pen for cattle or horses
a beast kept for sacrifice (太牢: ox, sheep, pig)
牢.shuowen: 閑，養牛馬圈也。从牛，冬省。取其四周帀也。
牢.shuowenEn: An enclosure: a pen for raising cattle and horses. From 牛 (ox) and an abbreviated 冬; it takes the sense of “closed on all four sides”.
牢.story: An ox under a cover. The beasts for the state sacrifices were kept in such pens, and the offerings took the name: the “great pen”, 太牢, was ox, sheep, and pig together. The crowd of passage 20 is as merry as guests at that feast. Later the pen held people: 牢 is the common word for a jail.
牢.gap: “Sacrifice” in English suggests loss. A 太牢 was the best meal of the year.

senses: a thing, a being, a creature
the world outside oneself; other people
物.shuowen: 萬物也。牛爲大物；天地之𢿙，起於牽牛，故从牛。勿聲。
物.shuowenEn: The ten thousand things. The ox is a great thing; the count of heaven and earth starts from the Ox-Leader star, and so it is from 牛 (ox). 勿 gives the sound.
物.story: An ox, with a sound part: the dictionary says that the ox is the great example of a thing. 物 covers beasts, plants, objects, and people as creatures. In the Laozi the Dao itself is called a 物 once: “there is a thing, formed in confusion, born before heaven and earth” (25). And the Dao “as a thing” is vague and elusive (21).
物.gap: English “thing” is lifeless. 物 includes all that lives; “creature” is often closer.

狂.shuowenEn: A mad dog. From 犬 (dog), with 㞷 for the sound.

parts.m: side form of 犬, a dog
sound part as now written (older 㞷)

狂.story: First a rabid dog, then any creature out of its mind. The word is not always blame. Confucius said that if he could not find people of the middle way, he would take the 狂, the wildly ambitious, as students. The “madman of Chu” who sings past Confucius’s carriage is a 狂. The Laozi uses it once, and with no admiration: the gallop and the hunt make a person’s heart break out in 狂 (12).
狂.gap: “Mad” in English is illness or anger. 狂 is an animal state: the bolting, snapping wildness of a dog.

senses: to be familiar with, to be at ease with
to treat with easy contempt, to take liberties
(as a loan for 狹) to make narrow, to cramp
狎.shuowenEn: A dog that can be made familiar. From 犬 (dog), with 甲 for the sound.
狎.story: The Shuowen starts from a tame dog: an animal with which one is at ease. Among people the word turns bad: familiarity that has lost respect. In passage 72 the received text says 無狎其所居, do not 狎 the place where they dwell. Read as written, the ruler is told not to treat the people’s homes with contempt. Most editors follow the Heshang Gong text and read 狹, narrow: do not cramp their dwellings. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to have 閘, a gate that shuts. The three graphs are near in sound.
狎.gap: “Familiar” is warm in English. 狎 is the cold side of it: the ease of one who walks in without knocking.

senses: a young or small dog (older usage)
狗.shuowen: 孔子曰：“狗，叩也。叩气吠以守。”从犬句聲。
狗.shuowenEn: Confucius said: “狗 is 叩, to knock: it knocks out its breath in barks and keeps guard.” From 犬 (dog), with 句 for the sound.

parts.m: side form of 犬, a dog

狗.story: 犬 is the picture of a dog, and 狗 is the later sound-compound, at first for the young or small animal. The dog guarded the house, was eaten, and was offered in the ancestral temple. In the Laozi it appears twice. The straw dog of the rite is the image for how heaven and earth treat all things (5). In the small state of passage 80, neighbors hear each other’s cocks and dogs and grow old with no visits between them: the dog’s bark there is the sound of a settled village.
狗.gap: The English dog is a pet and a friend. The early Chinese dog is a guard, a food animal, and an offering.

猶.def: like, similar to, just like, as
senses: watchful, in two minds (as in 猶豫)
猶.shuowen: 玃屬。从犬酋聲。一曰隴西謂犬子爲猷。
猶.shuowenEn: Of the ape kind. From 犬 (dog), with 酋 for the sound. Another account: west of Long, a puppy is called 猷.
猶.story: Most often a grammar word: “like”, “still”. In passage 15 it is the second half of the split word 猶豫, hesitation, and the old dictionaries make it an animal: a timid ape that climbs a tree at each sound, or a dog that runs ahead and back. In passage 17 the same word describes the best ruler, who is sparing with words.
猶.gap: No English word is both an ape, a doubt, and the word “as if”.

獨.shuowen: 犬相得而鬬也。从犬蜀聲。羊爲羣，犬爲獨也。
獨.shuowenEn: Dogs, when they come together, fight. From 犬 (dog), with 蜀 for the sound. Sheep make a flock; a dog makes one alone.

parts.m: sound; alone: a grub; old name of Sichuan

獨.story: The dictionary’s proverb says it: sheep flock, dogs go singly. To be 獨 is to be the kind that does not herd. In passage 20 the speaker says 我獨, “I alone”, six times, against the merry crowd. In passage 25 the Way itself “stands alone and does not change”.
獨.gap: “Lonely” is a feeling of lack. 獨 is a fact of number, and sometimes a point of honour.

senses: dark red-black, the color of deep dye
玄.shuowen: 幽遠也。黑而有赤色者為玄。象幽而入覆之也。
玄.shuowenEn: Hidden and far. Black with red in it is called 玄. The graph shows a hidden thing with a cover over it.

parts.m: a cover (as the Shuowen reads the top stroke)
a fine thread, a small twist of silk

玄.story: 玄 is first a color word: the black that still has red in it, as cloth has after many dips in the dye vat, or the sky has before dawn. Many scholars connect the lower part with a twist of silk thread, which fits the dye-house. From the color came the sense of depth: a thing so far in that light does not come back from it. The Laozi uses the word for the common source of having and not-having (passage 1), for the “dark female” (6), and for “dark virtue-power”, 玄德 (10, 51, 65). In the third century CE it named a movement, 玄學, “dark learning”. Qing dynasty printers had to avoid the graph, because it was in the personal name of the Kangxi emperor; they wrote 元 in its place.
玄.gap: English gives “mystery”, “profound”, or “dark”. The first two lose the color. The third brings in the Western link between darkness and evil or ignorance, which the Chinese word does not have. 玄 is the dark of depth and of the womb.

senses: precious, fine; a polite word for another person’s things
玉.story: At first three horizontals on a vertical, commonly explained as jade pieces on a cord; the dot was added later to tell it from 王, king. At the left of a character it is written with no dot. Jade was the stuff of rank and ritual in Zhou China. The Laozi names it four times, each time to step past it: a hall full of gold and jade cannot be kept (9); no wish to be rare like jade (39); a jade disc before a team of four horses is less than the gift of the Dao (62); the sage wears rough cloth and holds jade within (70).
玉.gap: “Jade” in English is a green ornament. 玉 was the measure of all worth, moral worth included: a person of fine character is “like jade”.

parts.m: three pieces on a cord (the early form; not “king”)
a later dot, added to tell jade from king

玉.shuowen: 石之美。有五德：潤澤以溫，仁之方也；䚡理自外，可以知中，義之方也；其聲舒揚，尃以遠聞，智之方也；不橈而折，勇之方也；銳廉而不技，絜之方也。象三玉之連，丨其貫也。
玉.shuowenEn: The beauty among stones. It has five virtues. It is glossy and warm: the way of humaneness. Its veins show from outside what is within: the way of rightness. Its sound is clear and carries far: the way of wisdom. It breaks and does not bend: the way of courage. Its edges are sharp and do not wound: the way of purity. The graph shows three pieces of jade joined; the vertical is the cord through them.

senses: (wàng) to rule as king; to be king over
王.story: Han scholars explained 王 by a pun on 往, “to go toward”: a king is the one to whom all under heaven go. They also read the graph as three lines, for heaven, earth, and humankind, joined by one vertical; modern scholars commonly see in the oldest forms the blade of a great axe, a sign of the power to punish. In the Laozi the king is one of the four great things (25), and lords and kings are told to hold to the Dao (32, 37). Passage 66 builds on the pun: the River and the sea are kings of the hundred valleys because all waters go down to them. Passage 78 says who is fit for the title: the one who takes on the state’s dirt.
王.gap: “King” in English is rank by blood or conquest. The Chinese pun gives another test: do people come? A king to whom no one goes is only a man in a hall.
王.shuowen: 天下所歸往也。董仲舒曰：「古之造文者，三畫而連其中謂之王。三者，天、地、人也，而參通之者，王也。」孔子曰：「一貫三爲王。」
王.shuowenEn: The one to whom all under heaven turn and go. Dong Zhongshu said: “Those who made the script in antiquity drew three strokes and joined them through the middle, and called it 王. The three are heaven, earth, and humankind; the one who passes through and joins them is the king.” Confucius said: “One that runs through three is 王.”

璧.def: piece of jade with hole in it

甘.shuowenEn: Fine. From a mouth that holds 一. The 一 is the way (of taste).

parts.m: a thing held in the mouth

甘.story: A mouth with something in it that one does not want to swallow yet: the graph of sweetness. In the scheme of five flavours, sweet is the middle one and goes with earth. The Laozi uses the word twice. Heaven and earth join and send down 甘露, sweet dew, which falls evenly with no command (32). And in the small state of passage 80 the people “find their food sweet”, where 甘 is a verb: they are content with it.
甘.gap: English “sweet” means sugar. 甘 is any taste that is good and mild, the opposite of bitter; fresh water can be 甘.

senses: the height of ease and pleasure (Shuowen)
甚.shuowen: 尤安樂也。从甘，从匹耦也。
甚.shuowenEn: The utmost ease and pleasure. From 甘 (sweet) and 匹, a mate, a pair.
甚.story: In the Shuowen’s reading the graph joins sweetness and a partner: as much delight as one can have. In common use it is only the adverb “very”. The Laozi uses it with care: “much love means great expense” (44) uses it, the court that is “very swept” while the fields are “very weedy” (53) uses it, and in passage 29 it stands by itself as the first thing the sage puts away: the extreme.
甚.gap: “Extreme” in English is neutral. 甚 keeps a taste of sweetness: it is too much of something one likes.

senses: to be born; to give birth to
to grow, to sprout; to arise
生.shuowenEn: To come forth. It shows grass and trees that grow out above the soil.
生.story: A sprout on a line of earth. It is the Laozi’s verb for every origin: having and not-having 生 each other (2); heaven and earth last because they do not live for themselves, 不自生 (7); the Dao gives birth to one (42); the Dao gives them birth and de rears them (51). It is also “life” as a thing that people cling to: those who make too much of life, 生生之厚, walk into death (50).
生.gap: “Produce” and “create” need a maker and a product. 生 is growth: the thing born is the continued life of that which bore it.

用.shuowen: 可施行也。从卜从中。衞宏說。
用.shuowenEn: That which can be put into practice. From 卜 (to divine) and 中 (to hit the mark). This is the explanation of Wei Hong.
用.story: The Shuowen reads the graph as a divination that hits the mark, and so a thing that can be acted on. Modern scholars doubt this, and the early form is disputed; a common view sees a bucket or other container. We give no picture. In the Laozi, 用 is a key word and nearly always a surprise: the use of Dao does not run out (4, 6, 35, 45); weakness is the 用 of Dao (40); the 用 of a wheel, a pot, and a room is at their emptiness (11). Later Chinese philosophy made a pair of 體 and 用, “body” and “function”: that which a thing is, and that which it does.
用.gap: “Use” in English sounds like usefulness to an owner, and “utility” is an economist’s word. 用 is the working of a thing, its function in act. That is the reason passage 11 can set it against 利, gain.

甫.def: begin; man, father; great; a distance of ten li
senses: a term of honour for a man
甫.shuowen: 男子美稱也。从用、父，父亦聲。
甫.shuowenEn: A term of honour for a man. From 用 and 父 (father); 父 is also the sound.
甫.story: A polite suffix in the names of gentlemen. In passage 21, 眾甫 is the “many fathers”, the beginnings of all kinds of things; the Mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 眾父.
甫.gap: Legge took the Shuowen’s “beautiful term” as “the beauties of things”. The word means the forefathers.

畏.shuowen: 惡也。从甶，虎省。鬼頭而虎爪，可畏也。
畏.shuowenEn: To dread. From 甶 (a ghost’s head) and an abbreviated 虎 (tiger). A ghost’s head and a tiger’s claws: fearsome.

parts.m: lower part; the Shuowen: tiger’s claws

畏.story: The Shuowen draws a monster: a ghost’s head on a tiger’s claws. The word covers both fear and awe. The masters are watchful as if they feared neighbours on four sides (15); the ruler one step down from the best is feared (17); “what others fear, I must fear” (20); when the people do not fear the dreadful, the great dread comes (72).
畏.gap: English separates “fear” (bad) from “awe” (noble). 畏 is one word.

senses: to rear, to keep and feed (read xù)
to support (a family, a people); to store up
畜.shuowen: 田畜也。《淮南子》曰：“玄田爲畜。”
畜.shuowenEn: To keep animals on the land. The Huainanzi says: “玄 (dark) and 田 (field) make 畜.”

parts.m: dark; related to a fine thread

畜.story: The farm word for keeping animals. The Laozi gives it to de: the Way gives birth and de rears, 畜 (51). Passage 10 uses it of the practitioner, 生之畜之, and passage 61 of a great state that wishes to gather and keep people. With grass on top it is 蓄, to store. The reading xù for the verb and chù for the noun is traditional.
畜.gap: “Nourish” and “nurture” are nursery words. 畜 is what a herdsman does: daily feeding with no control over the growth.

senses: to clear a passage, to let through
疏.shuowenEn: To pass through. From 𡿮 and 疋 (a foot); 疋 also gives the sound.
疏.story: The root sense is to open a way, as when a blocked river is cleared. From that come “with gaps”, “sparse”, and “not close”. In passage 73 the mesh of heaven’s net is 疏: it is mostly openings. In passage 79 a different word is used for closeness of kin (親); 疏 is its usual opposite.
疏.gap: “Coarse” and “loose” sound like faults in English. In 疏 the openness is the working part.

senses: to be sick of, to be distressed by
病.shuowenEn: A sickness that has grown heavy. From 疒 (sickbed), with 丙 for the sound.

parts.m: illness: explained by the Shuowen as a person leaning on a bed

病.story: Classical usage often sets 疾 as a sickness and 病 as a sickness grown grave. As a verb 病 means to suffer from, to be troubled by. The Laozi uses it as a diagnosis: gain or loss, which is the sickness (44)? And in passage 71 it turns the word on itself: 夫唯病病，是以不病, “only by being sick of the sickness is one not sick”.
病.gap: Translations write “worse” or “harm”. The medical picture, a condition that the patient may not feel, is the point.

senses: full (of a vessel); to fill to the brim
盈.shuowenEn: A full vessel. From 皿 (dish) and 夃 (to get much at market).

parts.m: upper part: in Qin speech, to get much when buying

盈.story: A dish at its brim. The word is the usual one for the full moon, the night before it starts to wane, and the Book of Changes says that the way of heaven lessens the 盈 and adds to the humble. The Laozi uses it as a warning mark. Dao is used and does not 盈 (4). Hold and fill it: better to have stopped (9). Those who keep this Dao do not wish to be 盈 (15). The hollow becomes 盈 (22). The valley holds to the One and is 盈 (39). Great 盈 seems empty (45). Han scribes often replaced the word with 滿, to avoid the name of Emperor Hui.
盈.gap: “Full” in English is good: a full life, a full heart. 盈 is the point of turning: full, and so about to spill or to wane.

senses: hexagram 42 of the Book of Changes
益.shuowen: 饒也。从水、皿。皿，益之意也。
益.shuowenEn: Abundance. From water and a dish; the dish shows the sense of “more”.

parts.m: water (written on its side, at the top)

益.story: Water that stands above the rim of a dish: more than full. It is the first form of 溢, to overflow. The Laozi is wary of it. To add to life is called ill-omened (55). In learning, add each day (48). Few in the world reach the 益, the benefit, of not-doing (43). A thing may be added to and so lessened (42).
益.gap: “Benefit” has no picture. 益 is a surplus, and a surplus spills.

senses: to steal, to take by stealth
to take what is not one’s own (of office, of fame)
盜.shuowen: 私利物也。从㳄，㳄欲皿者。
盜.shuowenEn: To take private gain from things. From 㳄 (drool): one who drools and wants the dish.

parts.m: drool: water beside an open mouth

盜.story: The Shuowen reads the graph as a scene: a mouth waters over a dish that belongs to another. In classical usage 盜 is the one who takes by stealth, and 賊 is the one who harms or kills; modern usage has moved the words. The Laozi names thieves four times, and each time it looks up, at the cause. Do not prize rare goods, and the people do not become 盜 (3). Cut off skill and profit, and there are no 盜 (19). Rulers with fine clothes and full stores while the fields lie waste are called 盜夸, “robber chiefs” (53). The more that laws are displayed, the more 盜 there are (57).
盜.gap: “Thief” names a type of person and a crime. The graph names a condition: wanting in front of a shown dish. The Laozi’s use is closer to the graph than to the law.

目.def: eye; look, see; division, topic; Kangxi radical 109
senses: an item, a heading, a mesh of a net
目.shuowenEn: The human eye. A picture. The inner lines are the pupil.
目.story: A picture of an eye, turned upright when writing moved to narrow strips. As a part of other characters it marks looking: 見, 相, 看, 眼, 盲. In the Laozi the eye is the organ of reaching outward. The five colors blind it (12). The sage is for the belly and not for the 目 (12). The people all fix their ears and 目 on the sage, and the sage treats them all as children (49).
目.gap: In the West the eye is the noble sense, the model for knowing: “I see”. This book is wary of it. The eye wants, and it has no measure.

senses: blindly, with no light or guide
盲.shuowenEn: An eye with no pupil. From 目 (eye), with 亡 for the sound.
盲.story: “Gone” above an eye. The sound part also gives the sense, as it does in 忘, to forget (gone, with a heart). In early China the blind had an honored trade: court musicians were blind men, and the music master of the Analects is led in by the hand. The Laozi uses the word once, and not of the born blind: the five colors make a person’s eye 盲 (12). It is a blindness that is produced, by too much to see.
盲.gap: The English word is flat: no sight. 盲 says that something has left: the pupil, the seeing part.

真.story: A word that the Confucian classics do not use and that the Laozi and the Zhuangzi made central. It is said of things and persons, not of statements. The essence in the dark is very 真 (21); the 真 of substance seems to change (41); cultivate it in the self, and one’s De is 真 (54).
真.gap: “True” belongs to sentences in English. 真 belongs to gold, pearls, and people.
真.shuowen: 僊人變形而登天也。从𠤎从目从乚；八，所乘載也。
真.shuowenEn: An immortal who changes form and rises to heaven. From 𠤎 (to transform), 目 (eye), and 乚 (hidden); 八 is that on which one rides. (The Shuowen enters the word under the graph 眞.)

矜.def: pity, feel sorry for, show sympathy
senses: to pity; to be careful of
矜.shuowenEn: The shaft of a spear. From 矛 (spear), with 今 for the sound.
矜.story: A spear-shaft, held upright; and so, of a person, stiff with self-regard. Not self-proud, so lasting (22); the self-proud does not last (24); achieve the result and do not be proud (30).
矜.gap: One graph for “proud” and “to pity”. English has no word that looks down in both ways.

senses: to know, to be aware of
to have charge of, to master
知.shuowenEn: A word, an utterance. From 口 (mouth) and 矢 (arrow).
知.story: An arrow and a mouth. Later scholars explain that what is known is spoken as fast and straight as an arrow flies. 知 and 智 were one word, and early manuscripts write both as 知. The Laozi is wary of knowing that aims outward and collects: “one who knows does not speak” (56), “to know that one does not know is best” (71). It values three knowings: to know the constant (16), to know enough and to know when to stop (32, 44), and to know oneself (33).
知.gap: English separates “know”, “knowledge”, and “wisdom” and ranks wisdom highest. In this book the highest word is not built on 知 at all; it is 明.

社.def: god of the soil and altars to him; group of families; company, society
senses: the god of the soil; the altar of the soil
a village community that shares such an altar

parts.m: an altar; things of spirits and rites

社.story: Altar and earth: a mound of soil where a community made offerings to the god of its land. Each state had one, paired with the altar of millet, 稷. The pair 社稷 came to mean the state itself. The modern word for “society”, 社會, is built on it: a gathering at the soil altar. In the Laozi the word comes once (78).
社.gap: “Altars” in English suggests a church. 社 is an open mound of the country’s own earth.
社.shuowen: 地主也。从示、土。《春秋傳》曰：「共工之子句龍爲社神。」周禮，二十五家爲社，各樹其土所宜之木。
社.shuowenEn: Lord of the earth. From 示 (altar) and 土 (earth). The Spring and Autumn tradition says: “Goulong, son of Gonggong, became the god of the soil.” By the rites of Zhou, twenty-five families make a 社, and each plants the tree that suits its soil.

senses: the spirit of a person; vital force
to be effective as a spirit is

parts.m: an altar; things of the spirits
sound part; early forms are commonly explained as lightning

神.story: The spirits of early China were many and local: of mountains, rivers, soil, grain, and the dead. They took offerings and gave or held back rain and harvest. The Laozi uses the word with respect and with a turn. The valley has a spirit that does not die (6). The world is a 神 vessel that cannot be handled by force (29). The spirits have their power from the One (39). When Dao is used to oversee the realm, the ghosts have no 神, no force to harm (60). In later Daoism 神 is the highest of three stuffs of the body, above essence and breath.
神.gap: “God” is too large and single. “Spirit” in English suggests the opposite of matter. 神 is a power that is present in a place or a body.
神.shuowen: 天神，引出萬物者也。从示，申聲。
神.shuowenEn: The spirits of heaven, which draw out the ten thousand things. From 示 (altar); 申 gives the sound.

senses: an omen, a sign (first good or bad)
祥.story: 祥 joins the altar sign and the sheep, the usual offering; the Shuowen glosses the sheep itself as “a good sign”. The word belongs to divination: it is how the unseen powers show their mind. The Laozi uses it three times with a twist. Weapons are 不祥 tools (31). To add to life by force is called 祥, where the word seems to mean a bad omen (55). And the one who takes on the state’s 不祥, its misfortunes, is the true king (78).
祥.gap: “Evil” judges; “unlucky” sounds light. 不祥 is in between: a taint that the spirits do not bless.
祥.shuowenEn: Blessing. From 示 (altar), with 羊 (sheep) for the sound. Another explanation: good.

senses: to offer food and drink to ancestors or spirits
with 祀: the regular round of offerings
祭.story: The modern shape shows a hand that sets meat on an altar, and the Shuowen explains the character in just that way. In early China the dead of a family lived on as ancestors while their descendants fed them at fixed times. A house with no sons had no one to lay the table, and to destroy a state fully was “to cut off its sacrifices”. So in passage 54 the unbroken sacrifice is the proof that a thing was well set up: it lasts because those who come after choose to continue it. The same part 示 is in 神, 福, 禍, and 祀.
祭.gap: “Sacrifice” suggests loss, or blood on a stone. 祭 is nearer to a meal that is shared with the dead: cooked food, wine, a set place.
祭.shuowenEn: To sacrifice. From 示 (the sign of the spirits), with a hand that holds meat.

senses: harm sent by the spirits or by Heaven
禍.story: The dark twin of 福, with the same altar sign: harm that comes down from above. The Laozi names its sources in human terms: no 禍 is greater than not to know what is enough (46), and none is greater than to take an enemy lightly (69). In passage 58 good fortune leans on it.
禍.gap: “Disaster” in English is a star gone wrong. 禍 is a response from the unseen, and so it invites the question of what one did.
禍.shuowen: 害也，神不福也。从示，咼聲。
禍.shuowenEn: Harm: the spirits do not bless. From 示, with 咼 for the sound.

senses: the blessing that comes from the spirits

parts.m: commonly explained as a full jar; gives the sound

福.story: A full vessel before the altar: the good that comes back from ancestors and Heaven to those who keep the rites. It hangs on doors at the New Year, often upside down, because “upside down” and “arrived” sound alike in modern Chinese. The Laozi uses the word with caution: fortune is where disaster crouches (58), and to rule a state without cleverness is the state’s 福 (65).
福.gap: “Luck” is chance and “blessing” is churchly. 福 is concrete well-being, long life, sons, enough to eat, and it was understood as sent.
福.shuowenEn: Help from above. From 示 (altar), with 畐 for the sound.

senses: ritual; the correct forms of court, family, and rank

parts.m: a ritual vessel with its offering; the older graph of the word

禮.story: An altar and a vessel. Of the right side alone the Shuowen says 行禮之器也, “a vessel for the performance of rites”. From sacrifice the word spread to all formal conduct, and for the Confucians it was the frame of a good society. The Laozi names it in two passages. In passage 31 the victory in war is to be marked with the rites of a funeral. In passage 38 it is the last step down: after the Dao, de, humaneness, and rightness are lost, ritual is left, the thin part of loyalty and trust.
禮.gap: “Propriety” and “etiquette” are small words. 禮 was religion, law, and manners in one.
禮.shuowen: 履也，所以事神致福也。从示，从豊，豊亦聲。
禮.shuowenEn: To tread a path; that by which one serves the spirits and brings blessing. From 示 (altar) and 豊 (ritual vessel); 豊 also gives the sound.

senses: to favor, to treat as one’s own
私.shuowen: 禾也。从禾厶聲。北道名禾主人曰私主人。
私.shuowenEn: Grain. From 禾 (grain plant), with 厶 for the sound. In the north the owner of the grain is called 私主人.

parts.m: a grain plant with a hanging ear
sound part; Han Fei: “to circle round oneself”

私.story: The Shuowen’s 私 is grain, and its 厶 is the older word for “private”: Han Fei said that the maker of the script drew “a circle round oneself” for 厶 and “a back turned on 厶” for 公, the public. In the old picture of the fields, each family had its 私 plot beside the lord’s 公 plot. By the Warring States 私 was a word of politics: private interest against the state. The Laozi uses it in two places. The sage is without 私, and so the sage’s 私 is completed (7). Show the plain, hold the uncarved; less 私, few desires (19).
私.gap: English “private” is neutral or even good: private life, privacy. “Selfish” is a moral fault. 私 is between them: one’s own share, fenced off.

senses: to tax; to levy a share of the harvest
稅.shuowenEn: Rent on land. From 禾 (grain), with 兌 for the sound.

parts.m: the grain plant, with a hanging ear
sound; by itself: to exchange, to be pleased

稅.story: The Spring and Autumn chronicle records for 594 BCE that the state of Lu “for the first time taxed by the acre”. From then on the word named the share of each field that went to the state. The ideal rate was one part in ten. In the Laozi the word appears once, in passage 75, as the thing that those above eat.
稅.gap: “Tax” is money and paperwork. 稅 is grain: the same substance that the taxed family eats.

稷.def: god of cereals; minister of agriculture
senses: the god of grain; the altar of grain
Lord Millet (后稷), ancestor of the Zhou house
稷.shuowenEn: A kind of millet. The chief of the five grains. From 禾 (grain), with 畟 for the sound.
稷.story: Millet was the staple of north China before wheat and rice, and its god received offerings beside the god of the soil. The Zhou kings traced their line to Hou Ji, Lord Millet, who taught the people to farm. With 社 it names the state: soil and grain, the two things without which there is no people.
稷.gap: English has no single word for a grain that is also a god and a sign of the state.

senses: (qǐ) to bow the head to the ground
稽.shuowenEn: To stay, to stop. From 𥝌 and 尤, with 旨 for the sound.
稽.story: The first sense in the Shuowen is “to stay”. To stay with a thing is to look into it, and the common classical sense is “to examine, to check one thing against another”, as accounts are checked against a tally. In passage 65 the received text has 稽式. Wang Bi glosses 稽 as 同, “the same”: the pattern that holds for the past and the present. The Heshang Gong text has 楷式, “model pattern”. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 稽. With 稽 the phrase has a use: it is the pattern against which a ruler’s methods are checked.
稽.gap: English separates “to examine”, “to tally”, and “to stay”. In 稽 they are one act: to stop at a thing long enough to compare it.

積.shuowenEn: To gather. From 禾 (grain on the stalk), with 責 for the sound.

parts.m: to demand; a debt; gives the sound

積.story: Sheaves in a stack. Passage 59 speaks of 德 piled up in layers, as a granary fills. Passage 81 turns the word round: the sage does not 積; the more is done for others, the more the sage has.
積.gap: “Accumulate” sounds like capital. 積 is a harvest image: what is gathered in for the bad year.

窬.def: a small door or window; a hole in the wall to cut through a wall

senses: to come to an end, to be used up
a dead end; with no way out

parts.m: the body (身 with 弓); sound part

窮.story: The Shuowen enters the older form 竆 under 穴, the cave, and defines it as “the far limit”. To be 窮 is to be at the back wall with nowhere to go, and so the word also means poor and stuck. Its opposite in early texts is 通 or 達, to get through. The Laozi uses it for what Dao does not do: many words meet the 窮 again and again (5); great fullness seems empty, and its use does not 窮 (45). Sunzi warns: do not press an enemy who is 窮.
窮.gap: “Exhausted” is about energy and “poor” is about money. 窮 is about space: no road left.

笑.shuowenEn: “This character was originally missing.” (The entry was lost; later editors restored it from other books.)

parts.m: a person who bends; young, supple

笑.story: Bamboo over a bent figure, and no certain explanation: the Shuowen entry was lost early, and old sources give more than one form of the graph. A remembered picture is bamboo that bends in the wind like a person who laughs. The Laozi has the word in one passage only, three times in two lines: the lowest scholar hears the Dao and laughs loudly at it, and if he did not laugh, it would not be enough to be the Dao (41).
笑.gap: English separates “laugh” and “smile”. 笑 is both, and with an object it is “to laugh at”.

等.def: rank, grade; to wait; equal, “and so forth”

senses: of a horse: to walk heavily and slowly
篤.shuowenEn: A horse that walks with heavy, slow steps. From 馬 (horse), with 竹 for the sound.
篤.story: The dictionary’s picture is a horse that sets each foot down with weight. From it comes the sense of the texts: solid, sincere, in earnest. Passage 16 pairs it with 極, the ridgepole: the top of the roof and the heavy tread.
篤.gap: “Sincerely” and “utterly” are adverbs of the mind. 篤 has weight in the legs.

精.shuowenEn: To pick out. From 米 (husked grain), with 青 for the sound.
精.story: Grain sorted until only the best is left. The meditation texts of fourth-century Qi used it for the fine vital stuff that makes life, becomes grain below and stars above, and lodges in a still heart. The Laozi finds it at the third step into the dark of the Way: “within it there is 精; this 精 is very real” (21). In passage 55 the infant’s 精 is at its height: it knows nothing of sex, and yet its member stirs.
精.gap: “Essence” is a philosopher’s word. 精 is first something on a threshing floor, and then something in the body.

senses: to sweep out, to clear away

parts.m: looks like rice; the Shuowen says it is waste
looks like a field; explained as a dustpan or basket

糞.story: The Shuowen lists the word under an older graph, defines it as “to throw out, to clear away”, and explains it as two hands that push a pan of waste. From sweeping out came the thing swept, and then its use on the land. In the Laozi it occurs once (46): in a world that has the Way, fast horses are sent back 以糞, to dung the fields.
糞.gap: English has polite words (“fertilize”, “manure”) and rude ones. 糞 is neither; it is the plain farm word, and the passage uses it as the sign of peace.

senses: the lead end of a silk thread
to sort threads; to put in order
紀.shuowenEn: To sort silk threads apart. From 糸 (silk), with 己 for the sound.

parts.m: sound jǐ; commonly explained as an old picture of a cord

紀.story: A skein of silk is useless until someone finds the head of the thread. That lead end is the 紀; when you hold it, the rest follows without a knot. From the silk room the word went to the state (綱紀, the head-rope of a net and the thread-end: the order that holds a country), to history (a king’s annals are his 紀), and to time (a 紀 was a cycle of twelve years; 世紀 is now “century”). Passage 14 ends with 道紀: the place where the Way, which no hand can seize, gives a hand something to hold.
紀.gap: “Essence” and “principle” make it a thing inside Dao. 紀 is a thread: you do not know it, you follow it. Legge’s “clue” (old English “clew”, a ball of thread) is the nearest English.

素.shuowen: 白緻繒也。从糸、𠂹，取其澤也。
素.shuowenEn: White, close-woven silk. From 糸 (silk) and 𠂹 (to hang down); chosen for its sheen.

parts.m: top: the Shuowen’s 𠂹, a thing that hangs

素.story: Silk cloth as it leaves the loom, before any dye. Thinkers of every school used it as the image of what a person is before teaching and habit colour them. The Laozi says it once: 見素抱樸, “show the undyed silk, hold the uncarved wood” (19). The Shuowen defines 樸, the wood, as 木素: the 素 of wood. Together the two became the ordinary word 樸素, plain.
素.gap: “Purity” is a moral word with dirt as its opposite. 素 has no dirt in view. Its opposite is colour and pattern.

細.shuowenEn: Minute. From 糸 (silk thread), with 囟 for the sound.

parts.m: here a changed form of 囟, which gives the sound

細.story: Thin as a filament of silk. Passage 63 says that the great affairs of the world start from the 細, and that the sage works on the great at that stage. Passage 67 uses the word of the Dao itself: if it resembled anything, it would long since have become 細, a small thing.
細.gap: “Small” is about size. 細 is about thinness: a line that can still be followed or cut.

senses: to sever, to break off; to end
絕.shuowenEn: To cut silk thread. From 糸 (silk), 刀 (knife), and 卩.
絕.story: A knife on a thread: a continuous thing is ended at one stroke. The three bans of passage 19 use it, and so does the line that follows them, 絕學無憂, “cut off learning: no worry” (20).
絕.gap: “Renounce” happens in the conscience. 絕 happens under a blade.

senses: the warp: the lengthwise threads on a loom
a constant, a norm, a rule
a classic text, a scripture (later also a Buddhist sutra)
to pass through, to go by way of
經.shuowenEn: To weave. From 糸 (silk thread), with 巠 giving the sound.

parts.m: sound part; commonly explained as warp threads stretched on a loom

經.story: On a loom the warp threads are strung first and stay fixed; the weft runs back and forth through them. 經 is the warp, and from it come the ideas of what stays constant and what everything else is woven through. A text that a culture treats as its warp is a 經: the Confucian classics, and later the Buddhist sutras. The Laozi was given this title in the Han dynasty, when the court began to treat it as a classic. The same word also means to pass through, as a thread passes through cloth.
經.gap: “Classic” keeps the sense of a canonical book but loses the loom. “Scripture” and “sutra” add a religious frame the title did not have at first. The thread image says something the English cannot: a 經 is what the rest of life is woven through.

senses: a net for fish, birds, or game
the net of law; a system that holds
網.shuowen: 庖犧所結繩以漁。从冂，下象网交文。
網.shuowenEn: What Paoxi knotted from cord, to fish with. From 冂 (a cover); the lower part shows the crossed pattern of a net. (The Shuowen enters the word under the older graph 网.)

parts.m: net (网) with 亡 added for the sound

網.story: The word was first written 网, a picture of crossed cords in a frame. Writers added 亡 for the sound and got 罔; when 罔 was borrowed for “have none” and “deceive”, they added 糸, thread, to mark the tool again. As the top part of other characters the net is written 罒: 羅 (a bird net), 買 (to buy), 罪 (crime; first a fish trap). In the Laozi the net appears once, in passage 73: 天網恢恢，疏而不失, heaven’s net is wide, its mesh is loose, and it loses nothing. The line became a proverb about justice.
網.gap: “Network” makes it a system of links. The Chinese word is a hunter’s and fisher’s tool: it catches and holds. The line then makes this net strange, with a mesh that lets things pass.

senses: (doubled) on and on, thin as a thread
緜.shuowenEn: Joined and fine. From 系 (a hanging thread) and 帛 (silk cloth).

parts.m: a thread that hangs, to tie on

緜.story: The loose floss drawn from silk cocoons: very fine, with no joints, and hard to break. The common modern form is 綿, with the silk radical on the left, and it later took the sense “cotton” too. Doubled, 緜緜 describes what goes on with no break: a vine of gourds and a people’s descent in the Book of Songs, a long rain, a range of hills. The Laozi uses it once, for the way the valley spirit is present: 緜緜若存, fine as floss, as if there (6).
緜.gap: “Continuous” and “everlasting” are ideas. 緜 is a material that every silk-working household knew by touch: nearly nothing, and it holds.

senses: slack, loose (of a belt or cord)
繟.shuowenEn: A belt that is slack. From 糸 (silk thread), with 單 for the sound.

parts.m: sound; the same sound-part as in 戰 (battle) and 彈 (to pluck, to shoot)

繟.story: A rare word. In passage 73 it describes the way of heaven: 繟然而善謀, slack, and good at planning. Other old editions write 坦 (level, at ease) or 默 (silent) in its place, and a modern collated edition of the Mawangdui silk texts has a loan graph. The picture is of the body: a sash that hangs loose at the waist.
繟.gap: “Relaxed” is close, but it is a state of mind. 繟 is a thing you can see: a cord with no pull on it.

senses: the carpenter’s inked line; a standard
doubled: on and on without a break
繩.shuowenEn: A rope. From 糸 (silk); the sound is from 蠅, abbreviated.
繩.story: A cord of twisted fibre. Carpenters snapped an inked cord against wood to mark a straight line, so 繩 became “a standard” and “to correct”. Passage 80 remembers a time before writing, when people kept records with knotted cords: 結繩. In passage 14 the doubled word 繩繩 pictures a thing that goes on like a rope paid out, and that cannot be named.
繩.gap: “Endless” or “ceaseless” keeps the idea and loses the rope and the hands on it.

senses: a knot or lump in silk thread
纇.shuowenEn: A knot in silk. From 糸 (silk thread), with 頪 for the sound.
纇.story: A weaver’s word for the place where a thread is not smooth. It occurs once in the Laozi: the level way seems 纇 (41). Wang Bi explains that the truly level way does not force one level on all things.
纇.gap: “Rough” and “uneven” lose the thread. The fingers know a 纇.

缺.def: be short of, lack; gap, deficit
缺.shuowenEn: A vessel is broken. From 缶 (earthen crock), with an abbreviated 決 for the sound.

parts.m: gives the sound; shared with 決, to breach

缺.story: The word begins with a pot that has lost a piece and widens to every kind of gap: a missing tooth, the dark of the moon, an empty office. In the Laozi the great completion is like it (45), and in passage 58 a government that looks sharply into everything leaves the people 缺缺, broken and wanting.
缺.gap: “Imperfect” and “deficient” are abstract. 缺 keeps the chipped rim of a bowl in view.

罟.def: net; snare; pressure come or go

罪.shuowen: 捕魚竹网。从网、非。秦以罪爲辠字。
罪.shuowenEn: A bamboo net for catching fish. From 网 (net) and 非. Qin used 罪 as the character for 辠 (guilt).

parts.m: is not, wrong; two wings back to back

罪.story: The character first meant a fish-net. “Guilt” was written 辠, a nose over the sign of punishment; the Shuowen says that the Qin changed it because 辠 looked like 皇, the First Emperor’s new title. The Laozi uses the word twice. No 罪 is greater than to approve of desire (passage 46, in most editions). By the Dao, one who has 罪 goes free (62).
罪.gap: Missionaries chose 罪 for “sin”, and Western readers now hear that. The old word is legal: an offence, and the punishment that waits for it.

美.shuowen: 甘也。从羊从大。羊在六畜主給膳也。美與善同意。
美.shuowenEn: Sweet to the taste. From 羊 (sheep) and 大 (big). Among the six farm animals the sheep is the chief one for the table. 美 shares one idea with 善.

parts.m: big; a person with arms spread

美.story: The Shuowen explains the word from the kitchen: a big sheep is good to eat. Many modern scholars explain the oldest forms as a person who wears a headdress of horns or plumes; the question is open. In both explanations beauty starts near the feast and the rite. The Laozi does not trust the word. When all know 美 as 美, the ugly is already there (2). Fine words, 美言, can buy honor (62), and words that are true are not 美 (81). The sheep also stands in 善, the good, and 義, right conduct.
美.gap: English “beautiful” belongs to the eye and to art. 美 began on the tongue and covers the fine, the good in quality, and the praised. Its opposite, 惡, is the foul and the hated. It is not “evil”.

senses: what is fitting; right conduct; duty
adopted, artificial (義父, a foster father)
義.shuowenEn: One’s own dignified bearing. From 我 (I; at first a weapon) and 羊 (sheep).

parts.m: sheep; a sign of good things
I, we; commonly explained as a toothed axe

義.story: The second great Confucian virtue, joined with 仁 by Mencius as a pair. It is duty as fitted to a role. The Laozi places it low: when the great Dao falls there are 仁義 (18); cut them off and the people return to family feeling (19); 義 comes after humaneness is lost and before ritual (38).
義.gap: “Righteousness” brings a judging God. “Justice” brings a law court. 義 is nearer to “doing the fitting thing in one’s place”.

senses: to fly repeatedly (of a young bird)
habit, custom; to be used to
習.shuowenEn: To fly again and again. From 羽 (feathers, wings) and 白.

parts.m: the base; its first form is debated

習.story: A fledgling that tries its wings. The Analects opens with the word: to learn and at due times to 習. With 學 it makes the modern word for study, 學習, which an old calendar text uses of young hawks. The Laozi ends passage 52 with 習常, to practise the constant; the silk texts write 襲常, to wear it.
習.gap: English “practice” is dry. 習 has wings in it, and the short repeated flight of a bird that is not yet sure.

senses: an elder; a term of respect
老.shuowen: 考也。七十曰老。从人、毛、匕。言須髮變白也。
老.shuowenEn: Aged. At seventy one is called 老. From person, hair, and change: it says that beard and hair have turned white.

parts.m: a person with long hair (short form)

老.story: 老 is a person whose hair has changed colour; early forms are commonly described as an old man with a stick. It is the first half of the name 老子, “the Old Master”. In the text itself the word is a warning sign: a thing forced to its prime “then grows old”, and that is called not-Dao (30, 55). The good old age of the book is called 壽 and 久, not 老.
老.gap: “Old” in English can be honourable or sad. In the Laozi’s own usage 老 means used up before one’s time.

者.def: that which; he who; those who

而.def: and; and then; and yet; but; Kangxi radical 126

耳.def: ear; merely, only; handle; Kangxi radical 128

senses: open all the way through; wise
a sage; the sage kings of old
聖.shuowenEn: To pass through, to be open. From 耳 (ear), with 呈 for the sound.

parts.m: lower part; commonly explained as a standing person

聖.story: The Shuowen takes the ear as the meaning and the rest as the sound. Early forms are commonly explained as a person with a large ear beside a mouth: one who listens and then speaks. The word is close to 聽, to listen, and 聲, sound. In the Warring States, 聖人 meant above all the ancient kings who set the world in order, and each school claimed them. The Laozi uses 聖人 about thirty times for a ruler who governs by attunement and not by force. Yet passage 19 says: cut off 聖, throw away wisdom, and the people gain a hundred times.
聖.gap: “Saint” brings a church and miracles. “Sage” brings a wise old man with sayings. 聖 is a quality of hearing: nothing blocks what comes in. In this book it is also a word about how to rule.

senses: not to listen, dull of understanding
聾.shuowenEn: To hear nothing. From 耳 (ear), with 龍 for the sound.
聾.story: A dragon over an ear. The Shuowen takes the dragon as the sound only, and readers have long enjoyed the picture of a great roar that ends hearing. The Laozi uses the word once: the five notes make a person’s ear 聾 (12). The notes are the scale of court music, played on bronze bells and stone chimes. The Zhuangzi has the same thought: the five sounds confuse the ear until it does not hear well.
聾.gap: “Deaf” in English is a condition. In this line 聾 is a result: the ear worn out by fine sound.

肆.def: indulge; excess; numeral four; particle meaning now, therefore; shop

senses: to resemble, to be like (as kin are alike)
不肖: unlike one’s forebears; unworthy, good for nothing
肖.shuowen: 骨肉相似也。从肉小聲。不似其先，故曰“不肖”也。
肖.shuowenEn: Bone and flesh that are alike. From 肉 (flesh), with 小 for the sound. One who is not like his forebears is therefore called 不肖.
肖.story: 肖 is family likeness: the child’s face that repeats the parent’s. 不肖, “not like”, was the common word for a son who fell short of his father, and then for any worthless person; it is the opposite of 賢, worthy. Passage 67 plays on both senses. The world says the speaker’s Dao is great and 不肖: like nothing, and so no good. The speaker answers that only the great is unlike; a thing that resembled another would long ago have been small. The sound part of the graph is 小, small. The modern word for a portrait is 肖像.
肖.gap: “Unlike” loses the insult and “unworthy” loses the likeness. The pun needs a family: a child of whom people say, “who does it take after?”

育.shuowenEn: To raise a child so that it does good. From 𠫓 (an inverted child), with 肉 for the sound.
育.story: The top is 子 upside down, commonly read today as a baby at birth, head first. The word runs from bearing to bringing up to teaching; modern 教育, education, keeps it. In the Laozi it occurs once, in the list of what is done for all creatures: 長之育之 (51).
育.gap: English splits “bear”, “rear”, and “educate”. 育 is one continuous act that begins at the birth.

能.def: to be able; can, permitted to; ability
能.shuowen: 熊屬。足似鹿。从肉㠯聲。能獸堅中，故稱賢能；而彊壯，稱能傑也。
能.shuowenEn: Of the bear kind. Its feet are like a deer’s. From 肉 (flesh), with 㠯 for the sound. The 能 beast is solid inside, and so the worthy are called 能; it is strong, and so the outstanding are called 能.

parts.m: upper left: commonly explained as the head; the Shuowen takes it as the sound
short form of 肉, flesh: the body

能.story: A picture of a bear, borrowed for “ability” because the animal is strong and solid. When the borrowed sense took over, fire dots were added to write the animal: 熊. In the Laozi, 能 is a plain helping word with a large role. Heaven and earth are able to last because they do not live for themselves (7). Passage 10 asks 能 six times: can the soul be held, can there be an infant, can the mirror be clean? Under heaven no one is able to know or to practice what is easy to know and practice (70).
能.gap: English “can” is a colourless helper. 能 still has an animal’s solid strength in it.

脆.shuowen: 小耎易斷也。从肉，从絕省。
脆.shuowenEn: Small, soft, and easily broken. From 肉 (flesh) and a reduced 絕 (to cut off). (The Shuowen writes the graph 脃.)

parts.m: flesh (the form of 肉 at the left of a graph)
the right side in the later form; by itself, danger

脆.story: The quality of a fresh shoot: full of water and easy to snap. The Laozi uses it twice. While a thing is tender it is easy to break up (64). Grasses and trees, alive, are soft and tender (76).
脆.gap: English “brittle” belongs to hard, dry things. 脆 belongs to soft, wet ones.

腹.shuowenEn: The thick part. From 肉 (flesh), with 复 for the sound.
腹.story: The belly stands in the Laozi for need that has a limit. The sage fills the belly (3) and acts “for the belly, not for the eye” (12). Wang Bi explains: the belly feeds a person with things, and the eye makes a person the servant of things. Later breath practice set the body’s center in the lower belly, and read these lines as a direction for attention. Both uses start from a plain fact: a belly gets full, and an eye does not.
腹.gap: Modern versions say “center” or “core”. Those are abstractions. 腹 is the soft front of the body, where food goes.

senses: a subject, a minister; one who serves a lord
臣.shuowen: 牽也。事君也。象屈服之形。
臣.shuowenEn: To be led. To serve a lord. It shows the form of one who bends in submission.
臣.story: The Shuowen sees a bowed body; modern scholars commonly see an eye turned on end, the eye of one whose head is lowered. From captive to minister, the word kept the sense of service to one above. In the Laozi the uncarved wood is small, and no one in the world can make it a 臣 (32); the loyal 臣 appears when state and house are in the dark (18).
臣.gap: “Minister” has rank and “subject” has none; “servant” is too low. 臣 is all of them: anyone seen from the throne.

parts.m: commonly explained as an eye turned on end: a bowed head

自.def: self, private, personal; from; Kangxi radical 132
senses: of itself, by its own nature
自.shuowenEn: The nose. It shows the shape of a nose.
自.story: A picture of a nose, taken for “self” because a person who means “me” points at the nose. The nose itself was then written 鼻. The Laozi uses 自 in two directions. With suspicion, for the self that shows, approves, praises, and admires itself (22, 24). And with trust, for what happens of itself when no one forces it: the people transform of themselves, right themselves, grow rich of themselves (57); and 自然, “so of itself”.
自.gap: English “self” is a noun, a thing one has. 自 is mostly an adverb: a direction that an action takes, back to its own starting point.

至.def: reach, arrive; extremely, very; Kangxi radical 133
senses: the utmost, the furthest point; most
solstice (the sun’s arrival at its limit)
至.shuowen: 鳥飛从高下至地也。从一，一猶地也。象形。
至.shuowenEn: A bird flies from on high down to the ground. From 一, and the 一 is like the earth. A picture.
至.story: The Shuowen sees a bird that lands; many modern scholars see an arrow that has struck the ground. From arrival comes the limit, and 至 before a word makes it “the most”: the softest and the hardest under heaven (43), the height of harmony in the infant (55). As a verb: push emptiness to its limit, 致虛極, uses the related 致 (16).
至.gap: “Most” and “utmost” are only grammar in English. 至 still has a flight and a landing in it.

senses: a high platform of rammed earth; a terrace
臺.shuowen: 觀，四方而高者。从至从之，从高省。與室屋同意。
臺.shuowenEn: A lookout, four-sided and high. From 至 (to arrive) and 之, with a reduced 高 (high). It is made on the same idea as 室 and 屋.
臺.story: A 臺 was built of earth carried in baskets and beaten hard between boards, layer on layer, and a hall or tower stood on top. Rulers of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods built them to see far and to be seen, and writers often treated a famous terrace as a sign of a ruler’s excess. The Laozi has the word twice. In passage 20 the crowd is merry as if it climbed a terrace in spring. In passage 64 a terrace of nine storeys rises from heaped earth: the tallest work of a state begins as one load.
臺.gap: “Tower” suggests stone and a narrow shape; “terrace” suggests a garden. A 臺 is a broad, solid mass of packed earth, and its making is mass labour.

與.def: and; with; to; for; give, grant

色.def: color, tint, hue, shade; form, body; beauty, desire for beauty; Kangxi radical 139
senses: the look of the face, complexion, expression
色.story: The first sense is the color that comes and goes in a face: a look. From it come “color” in general and “beauty”, and then desire for beauty; Mencius has a speaker say that appetite for food and for 色 is human nature. Chinese Buddhists later chose the word for form, the visible world: “form is emptiness”. The Laozi uses it once, in the phrase for the five ritual colors that make the eye blind (12).
色.gap: English “color” is a property of surfaces. 色 began on the human face and keeps a link with desire.

芸.def: rue, herb used to keep insects away; to cut grass or weeds; art, talent, ability, craft, technique, performance, acting, trick, stunt

senses: straw (as in 芻狗, a straw dog)
芻.shuowenEn: Cut grass. It shows the form of grass wrapped in bundles.

parts.m: a sprout, a blade of grass (twice)

芻.story: A picture of two bound bundles of grass, one on the other. The word is plain farm language: hay for oxen and sheep. The Mencius uses 芻豢 for grass-fed and grain-fed meat, the food that pleases the mouth. In the Laozi the word stands only in 芻狗, the straw dog of the rite (5). The Zhuangzi tells how such a dog was boxed, covered with embroidery, and handled by priests who had fasted, and how after the offering people walked on it and the grass-cutters burned it. In modern Chinese, 芻議 is a modest name for one’s own proposal: “hay talk”.
芻.gap: “Straw” in English means worthless: a straw man, the last straw. The straw dog is not worthless in its hour. It is honored, and then its hour ends.

茍.def: to be circumspect, cautious in one's behaviour (distinguish DKW 30790 gou3)

senses: the chaste tree, a tough shrub; a rod cut from it
Jing: an old name for the state of Chu
荊.shuowenEn: The tree of Chu. From 艸 (plants); 刑 gives the sound.
荊.story: 荊 is a hardy bush of waste ground whose rods were used to beat offenders. It is also another name for Chu, the great state of the south. Laozi 30 pairs it with 棘 for the scrub that follows an army, and the Mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 楚 in its place.
荊.gap: “Thorns” loses the name of a country. A reader from Chu saw home in the word.

senses: to preside over, to attend (as a superior)
莅.story: A formal verb, also written 蒞 and 涖: a lord comes to court, an official comes to a post, and looks over it from above. Passage 60 uses it of the Dao and the realm: 以道莅天下. The silk texts are reported to have 立, “to stand, to set up”, in its place.
莅.gap: “Govern” is too active and “attend” too humble. 莅 is presence from above.

莫.def: do not, is not, can not; negative

華.story: A picture of a plant in bloom. The plain sense went to the later character 花, and 華 kept the high ones: glory, the capital’s splendor, the name of the Chinese world. In passage 38 it is one of a pair with 實, fruit: foreknowledge is the 華 of the Dao, and the full-grown person stays in the fruit and does not dwell in the flower.
華.gap: English “flower” is praise (“the flower of youth”). Here the flower is that which is early, bright, and soon gone.

senses: all, the whole number of; very many
萬.shuowenEn: A creature (an insect). From 厹; a picture.
萬.story: The early graph is a scorpion, with claws and a tail; it was borrowed for the number of like sound. Ten thousand was the largest common unit of counting, so 萬物, “the ten thousand things”, means all that exists, each thing counted singly. The Laozi uses 萬物 in more than twenty passages. They are born, fed, and come home; they are never added up into a “universe”. The short form 万 is old.
萬.gap: “The universe”, “all things”, “creation” make one collective. 萬物 is a crowd.

蕪.shuowenEn: Choked with weeds. From 艸 (grass), with 無 for the sound.
蕪.story: Grass over 無. Farmland in north China goes back to weeds in one season when no one works it, and in the Warring States the usual reason was that the men had been taken for war or labour. The Laozi uses the word once: the court is very fine and the fields are very 蕪 (53). 荒蕪 is still the common word for abandoned land.
蕪.gap: “Weedy” sounds like a careless gardener. 蕪 is the mark of a countryside whose people have been called away.

虎.shuowen: 山獸之君。从虍，虎足象人足。象形。
虎.shuowenEn: Lord of the beasts of the mountains. From 虍 (tiger stripes); the tiger’s feet are like human feet. A picture.

parts.m: legs; the Shuowen says they are like a person’s (the standard traditional form writes 几)

虎.story: Tigers lived across China in the Warring States period and were a real danger on mountain roads. The early forms draw the whole animal on its side; the script later stood it upright. In the Laozi the tiger comes once, with the 兕: the one who holds life well walks the land and the tiger finds no place for its claw (50).
虎.gap: For a modern reader the tiger is rare and far away. For this text it is what waits in the hills beside the road.

虛.def: false, worthless; empty, hollow; 11th lunar mansion, determinative star β Aquarii (Sadalsuud)
senses: a great mound; a deserted site (later 墟)
虛.shuowen: 大丘也。崐崘丘謂之崐崘虛。古者九夫爲井，四井爲邑，四邑爲丘。丘謂之虛。从丘虍聲。
虛.shuowenEn: A great mound. The Kunlun hill is called the Kunlun 虛. In old times nine men made a well-field, four well-fields a town, four towns a hill-district; a hill-district is called a 虛. From 丘 (hill), with 虍 for the sound.
