虛.story: First a wide, bare height, and the site of a city that is gone. From open ground came “empty”. The Laozi uses it for productive openness: empty the heart, fill the belly (3); the bellows is empty and not used up (5); reach emptiness, the limit (16).
虛.gap: “Void” and “vacancy” suggest lack. 虛 is open land: nothing stands on it now, so anything may.

senses: háo: to howl, to wail, to cry out
hào: to proclaim; an order, a signal
hào: a title, a name; (modern) a number
號.shuowenEn: To call out. From 号 (a cry of pain) and 虎 (tiger).

parts.m: a cry: a mouth over blocked breath

號.story: A cry of pain with a tiger beside it: a full-throated howl. In passage 55 the infant 號 all day and is not hoarse, and the text calls that the peak of harmony. From “cry out” the word grew to “proclaim”, then “title”, “name”, and in modern use “number”.
號.gap: English “cry” can be quiet tears. 號 is loud; it is the word for wailing at a funeral and for a roar.

蠆.def: a kind of scorpion; a sting in the tail

行.def: go; walk; move, travel; circulate; Kangxi radical 144
senses: to do, to put into practice; conduct
行.shuowenEn: A person’s walking and hurrying. From 彳 and 亍 (left step and right step).
行.story: The old form is commonly explained as a crossroads seen from above; the Shuowen divides it into a left step and a right step. From walking comes “to carry out”: 行 is what is done, as against what is said. The Laozi has both senses. The sage does not 行 and yet knows (47); a journey of a thousand li begins under the foot (64); and “my words are very easy to 行” and no one can 行 them (70).
行.gap: English keeps “walk” and “practise” apart. In Chinese to practise a teaching is to walk it.

術.def: art, skill, special feat; method, technique

senses: to guard, to stand guard around
a guard, an escort; the night watch
Wei: a state of the central plain
衛.shuowen: 宿衞也。从韋、帀，从行。行，列衞也。
衛.shuowenEn: The night guard. From 韋 and 帀 (to go round), and from 行; 行 is the ranks of the guards. (The Shuowen writes the graph 衞.)

parts.m: commonly explained as feet circling a walled place

衛.story: 衛 is a patrol: guards who walk around a place at night. It named a ruler’s bodyguard and the border posts of a state, and it is the name of an old state near the Yellow River. In the Laozi it comes once, in the last line of passage 67: 天將救之，以慈衛之, heaven will rescue them and guard them with tenderness. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to have “wall them round” in its place. Later medicine took the word for the body’s defensive energy, 衛氣, which circles at the surface.
衛.gap: “Protect” is general. 衛 is a ring of sentries in motion, a military picture used for a mother’s care.

衣.def: clothes, clothing; cover, skin; Kangxi radical 145
senses: an upper garment, a robe; clothes
(yì) to clothe, to put clothes on someone
衣.shuowen: 依也。上曰衣，下曰裳。象覆二人之形。
衣.shuowenEn: That which one leans on. The upper piece is called 衣, the lower is called 裳. It shows two people covered.
衣.story: A picture of a robe: collar at the top, lapels crossed below. The Shuowen explains the word by its near-homophone 依, to lean on, and sees two people under a cover; modern scholars see collar and lapels. In passage 34 it is a verb beside 養, to feed: the Dao clothes and feeds the ten thousand things and does not act the lord. Elsewhere in the Laozi, clothes are a mark of class: the court wears patterned silk while the fields are full of weeds (53), and the sage wears rough cloth with jade inside (70).
衣.gap: English “clothe” is rare and a little solemn. 衣 as a verb is a daily word, what a parent does for a child each morning.
衣.pyNote: Read yì when it is a verb, “to clothe”, as in passage 34.

senses: to mend a garment, to patch
to repair; to make up a lack; to fill a vacant post
補.shuowenEn: To make a garment whole. From 衣 (clothing), with 甫 for the sound.

parts.m: clothing (the form of 衣 at the left of a graph)

補.story: A word from the sewing basket. In the Laozi it appears only in passage 77: the way of heaven takes from what has more than enough and mends what has not enough. A modern collated edition of the Mawangdui silk texts prints 益, to add, in the summary line; the received text keeps the image of the patch.
補.gap: “Supplement” is a quantity. 補 is repair: a piece cut to fit a tear.

senses: coarse cloth of hemp or hair; a garment of it
the dress of the poor; a commoner
褐.shuowen: 編枲韤。一曰粗衣。从衣曷聲。
褐.shuowenEn: Socks plaited of hemp. Also: coarse clothing. From 衣 (garment), with 曷 for the sound.
褐.story: 褐 was the rough, undyed cloth of farmers and labourers, against the silk and fur of the rich. To “wear 褐” was to be a commoner, and Mencius uses the phrase for the followers of a teacher who lived by farming. The Laozi has the word once: 聖人被褐懷玉, the sage wears coarse cloth and holds jade in the bosom (70). The line gave Chinese a lasting phrase for hidden worth. The modern sense, the colour brown, comes from the look of the cloth.
褐.gap: “Hair cloth” and “sackcloth” suggest Christian penance. 褐 is not a sign of repentance. It is ordinary poor clothing, worn with no message.

senses: a robe closed to the left: burial dress (Shuowen)
to put one garment over another; layered, doubled
to inherit, to continue, to follow
襲.shuowenEn: A robe that closes to the left. From 衣 (garment); a short form of 龖 gives the sound.

parts.m: sound part (short for two dragons, 龖)

襲.story: The first sense is a garment put on the dead, closed on the opposite side from the clothes of the living. From “dress over” came “to add a layer”, “to take on what came before” (to inherit a title), and “to come upon under cover” (a surprise attack). The Laozi has two rare phrases with it: 襲明 (27), light that is covered, handed on, or followed, and 襲常 (52), where the same choices arise with “the constant”.
襲.gap: No English word joins a robe, an inheritance, and an ambush. Each translation of 襲明 must drop two of the three.

見.def: see, observe, behold; perceive; Kangxi radical 147
senses: (xiàn) to appear, to show, to make seen (later 現)
見.shuowenEn: To look. From 儿 (a person) and 目 (eye).
見.story: An eye on legs: a person who sees. The same graph, read xiàn, is the reverse: to be seen, to show. The Laozi uses both. Look for it and it is not seen (14). Show plainness and hold the uncarved wood (19). One who does not show the self is bright; one who shows the self is not bright (22, 24). Without looking out of the window, see heaven’s way (47). The sage knows the self and does not show the self (72), and does not wish to show worth (77).
見.gap: English keeps “see” and “show” apart. In 見 they are one act with two directions, so that display is a kind of looking at oneself.

senses: to keep the eyes open: to be alive (久視)
視.shuowenEn: To look toward. From 見 (to see) and 示 (to show; an altar).
視.story: To direct the eyes at a thing. Passage 14: look at it, and it is not seen. Passage 35: look, and there is not enough to see. In passage 59 久視, “to see for a long time”, means to stay alive, and with 長生 it became the motto of the arts of long life.
視.gap: English “lasting sight” is odd; “longevity” loses the open eyes.

親.shuowenEn: To come right up to. From 見 (to see), with 亲 for the sound.
親.story: The word for one’s own family, and for the nearness that family has. Passage 17 uses it for the second-best ruler, whom the people hold dear. Passage 18 has the six 親, the close relations; passage 56 says the one who has reached “dark sameness” can be neither held close nor kept far; passage 79 says the Way of heaven has no kin: 天道無親.
親.gap: “Love” is too wide. 親 is the closeness of people who see each other every day.

senses: to look at with attention, to observe, to contemplate
guàn: a gate tower; a Daoist temple
觀.shuowenEn: To look at with close attention. From 見 (to see), with 雚 for the sound.

parts.m: a water bird (stork or heron); gives the sound
to see: an eye on legs

觀.story: 觀 is the long, careful look. Passage 1 uses it twice: without desire, look at the fine points; with desire, look at the edges. Passage 16 uses it for the return of all things: 吾以觀復, “by this I watch them go back”. Passage 54 makes it a method: by the body look at the body, by the realm look at the realm. The sound-part draws a tall water bird, and readers like to see in it the heron that stands still and watches, though sound was the scribes’ reason. Read guàn, the word later named the Daoist temple.
觀.gap: “Observe” sounds like science and “contemplate” like religion. 觀 is both and neither: steady looking that does not yet judge or plan.

角.def: horn; angle, corner; point; Kangxi radical 148; 1st lunar mansion, determinative star Spica

言.def: words, speech; speak, say; Kangxi radical 149

senses: to entrust, to commit to someone’s care
託.shuowenEn: To lodge with. From 言 (speech), with 乇 for the sound.
託.story: To put a thing in another’s hands by word. A dying ruler 託 his young heir to a minister; that is the classic use, and the Analects praises the person to whom an orphan prince can be 託. The Laozi uses it once, as the twin of 寄: to the one who cherishes the body as all under heaven, all under heaven can be 託 (13). The Zhuangzi quotes the two lines with the verbs in the other order.
託.gap: “Entrust” is close. English has no pair like 寄 and 託, two words that the oldest dictionary defines by each other.

訥.shuowenEn: Speech is difficult. From 言 (speech) and 內 (inside).
訥.story: 訥 is speech that stays inside. Confucius praised it: the noble person wishes to be 訥 in word and quick in deed (Analects 4.24), and the plain and 訥 are near to humaneness (13.27). The Laozi says that great eloquence is like it (45). The two schools disagreed on much and agreed on this: fluent talk is a reason for doubt.
訥.gap: “Stammering” and “inarticulate” are defects in English, whose tradition honours the orator. 訥 can be said with respect.

設.def: build; establish; display; particle of hypothesis, supposing

詐.def: cheat, defraud, swindle; trick; to feign

senses: to call to account, to punish
詰.shuowenEn: To question. From 言 (speech), with 吉 for the sound.
詰.story: A word of the court and the law office: to press a person for an answer. In passage 14 the three names “cannot be brought to full questioning”. They do not hide an answer. They are not the kind of thing that a question can open.
詰.gap: “Cannot be analyzed” makes it a limit of logic. The Chinese picture is an interrogation that gets no reply.

誅.def: execute, kill, put to death; punish

senses: yes, I will (the word of assent)

parts.m: to accord with; gives the sound

諾.story: The word that one says to accept a request. Passage 63 warns that a light 諾 is short on trust; the phrase 輕諾寡信 is still in use. A saying about the Chu general Ji Bu, a man known for keeping his word, held that one 諾 of his was worth more than a hundred catties of gold.
諾.gap: “Promise” is a noun and a contract. 諾 is the spoken syllable itself, the moment of saying yes.
諾.shuowenEn: To answer in assent. From 言 (speech), with 若 for the sound.

謂.def: say, tell; call, name; be called

譽.shuowenEn: To speak well of. From 言 (speech), with 與 for the sound.

parts.m: sound part; alone: to give, with

譽.story: Praise that is spoken, and so reputation. The second-best ruler of passage 17 receives it. Passage 39 warns in one edition: 至譽無譽, “the highest praise is no praise”.
譽.gap: It is public and audible: nearer to “acclaim” than to private esteem.

senses: a low place where water gathers
谷.shuowen: 泉出通川爲谷。从水半見，出於口。
谷.shuowenEn: Where a spring comes out and runs through to a river, that is a valley. From water half seen, as it comes out of an opening.

parts.m: upper strokes: water half seen (Shuowen); or two slopes

谷.story: The valley is the main landscape of the Laozi. It is low, and so water comes to it. It is empty, and so there is room in it. The valley spirit does not die (6). The old masters were open like a valley (15). Know glory and keep to disgrace, and be the valley of the world (28). Dao in the world is like streams and valleys that run to the river and the sea (32). The valley is full when it holds to the One (39). The highest power is like a valley (41). The rivers and seas are kings of the hundred valleys because they lie below them (66).
谷.gap: The English valley is a view, or a place of shadow and sorrow. 谷 is the fertile low ground with a stream in it: the best place, because it does not rise.

谿.shuowen: 山瀆無所通者。从谷奚聲。
谿.shuowenEn: A mountain watercourse that leads through to nowhere. From 谷 (valley); 奚 gives the sound.
谿.story: 谿 is the narrow, closed cut in a mountainside down which water runs; it is also written 溪. The Shuowen sets it apart from 谷, the open valley where a spring reaches a river. In Laozi 28 the one who keeps to the hen is “the ravine of all under heaven”; Wang Bi comments that a ravine does not seek things and things come to it of themselves.
谿.gap: English “stream” names the water. 谿 names the low ground that the water has no choice except to enter.

senses: a sign in the sky; a hexagram figure
象.shuowen: 長鼻牙，南越大獸，三秊一乳，象耳牙四足之形。
象.shuowenEn: Long nose and tusks; a great beast of the far south; it bears young once in three years. The graph shows ears, tusks, and four feet.

parts.m: a whole picture of the animal: trunk at the top, body and legs below

象.story: Elephants lived in north China in the Shang and withdrew south as the land was cleared. By the Warring States most people knew them only from ivory and bones. The Han Feizi uses this to explain how the animal’s name came to mean “image”: people find the bones of a dead elephant and from that pattern imagine the living one, “so whatever people picture in the mind is called 象”. The word then covered each kind of likeness: the signs that heaven hangs in the sky, the figures of the Book of Changes. In the Laozi, 大象, “the great image” (35, 41), has no shape, and Dao “looks” older than Di (4).
象.gap: English keeps “image”, “symbol”, “seems”, and “elephant” apart. In Chinese one word holds them, with a hint that every image is a reconstruction from remains.

senses: wary, to hesitate (as in 猶豫)
豫.shuowen: 象之大者。賈侍中說：不害於物。从象予聲。
豫.shuowenEn: A large kind of elephant. The palace attendant Jia says: it does no harm to other creatures. From 象 (elephant), with 予 for the sound.
豫.story: For the Shuowen this is an animal name: a great elephant that harms nothing. Old tradition made the elephant a careful beast that tests the ground, and so explained the sense “to hesitate”. Modern linguists treat 猶豫 as one two-syllable word and the animals as borrowed graphs. In passage 15 it opens the portrait of the old masters: wary, as if crossing a river in winter.
豫.gap: English “hesitant” or “irresolute” sounds like a weakness of will. 豫 also means prepared and at ease: the care of a large body that has no need to hurry.

senses: to test by divination (the oracle-bone sense)
a standard, that which is correct
貞.shuowenEn: To ask by divination. From 卜 (the crack in the bone), with 貝 (cowrie) as the gift offered.

parts.m: cowrie; in early forms a tripod, 鼎

貞.story: The verb that opens the questions on the Shang oracle bones. From the tested answer came “firm” and “true”, and the word is one of the four at the head of the Book of Changes. In passage 39 lords and kings, by the One, become the 貞 of all under heaven; the silk texts are reported to write 正, a standard.
貞.gap: Dictionaries give “chaste, virtuous”, the late and narrow sense. In early texts it is closer to “proved true”.

senses: to turn the back on; to betray
負.shuowen: 恃也。从人守貝，有所恃也。一曰受貸不償。
負.shuowenEn: To rely on. From a person who guards cowries: he has something to rely on. Some say: to take a loan and not repay it.
負.story: A person above a cowrie shell. The dictionary begins from “rely on” and “owe”; the usual sense in texts is to bear a load on the back, and so to have one’s back to something. In passage 42 the ten thousand things 負 shade: they carry it behind them. The Shuowen’s second sense, a loan not repaid, sits oddly well beside passage 41, where the Dao is a lender.
負.gap: English “bear” or “carry” does not say where. 負 is on the back, out of sight.

貨.shuowenEn: Wealth. From 貝 (shell, money), with 化 for the sound.
貨.story: Things that move from hand to hand. The shell at the bottom was early money. The Laozi uses the word mostly in one phrase, 難得之貨, “goods hard to get”: do not prize them and there are no thieves (3); they hinder a person’s walk (12); the sage does not prize them (64). Passage 44 asks the question outright: your person or your 貨, which counts for more?
貨.gap: “Goods” in English sounds good. 貨 is neutral: stuff that is traded, and that draws the eye for that reason.

senses: to demand payment, to press a claim
to blame, to reproach, to hold to account
a duty; a debt (later written 債)
責.shuowenEn: To demand. From 貝 (cowrie shell), with 朿 (thorn) for the sound.

parts.m: a thorn; the sound-part (now reduced to four strokes)

責.story: First the creditor’s act of asking for what is due; then blame of any kind; then the duty itself. In the Laozi the word comes once: the sage holds the left tally and does not 責 anyone (79).
責.gap: English keeps “to bill” and “to blame” apart. 責 is one act: to present someone with what they owe.

senses: to value, to prize, to honor
(old gloss, in passage 13) to treat as grave, to fear
貴.shuowenEn: Of things: not cheap. From 貝 (shell, money), with 臾 for the sound.
貴.story: First a word of the market: dear, the opposite of 賤, cheap. Then of persons: high in rank. As a verb: to hold dear. The Laozi uses all three and keeps reversing them. Do not 貴 rare goods (3, 64). Rich and 貴 and proud: ruin (9). 貴 the body as all under heaven (13). The 貴 has the lowly as its root (39). Those who know “me” are few, and so “I” am 貴 (70). The sage cares for the self and does not 貴 the self (72).
貴.gap: English keeps “expensive”, “noble”, and “to value” apart. 貴 is one word, and it shows that rank and price are one kind of thing.

senses: to lend; to give out, to bestow
貸.shuowenEn: To give out. From 貝 (cowrie, money), with 代 for the sound.

parts.m: to take the place of; the sound part

貸.story: A money word. In the Laozi it comes once, in the last line of passage 41: only the Dao is good at 貸 and at completing. Life, form, and ability are loans. The silk text is reported to have 始, “to begin”, in its place.
貸.gap: “Bestow” and “provide” make it a gift. A loan is to be returned.

senses: material to work with, a resource
資.shuowenEn: Goods. From 貝 (shell money); 次 gives the sound.
資.story: 資 is what one has to work with: a merchant’s stock, a traveller’s funds, a craftsman’s material. Wang Bi glosses it “to take from”. In Laozi 27 the not-good person is the 資 of the good person, and the good person is told to hold that material dear. The later compound 師資, from the same two lines, came to mean a teacher.
資.gap: “Resource” makes a person into a quantity. The Laozi adds the verb 愛, to care for, which a mere resource does not receive.

senses: to injure, to ruin, to murder
one who does violent harm: a bandit, a rebel, a traitor
賊.shuowenEn: To ruin. From 戈 (dagger-axe), with 則 for the sound.
賊.story: 賊 is harm done with a weapon. In early texts it is the word for an assassin, a rebel, or a person who destroys a thing from inside; Mencius says that a king who does violence to humaneness is a 賊 and no king. The Laozi uses it three times. Passage 19: give up skill and profit, and robbers and 賊 will be gone. Passage 57: the more laws are displayed, the more robbers and 賊 there are. Passage 65: to govern a state by cleverness is to be the state’s 賊. In each case the 賊 is produced by the cleverness of those above.
賊.gap: “Thief” is too light; “bane” and “curse” lose the person. 國之賊 names the ruler as a criminal against the state.

senses: a guest, a visitor of rank
to treat as a guest; to honour
to come as a guest: to submit, to offer allegiance
賓.shuowenEn: One who is treated with respect. From 貝 (shell, a gift); 𡧍 gives the sound.
賓.story: 賓 is the honoured guest: a person under one’s roof, with gifts given or brought. In the Zhou order, states and peoples that acknowledged the king “came as guests”, so the word also means to give allegiance. Laozi 32 sets it against 臣, a subject: the uncarved cannot be made a servant, and if rulers kept to it, the ten thousand things would 自賓, come as guests of themselves.
賓.gap: “Submit” loses the honour, and “guest” loses the politics. 賓 is allegiance that keeps its dignity.

senses: to surpass, to be better than
賢.shuowenEn: Much ability. From 貝 (shell, money), with 臤 for the sound.
賢.story: The Shuowen says that the old script wrote this word 臤, hand and servant, glossed as “firm”; the shell was added. Some editions of the Shuowen define 賢 as “much wealth”. By the Warring States, 賢 was the key word of political reform: the Mohists asked rulers to 尚賢, to raise able men of any birth, and Confucians asked for the same. The Laozi answers “do not exalt the worthy” (3). In passage 77 the sage does not wish to 見賢, to show worth. In passage 75 the word is a plain comparative: “better than”.
賢.gap: “Worthy” is moral and “talented” is technical. 賢 is both, and it is also a job title: the kind of man a court hires.

senses: to hold cheap, to look down on
賤.shuowenEn: The price is low. From 貝 (cowrie shell), with 戔 for the sound.
賤.story: The partner of 貴. Passage 39 says that the high takes the low, 賤, as its root, and that kings call themselves orphaned and unworthy for that reason. Passage 56 says of the one in the dark sameness: cannot be raised high, cannot be brought low.
賤.gap: “Base” and “humble” are moral in English. 賤 is a rank and a price; a good person can be 賤.

senses: to give in pawn, a pledge
an attached thing with no use
a wart, a growth on the skin
贅.shuowen: 以物質錢。从敖、貝。敖者，猶放；貝，當復取之也。
贅.shuowenEn: To give a thing in pledge for coins. From 敖 and 貝. 敖 is like “to let go”; the shell shows that one must take it back again.
贅.story: The Shuowen starts 贅 in a pawnshop: a thing let go for money, with a shell below to show that it must be redeemed. What is pawned hangs between two owners, and from that the word came to mean anything attached and useless. The Shuowen glosses the word for wart, 肬, as 贅. A man who married into his wife’s family was a 贅婿, a “pledged son-in-law”. Laozi 24 sets 贅 beside leftover food as the two pictures of self-display.
贅.gap: English “superfluous” is clean and abstract. 贅 is a growth on the skin that you would like to be rid of.

贍.def: support, aid; to be sufficient; rich, elegant

赤.shuowenEn: The colour of the south. From 大 (a person; great) and 火 (fire).

parts.m: a person with arms out; great

赤.story: 赤 is the oldest and plainest of the Chinese reds: a person, or a great blaze, over 火. In the scheme of five phases it belongs to the south, summer, and fire. It also means bare and with nothing added. Both senses meet in 赤子, the “red child”: the newborn, red-skinned and naked. Passage 55 takes the 赤子 as the likeness of a person full of 德. Mencius speaks of “the heart of the red child”, and rulers called the people their 赤子.
赤.gap: “Infant” and “baby” have no colour. 赤子 keeps the raw fact of the first days: red, and bare.

走.def: walk, go on foot; run; leave; Kangxi radical 156
senses: to walk, to go, to leave (modern)
走.shuowen: 趨也。从夭、止。夭止者，屈也。
走.shuowenEn: To hurry. From 夭 and 止 (foot). 夭 with 止 means to bend.

parts.m: a bent figure (now written like 土)

走.story: In classical Chinese 走 is to run and 行 is to walk; the modern sense “walk” came much later. Many modern scholars explain the old form as a person with swinging arms over a foot. 走馬 in passage 46 are therefore running horses, swift horses kept for war and for the relay post.
走.gap: A reader who knows modern Chinese will see “walking horses”. The classical word is the opposite: speed.

起.def: rise, stand up; go up; begin

足.def: foot; attain, satisfy, enough; Kangxi radical 156
senses: to be worth (不足: not worth…)
足.shuowenEn: A person’s foot. It is below. From 止 (foot) and 口.

parts.m: a round shape above (knee or leg)

足.story: 足 is the foot with something of the leg above it. The same graph writes “enough”, commonly explained as a loan for a like-sounding word. 知足, “to know enough”, is one of the Laozi’s fixed phrases: the one who knows it is rich (33), is not disgraced (44), and has the lasting kind of enough (46). It makes a pair with 知止, to know when to stop, whose 止 is also a foot. Passage 64 has the literal sense: a journey of a thousand li starts under the foot.
足.gap: “Contentment” is a mood. 知足 is a piece of knowledge: knowing the amount.

senses: to step across, to stride over
跨.shuowenEn: To cross over. From 足 (foot); 夸 gives the sound.

parts.m: sound part; by itself: extravagant, to brag

跨.story: 跨 is the long step that takes a person over a ditch or onto a horse. Its sound part, 夸, means “extravagant” in the Shuowen and later “to brag”, so the graph happens to set a foot beside a boast. Laozi 24 says that one who strides, or straddles, does not walk: the legs have taken all the ground they can and the next step will not come. The line is reported missing from the Mawangdui silk texts.
跨.gap: English must pick “stride” or “straddle”. 跨 is the one position of the legs that both words describe.

身.shuowenEn: The body. It shows a person’s body.
身.story: Early forms are commonly explained as a person in side view with a round belly. The word runs from the physical body to the whole person and the span of a life. It is central in the Laozi. The sage puts the 身 behind and it is in front (7). The work done, the 身 withdraws (9). “I have great trouble because I have a 身” (13). Name or 身, which is nearer? (44). Cultivate it in the 身, and its power is real (54). To the end of the 身, that is, all one’s life, there is no danger (16, 52).
身.gap: “Self” brings in an inner owner of the body. “Body” alone can sound like mere flesh. 身 is the living person, body and life together.

車.def: cart, vehicle; carry in a cart; Kangxi radical 159

輒.def: then; each; rack on chariot for luggage or weapons

senses: side pieces tied to a cart to strengthen it
to assist, to support from the side
輔.shuowenEn: The cheek-frame (jaw) of a person. From 車 (cart), with 甫 for the sound.
輔.story: The graph has a cart in it, and the Book of Songs uses the word for props that are fastened to a loaded cart. The Shuowen defines it as the jaw. A proverb in the Zuozhuan joins the two: 輔車相依, prop and cart, or cheek and jaw, depend on each other. From this came the sense “to assist”, and the title of the ministers who stood at a ruler’s side. In passage 64 it is the last verb of the sage: 輔萬物之自然, to assist the self-so of the ten thousand things. The helper takes load and does not steer.
輔.gap: “Help” and “assist” are weak in English and can hide control (“let me help you”). 輔 is structural: a part at the side that bears weight and has no power of direction.

senses: to treat as light, to slight (verb)
輕.shuowenEn: A light chariot. From 車 (chariot); 坙 gives the sound.
輕.story: The Shuowen ties 輕 to a vehicle: the light chariot that an army sends ahead for speed. From there it means light in general, and then light in conduct: hasty, easy to move, of little account. As a verb it means to hold something cheap. In Laozi 26 it is the opposite of 重 and occurs three times: the light has its root in the heavy; a great lord must not make his person light; the light one loses the root.
輕.gap: English “light” also means brightness and is mostly pleasant. 輕 has no brightness in it, and in a ruler it is a fault.

輜.def: a supply cart, covered wagon, dray
senses: 輜重: an army’s supply train, baggage
輜.shuowen: 軿車前，衣車後也。从車甾聲。
輜.shuowenEn: A wagon closed in like a curtained carriage in front and like a clothes cart behind. From 車 (cart); 甾 gives the sound.
輜.story: 輜 is the slow, covered cart that carries what an army or a traveller needs. With 重, “the heavy things”, it forms the standing term for the supply train. Sunzi warns that an army without it is lost. Laozi 26 makes it the picture of what a person must not ride away from, and the Han Feizi glosses it for rulers: the state is a lord’s baggage train.
輜.gap: “Baggage” in English is something one would like to drop. 輜重 is what keeps the traveller alive.

輟.shuowen: 車小缺復合者。从車叕聲。
輟.shuowenEn: Carts with a small gap that close up again. From 車 (cart), with 叕 for the sound.

parts.m: to join, to stitch; gives the sound

輟.story: A column of carts opens a small gap and closes it again: that is 輟. So the word means a pause, not an end. Passage 54 says the sacrifices of the descendants 不輟, do not pause even once. The silk texts are reported to have the stronger word 絕, “cut off”.
輟.gap: English “cease” is final. 輟 is the smaller thing: a missed beat.

senses: the box of a cart or chariot
a cart, a carriage; a sedan chair
the many, the public (輿論, public opinion)
輿.shuowenEn: The box of a cart. From 車 (cart), with 舁 for the sound.

parts.m: four hands that lift; also the sound

輿.story: A cart in the middle and hands at the four corners: the part that carries. In passage 39 the pinned text says that if you count out the 輿, there is no 輿; other editions read 譽, praise. In passage 80 the small state has boats and carts, 舟輿, and no one rides them.
輿.gap: None in the word. The gap is in the line: cart or praise, and no one is sure.

senses: by extension: a cart, a center where things gather
轂.shuowenEn: That on which the spokes converge. From 車 (cart), with 㱿 for the sound.
轂.story: The hub was a short cylinder of hard wood with a ring of mortises for the spokes and a bore through the center for the axle. It took the most wear of any part, and the Kaogongji gives careful rules for its wood, length, and bore. Crowded streets were described as 轂擊, “hub knocks on hub”. In the Laozi it occurs once (11), and it made the hub one of the lasting images of Chinese thought: a center that holds everything because it is hollow.
轂.gap: English “hub” now means a busy center, a place full of activity. The Laozi’s hub is important for the opposite reason: its middle is the one empty place in the wheel.

辭.story: The Shuowen begins with the law court: words set in order as a plea. From formal words came the polite refusal, and from that, a departure. In the Laozi the word comes two times in the phrase 不辭 (2, 34). It can be heard as “does not refuse”, of a host who turns no one away, or as “does not speak”, of a giver who makes no statement about the gift. Both fit the Dao of passage 34.
辭.gap: English has to choose between “refuse” and “speak”. The Chinese word holds a refusal that is made of words.

辯.shuowenEn: To set in order. From 言 (speech) between the two parts of 辡.
辯.story: The graph is a court scene: speech between two litigants. In the Warring States, 辯 was a profession. Travelling advisers lived by set speeches, and the “disputers”, 辯者, such as Hui Shi and Gongsun Long, argued paradoxes for their own sake. The Laozi keeps its distance: great 辯 is like slow speech (45), and the good do not 辯 (81).
辯.gap: “Eloquence” sounds like a gift. 辯 has a contest in it, and someone must lose.

senses: to be so kind as to (polite speech: “you disgrace yourself by…”)
辱.shuowen: 恥也。从寸在辰下。失耕時，於封畺上戮之也。辰者，農之時也。
辱.shuowenEn: Shame. From 寸 (a hand) under 辰. One who missed the time of plowing was punished at the boundary mound. 辰 is the farmers’ season.

parts.m: the farming season and its star; commonly explained as a shell blade for field work

辱.story: The Shuowen reads the graph as a public punishment for failing the season; modern scholars see a hand with a farm tool and doubt the story. The word is the partner of 榮, glory, and of 寵, favor. The Laozi treats it as a place that one can choose to stand in. Favor and 辱 are both like a fright (13). Know glory and keep to 辱: be the valley of the world (28). The great white seems 辱, soiled (41). Know what is enough and there is no 辱 (44).
辱.gap: “Disgrace” is a fall from grace, a word of court and church. 辱 is exposure before one’s neighbors. The Laozi advises a person to keep to it, which no English moralist would say of disgrace.

迷.shuowenEn: To be in doubt, astray. From 辵 (walking); 米 gives the sound.
迷.story: 迷 is the state of a traveller who no longer knows the road. The Shuowen glosses it with 或, the old way to write 惑, doubt. In the Laozi it is what people have long been in (58), and in passage 27 what the clever person falls into who neither prizes a teacher nor cares for the material: 雖智大迷, “however clever, greatly lost”. Buddhists later made it the standing opposite of 悟, to awaken.
迷.gap: “Deluded” is a state of mind. 迷 keeps its feet: it is being on the wrong path.

parts.m: right part as now written; in the older form 𢓴 the parts are a step, the sun, and a trailing foot

退.story: The Shuowen enters an older graph, 𢓴, and glosses it as “to draw back; another sense, to walk slowly”. The word is the partner of 進, to advance, and the pair covers armies, careers, and manners. The Laozi takes the side of 退. The work carried through, the body steps back: the way of heaven (9). The Dao that goes forward seems to 退 (41). “I do not dare advance an inch; I 退 a foot” (69). The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to write an old form of the word, which some editions print as 芮, and to have it also in passage 7.
退.gap: “Retreat” is a defeat and “retire” is the end of a career. 退 is a step backward, taken in good order, and it can be the strongest move.

senses: to go away, to pass on
to flow past (of water, of time)
逝.shuowenEn: To go away. From 辵 (walking); 折 gives the sound. Read like 誓.

parts.m: sound part; by itself: to break off

逝.story: 逝 is departure that does not look back. Confucius used it beside a river for all that passes, day and night. It became a gentle word for death. In Laozi 25 it is the first thing that “great” turns into: what is great does not stay to be measured. The chain then runs on: gone, so far; far, so back again. The Mawangdui silk texts are reported to write the word with the sound-loan 筮.
逝.gap: “Flowing” keeps the river and loses the leaving. “Departing” keeps the leaving and loses the river.

senses: to pass, to go by, to cross
to exceed, to go too far
過.shuowenEn: To cross over, to pass. From 辵 (to walk), with 咼 for the sound.
過.story: 過 is a word of walking: to pass a place. From “go past” came “go beyond the mark”, and from that the common word for a fault. In Chinese ethics an error is first an overshoot, and Confucius says that to go too far is as bad as not to reach. The Laozi plays on both senses in passage 64: the sage 復眾人之所過, goes back to what the many pass by, or makes good what the many overdo. In passage 35 the same graph is plain: music and food make the passing guest (過客) stop.
過.gap: “Sin” and “fault” in English suggest a broken rule or a stain. 過 is spatial. The thing was there, and one went past it.

senses: to lead, to guide (later written 導)
method, teaching, a craft’s or a school’s way
Dao: the course that everything follows
道.shuowen: 所行道也。从辵从𩠐。一達謂之道。
道.shuowenEn: That on which one walks. From 辵 (to walk) and 𩠐 (head). A road that goes through in one direction is called 道.
道.story: Before it was a philosophical term, 道 was the road under a traveler’s feet, and each school of the Warring States had its own: the 道 of the former kings, the 道 of war, the 道 of Heaven. To “have Dao” meant that a state was in order. The word was also an everyday verb, “to say”, and a verb for guiding. The Laozi took this common word and used it for that which comes before heaven and earth, while it kept the road in view. The graph joins walking and a head. Some read a person on a journey, and others a leader who shows the direction; both are later readings of the shape, and neither should be pressed.
道.gap: “Way” is nearest, but English adds an article, a capital letter, and a singular. “God”, “Reason”, “Logos”, and “Nature” were all tried by early translators, and each brought in a Western system. Modern versions that write “Absolute”, with a capital, do the same. Dao is a road that things walk. It does not stand behind them as a second thing.

違.def: disobey, violate, defy; be apart from

senses: to go far; to keep at a distance
遠.shuowenEn: Distant. From 辵 (to walk, movement), with 袁 for the sound.
遠.story: 遠 has the same walking sign as 道: distance is a matter of feet. In the Laozi it is a quality of the Way itself: to be great is to pass on, to pass on is to go 遠, to go far is to return (25). In passage 47 it is the error of the seeker: the farther out, the less known. In passage 65 the dark power is deep and 遠. The book lets the Way go far and asks the person to stay near.
遠.gap: “Far” in English is neutral or adventurous. In this book distance from the root is usually a loss, unless it turns back.

senses: to turn round; to give back
還.shuowenEn: To return. From 辵 (walking); 瞏 gives the sound.
還.story: 還 is the journey home, and by extension anything that comes round to its start. In Laozi 30, the business of arms “is fond of 還”: it rebounds on the one who began it, or, as Wang Bi reads, the one with the Dao is always turning back toward not-doing. The word belongs with 復, 歸, and 反, the book’s family of returns.
還.gap: “Retaliation” is one narrow kind of return. 還 says only that the thing comes back.

邪.def: wrong, evil, depraved, vicious, perverse, heterodox

senses: the open land outside a city wall
the offering to Heaven made there
郊.shuowen: 距國百里爲郊。从邑交聲。
郊.shuowenEn: A hundred li from the capital is the 郊. From 邑 (walled town), with 交 for the sound.

parts.m: to cross, to meet; gives the sound

郊.story: Outside a Zhou city wall lay the 郊, and beyond it the wilds. The ruler made the great offering to Heaven there, and armies met there. The sound part 交 means “to cross, to meet, to join battle”, which suits the place though the dictionary treats it only as sound. In passage 46 war horses are born at the 郊: the war has come to the edge of the city.
郊.gap: “Suburb” suggests houses and gardens. The 郊 is open ground where a state meets Heaven and its enemies.

senses: xiàng: to face toward (later written 嚮, 向)
鄉.story: The early form is commonly explained as two people who kneel face to face over a vessel of food. That picture wrote three words: 鄉, the community; 饗, to feast; and 卿, a minister. A village is the people who eat together. In passage 54 it is the third rung of the ladder, between the household and the state, and its fruit is 長, “lasting”.
鄉.gap: “Village” is a place on a map. 鄉 is first a group that shares feasts, elders, and rites.

senses: a border district of five hundred households
鄙.shuowenEn: Five 酇 (of a hundred households each) make a 鄙. From 邑 (settlement), with 啚 for the sound.

parts.m: sound; alone: a granary, the outlands

鄙.story: A word of the map that became a word of contempt: the outer lands, and so everything that was not of the capital. The speaker of passage 20 is “a block, like a man of the 鄙”.
鄙.gap: “Rustic” is mild. 鄙 is what the court called people whose accent it laughed at.

鄰.shuowenEn: Five families make a 鄰. From 邑 (a settlement), with 粦 for the sound.

parts.m: a settlement (the form of 邑 at the right of a graph)

鄰.story: The smallest unit of village life. The Laozi uses it for wariness and for nearness. The masters of old were watchful, as if in fear of neighbours on all four sides (15). In passage 80 neighbouring states are within sight and hearing of each other.
鄰.gap: English “neighbour” is a person. 鄰 is first a unit: the five houses that share a lane.

senses: to pair, to mate, to be the partner of
to match, to be equal to
to blend, to mix in proportion
配.shuowenEn: The colour of wine. From 酉 (wine jar), with 己 for the sound.

parts.m: now the sound; commonly explained as a reshaped kneeling person

配.story: The early graph is commonly explained as a person kneeling beside a wine jar. The lasting sense is “to be the partner of”: a spouse, a match, a fit. In Zhou ritual the word had a special use. When the king sacrificed to heaven, a founding ancestor was 配天, set as heaven’s pair to share the offering. The Laozi borrows the term once. The one who does not contend and goes below others is said to 配天, at the ridgepole of the ancients (68). The highest seat in the old religion is given to the lowest posture.
配.gap: “Match” and “equal” suggest a contest or a measure. 配 is a pairing, as of husband and wife or host and guest: two that belong at one table.

釁.def: smear with blood in sacrifice; rift, quarrel

里.def: unit of distance; village; lane; Kangxi radical 166

senses: weighty, grave, important; to treat as important
重.shuowenEn: Thick. From 壬; 東 gives the sound.

parts.m: a person (fused into the modern form)
a bundle or sack; sound part

重.story: Bronze forms of 重 are commonly described as a person fused with a bundle, 東, which may also give the sound. Weight is thus pictured from the carrier’s side. The word spread to everything that has weight in a life: grave conduct, important matters, respect (to 重 someone is to take that person seriously). Armies called their supply train 輜重, “the wagons and the heavy things”. Laozi 26 plays on both: the heavy is the root of the light, and the one who travels does not leave the baggage.
重.gap: English splits “heavy”, “serious”, “important”, and “baggage”. 重 holds them as one idea, so the first line of Laozi 26 is physics and ethics at once.

金.def: gold; metals in general; money; Kangxi radical 167
senses: one of the five phases (west, autumn, white)
金.shuowenEn: The metals of five colors. The yellow one is their chief.
金.story: For the Warring States, 金 is metal in general and most often bronze, the stuff of ritual vessels, bells, and weapons; gold is “yellow 金”. The Shuowen praises gold: long buried, it grows no coat; refined a hundred times, it is no lighter. It reads the graph as earth, 土, with dots that show the ore in it. The Laozi names 金 once: 金 and jade fill the hall, and no one can guard them (9). Later Daoist alchemy made 金 its great aim: 金丹, the golden elixir.
金.gap: “Gold” is too narrow for the early word. A hall “full of gold” was mostly a hall full of bronze.

senses: the picked front troops of an army
銳.shuowenEn: An awn, a fine point. From 金 (metal), with 兌 for the sound.
銳.story: The beard of an ear of grain, then any point: of a blade, of a mind, of an army. The Laozi says twice 挫其銳, “blunt the point” (4, 56), and warns in passage 9 that a blade which is hammered to a fine edge cannot be kept long.
銳.gap: “Sharp” is praise in English when said of a mind. The Laozi counts it as a risk to its owner.

senses: to press down with a weight
a weight (for a mat, for paper)
to garrison, to hold a district; a market town
鎮.shuowenEn: To press down broadly. (The Shuowen enters the character in the form 鎭.)
鎮.story: A metal weight. Bronze weights held down the corners of sitting mats; the king’s jade tablet was the 鎮圭; the chief mountain of a region was its 鎮. From the weight came the garrison and the town. The Laozi uses the word once: when wanting stirs among things that have changed of themselves, “I will 鎮 it with the nameless uncarved wood” (37). The weight in that line is plain wood.
鎮.gap: “Calm” and “restrain” lose the object. 鎮 is a heavy thing set on a light thing.

長.def: long; length; excel in; leader; Kangxi radical 168
senses: zhǎng: an elder, a chief; to be head of
長.story: Early forms are commonly explained as a person with long hair, perhaps an elder with a staff. The two readings are two sides of that picture: cháng, long, and zhǎng, to grow old, to be senior, to lead. The Laozi uses both. Long and short shape each other (2). Heaven is long (7). What is hammered sharp cannot be kept long (9). To raise things and not rule them, 長而不宰, is the dark power (10, 51). The one who shows off does not last or lead (22, 24).
長.gap: English keeps “long”, “grow”, and “leader” in three words. In Chinese they are one word: the one who has lasted is the one in front.

門.def: gate, door, entrance, opening; Kangxi radical 169
senses: a household; a school or lineage of teaching
門.shuowenEn: “To hear” (a gloss by like sound). From two door leaves. A picture.

parts.m: one door leaf; 門 is two of them, face to face

門.story: 門 is one of the clearest pictures in the script: two leaves that hang on posts. The Shuowen glosses it with a word of like sound, 聞, “to hear”; a gate is where news comes in. A 門 was the large outer gate of a compound or a city, and a 戶 was the small inner door. The word then came to mean a family and a school of teaching: to be a student is to “enter the gate”. In the Laozi the gate is where things come out of the dark (1, 6) and a thing in the body that can open and close (10, 52, 56). A gate is useful where the wall is absent, which is the lesson of passage 11.
門.gap: English “gate” and “door” are only openings. 門 is also a threshold of belonging: a house, a lineage, a way of practice.

閉.shuowen: 闔門也。从門；才，所以歫門也。
閉.shuowenEn: To shut the gate. From 門 (gate); 才 is that with which the gate is held against entry.

parts.m: here: the bar across the gate

閉.story: A gate with its bar in place. In passages 52 and 56 the line 閉其門 asks a person to shut the gate of the senses. Passage 27 says that a skilled closer needs neither bar nor bolt, and still nobody can open what is closed. So the best closing in this book is not locked: it holds because nothing pulls outward.
閉.gap: “Close” can be gentle and “lock” needs a key. 閉 is the bar dropped across from inside.

senses: to separate; to find a gap in (jiàn)

parts.m: sun (the older form has 月, moon)

間.story: The older graph is 閒: a door with the moon in it. The Shuowen defines that form as a crack or gap: light seen between two door leaves. From the gap in a door the word spread to every in-between: the space between things, a span of time, the world of people (人間). In the Laozi, the whole world is 天地之間, the gap between heaven and earth, and it is compared to a bellows (5). Passage 43 says that what has no substance can enter where there is no 間, no gap at all.
間.gap: English “space” is an abstract container. 間 is a crack with light in it: an opening between two things that are there.
間.shuowenEn: A crack. From gate and moon. (The Shuowen enters the older form 閒, with the moon; 間, with the sun, is the later graph.)

senses: to count off at a gate; to inspect, to review
閱.shuowen: 具數於門中也。从門，說省聲。
閱.shuowenEn: To count off the full number in the gateway. From 門 (gate); the sound is from 說, abbreviated.
閱.story: Troops or goods counted as they file through a gate. In passage 21 the origins of all things are reviewed in this way, by means of the name that does not go away.
閱.gap: “See” and “observe” are still. 閱 has movement: things pass, one by one.

senses: to peep, to look through a gap
闚.shuowenEn: To glimpse through a gate. From 門 (gate), with 規 for the sound.
闚.story: 闚 is a narrow look, through a gate that stands ajar. Many editions write the same word as 窺, with 穴, a hole, on top, which the Shuowen glosses as “a small look”. Both graphs were used for spying on another state. In passage 47 one sees heaven’s way without this kind of look from the window.
闚.gap: English “look out of the window” is neutral. 闚 says that such a look is partial and a little furtive.

阿.def: prefix for people's names; used in transliteration

附.def: adhere to, append; rely on near to

陰.def: the passive, female principle in Chinese philosophy (yin); dark; secret
senses: shade; the shaded side: north of a hill, south of a river
yin, the partner of 陽 in later cosmology
陰.shuowen: 闇也。水之南、山之北也。从𨸏侌聲。
陰.shuowenEn: Dark. The south side of a river, the north side of a mountain. From 𨸏 (hill), with 侌 for the sound.

parts.m: 今 over 云 (cloud): overcast; also the sound

陰.story: A hill under cloud, or the slope that the sun does not reach. The Laozi names it once, with 陽 (42). The book’s liking for the dark, the low, the female, and the valley made later readers call it a yin book, but it does not itself use the word so. The short form 阴 is hill plus moon.
陰.gap: “Negative” and “passive” make it a lack. Shade is a place: cool, moist, where seeds start.

陽.def: the active, male principle in Chinese philosophy (yang); light; sun
senses: sunlight; the sunny side: south of a hill, north of a river
yang, the partner of 陰 in later cosmology
陽.shuowenEn: High and bright. From 𨸏 (hill), with 昜 for the sound.

parts.m: the sun above, with rays: to open, bright; also the sound

陽.story: A hill with the sun on it. Place names keep the first sense: a town named with 陽 lies on the sunlit side of a hill or river. The Laozi uses the word once: the ten thousand things carry shade on the back and hold 陽 in the arms (42). The great system of yin and yang, with its lists of pairs, is later than that line. The short form 阳 is hill plus sun.
陽.gap: “The male principle”, “positive”, “active” are late and abstract. 陽 is first a warm slope at midday.

隅.shuowenEn: A corner. From 𨸏 (hill, mound), with 禺 for the sound.

parts.m: a kind of monkey; the sound part

隅.story: The angle of a wall or of a piece of land. Confucius used the word for teaching: if he holds up one corner and the student cannot come back with the other three, he does not repeat the lesson. The Laozi has it once: the great square has no 隅 (41). The sound part 禺 is the monkey that is also in 愚, foolish.
隅.gap: None in the word. The line needs the old moral sense of “square”, upright, which English has almost lost.

隨.def: follow, listen to, submit; to accompany; subsequently, then; hexagram ䷐

senses: a cock; the male of birds and animals
雄.shuowenEn: The father of birds. From 隹 (bird); 厷 gives the sound.

parts.m: sound part; by itself: the upper arm

雄.story: 雄 is the cock. From the male bird the word spread to any male animal and to the qualities of display and attack; later 英雄 is “hero”. Wang Bi reads it as “the kind that goes first”. Laozi 28 does not reject it: the first verb is 知, to know it and have command of it. Only then does one keep to the hen.
雄.gap: “Masculine” is an abstraction. 雄 is a rooster on a wall.

senses: a hen bird, a female bird
雌.shuowenEn: The mother bird. From 隹 (bird), with 此 for the sound.
雌.story: Chinese names the sexes of birds 雌 and 雄, and of beasts 牝 and 牡. The cock leads the song and the hen answers; Wang Bi explains the word in this passage by that image. The Laozi uses it twice. Heaven’s gate opens and shuts: can it be as the 雌? (10). Know the cock and keep to the 雌, and be the ravine of the world (28). In later Chinese, 雌雄 also means “loser and winner”: to decide the hen and the cock is to fight it out.
雌.gap: “Feminine” is a set of cultural traits. 雌 is a hen on a nest: a role in a pair, defined by what she does.

senses: a chicken; a cock or hen
雞.shuowenEn: The domestic animal that knows the time. From 隹 (short-tailed bird), with 奚 for the sound.
雞.story: The household clock of early China: the cock that calls before dawn. With the dog it stands for a settled village. In passage 80 the sound of chickens and dogs is heard from one state to the next, and the phrase 雞犬相聞 became a fixed expression for neighbours within earshot.
雞.gap: For a modern reader a rooster is a farm sound. For the first readers it was the hour.

離.def: leave, depart; go away; separate; trigram ☲; hexagram ䷝

senses: to find hard, to treat as hard
難.story: The character has a bird, 隹, at its right, and was at first the name of a bird; it was borrowed for “difficult”. In the Laozi 難 is the partner of 易: the two complete each other (2). Goods that are 難 to get make people thieves (3). In passage 63 the word comes five times, as adjective, noun, and verb: the sage treats things as 難 and so has no 難.
難.gap: English needs “hard”, “difficulty”, and “to find difficult”. One Chinese word moves through all three.

senses: to be exposed, to show; in the open
露.shuowenEn: That which moistens. From 雨 (rain); 路 gives the sound.

parts.m: rain: things that fall from the sky
sound part; by itself: a road

露.story: Dew is written under the rain sign because it was thought to fall from heaven in the night. It wets every surface alike and is gone by mid-morning. 甘露, sweet dew, became a standing omen of good government under the Han and later the Chinese Buddhist word for the nectar of deathlessness. In Laozi 32 it is the picture of a gift that needs no one to hand it out.
露.gap: English dew is only weather. 露 in Chinese letters is also grace: what comes down unasked.

senses: a spirit’s power to respond; numinous, potent
a spirit; the soul of the dead
a spirit-medium (in the songs of Chu)
靈.story: Rain above, three drops, a dancing medium below: a rain rite, and the word for the power that makes it work. The Shuowen explains the upper part, 霝, as falling rain, and the silk texts of the Laozi are reported to write only that part. A god, a place, a medicine, or a person is 靈 when it answers. In passage 39 the spirits got the One and so are 靈; without it they would give out, like breath. The short form is 灵.
靈.gap: “Divine”, “spiritual”, “soul”, and “efficacious” each take one corner. 靈 is power that is proved by a response.
靈.shuowenEn: (Of the older form with 玉 at the foot:) one who serves the spirits with jade. From 玉 (jade), with 霝 for the sound. The Shuowen gives 靈 as the variant written with 巫.

靜.shuowenEn: To examine closely. From 青 (the green of living things), with 爭 for the sound.

parts.m: sound; alone: to pull, to contend

靜.story: The opposite of 動, movement. A practice word of the fourth-century meditation teachers and of the Laozi: muddy water made still slowly clears (15); keep stillness firmly, and return to the root is called stillness (16); stillness is the lord of haste (26); the female overcomes the male by stillness (61); “I love stillness and the people right themselves” (57).
靜.gap: “Peace”, “serenity”, and “tranquillity” are feelings. 靜 is a fact: not moving. The feelings may come or not.

非.def: not, negative, non-; oppose; Kangxi radical 175

音.def: sound, tone, pitch, pronunciation; Kangxi radical 180

順.def: obey, submit to, go along with
senses: to go along with, to follow the course of
to obey, to comply (in Confucian use)
順.shuowenEn: To follow the lines of a thing. From 頁 (head) and 巛 (stream).
順.story: A head beside a stream: to face the way the water runs. The word names any movement with the grain: a wind behind the boat, a year of good weather, a text that reads smoothly. Its opposite is 逆, to go against. Confucian writers used it for the obedience of a child or a subject. The Laozi has it once, as the last word of passage 65: 大順, the great going-along, reached only after dark de has turned back with all things. Cousins on 川: 訓, to instruct, and 馴, tame.
順.gap: “Harmony” belongs to 和, a blend of unlike things. “Obedience” adds a master. 順 has neither: it is motion in the direction that a thing already goes.

須.def: must, have to, necessary; moment; whiskers

風.def: wind; air; manners, atmosphere; Kangxi radical 182
senses: the air of a place: customs, manners
風.shuowen: 八風也。東方曰明庶風，東南曰清明風，南方曰景風，西南曰涼風，西方曰閶闔風，西北曰不周風，北方曰廣莫風，東北曰融風。風動蟲生。故蟲八日而化。从虫凡聲。
風.shuowenEn: The eight winds. [It names one for each of eight directions.] When the wind stirs, insects are born; so insects take eight days to transform. From 虫 (a creeping creature), with 凡 for the sound.

parts.m: frame: the sound; a trace of the phoenix 鳳

風.story: The oracle bones wrote “wind” with the graph of the phoenix. The later character keeps the bird’s frame and puts an insect inside; the Shuowen says that wind wakes the insects. In passage 23 a whirlwind, 飄風, does not last the morning.
風.gap: English “wind” is only moving air. 風 is also the mood and manners of a people, which blow from the ruler down.

senses: sì: to feed, to give food to
食.shuowen: 一米也。从皀亼聲。或說亼皀也。
食.shuowenEn: Grain gathered together. From 皀 (fragrant grain), with 亼 for the sound. Some say: 亼 (to gather) and 皀.
食.story: The early graph is commonly explained as a vessel of food with a lid. Read sì, the same graph means “to feed”. Passage 20 ends with 食母, the mother who feeds; passage 53 scolds those who are glutted with drink and 食 while the fields are bare; passage 80 wishes the people to find their food sweet.
食.gap: English keeps “eat” and “feed” apart. One graph does both, and 食母 leans on that.

parts.m: to bring together; commonly explained as a lid

senses: a cake of steamed rice or flour
餌.story: Food at the left and 耳 for the sound. The word is a pleasant cake at a feast and the bait on a fish-hook, and classical writers use the double sense often. In passage 35 music and 餌 stop the passing guest. Read as cake, the line is a kind remark about tired travelers. Read as bait, it is a remark about how the world catches people. The Dao that follows has no flavor, so it cannot bait a hook.
餌.gap: English must choose “cakes” or “bait”. The pinned word is both, and the passage needs both.

senses: what is left over, the remainder
餘.shuowenEn: Abundance. From 食 (food), with 余 for the sound.
餘.story: Food beyond what is eaten. 有餘, “to have surplus”, is a set term in the Laozi. The crowd all have surplus, and I alone seem to have lost everything (20). Goods in surplus mark the robber court (53). Heaven’s way takes from surplus to fill what lacks; the human way does the opposite (77).
餘.gap: In the language of business a surplus is a success. In this book it is a question: from whom was it taken?

饌.def: feed, support, provide for; food; fine meats, delicacies

senses: famine; a year when the grain fails
饑.shuowenEn: When the grain does not ripen, that is called 饑. From 食 (food), with 幾 for the sound.

parts.m: sound jī; by itself: how much? almost

饑.story: The Shuowen keeps 饑, a failed harvest, apart from 飢, the hunger of a body. Early manuscripts often mix the two. Passage 75 uses the harvest word and then gives it a cause that is not the weather: those above eat too much of the tax.
饑.gap: “Hunger” is a feeling. 饑 is an event that happens to a whole region.

首.def: head; first; leader, chief; a poem; Kangxi radical 185

馬.shuowen: 怒也。武也。象馬頭髦尾四足之形。
馬.shuowenEn: Fury; war. It pictures the horse’s head, mane, tail, and four legs.
馬.story: A picture of the animal, turned on end: head and mane above, back and tail in the long hooked stroke, four dots for the legs. The Shuowen defines it by sound as “fury” and “martial”. In the Warring States the horse was the engine of chariots and, after 307 BCE, of cavalry. The Laozi names it twice: the running horses and war horses of passage 46, and the team of four that goes before a jade disc in passage 62.
馬.gap: For a modern reader a horse is sport or countryside. For this text it is state power, as a tank or an aircraft is now.

senses: to drive horses hard; to gallop, to race
to spread fast (of fame, of thought)
馳.shuowenEn: To drive hard. From 馬 (horse), with 也 for the sound.
馳.story: A horse at speed. With 騁 it makes the set phrase 馳騁, a full gallop in the hunt or in war. The Laozi uses the phrase two times, with opposite values: the gallop and the hunt drive the heart mad (12); the softest thing under heaven gallops over the hardest (43). The short form is 驰.
馳.gap: “Overcomes” and “penetrates”, common in English versions, lose the animal.

senses: to give free rein to (the eye, the mind)
騁.shuowenEn: To race straight ahead. From 馬 (horse), with 甹 for the sound.
騁.story: The partner of 馳: a run at full stretch with no turn. Later writers use it for the eye that ranges over a view and the mind that runs free. In the Laozi it occurs only in the pair 馳騁 (12, 43).
騁.gap: None in the word. English has “gallop” for both 馳 and 騁 and so cannot double the verb as the Chinese does.

senses: fierce (of the sun, of an army)
驕.shuowen: 馬高六尺爲驕。从馬喬聲。
驕.shuowenEn: A horse six chi tall is called 驕. From 馬 (horse), with 喬 for the sound.
驕.story: First a big horse, then the bearing of a person who is like one. Military writers used the word with care: an army that is 驕 after victory will be beaten, and a good general makes the enemy 驕 on purpose. The Laozi uses it twice. Rich, of high rank, and 驕: one leaves ruin to oneself (9). The one who helps a ruler with Dao wins and stops: the result is reached, and there is no 驕 (30).
驕.gap: English “pride” can be a virtue: pride in one’s work. 驕 cannot. It is the high head of an animal that is hard to hold.

senses: (of a horse) to shy, to bolt
to start in fear; to startle
驚.shuowenEn: A horse takes fright. From 馬 (horse), with 敬 for the sound.
驚.story: First the sudden jump of a frightened horse, then the same jump in a person. It is a movement of the body before thought. The Laozi uses it in one passage, five times: favor and disgrace are like a 驚; to get favor is like a 驚, and to lose it is like a 驚 (13). One of the twenty-four terms of the farmers’ year is 驚蟄, “the startling of the sleeping insects”, when the first thunder wakes them.
驚.gap: “Alarm”, “anxiety”, and “surprise” are states of mind. 驚 is a jolt of the whole animal.

senses: of a horse: a fast pace
驟.shuowenEn: A horse’s fast pace. From 馬 (horse), with 聚 for the sound.
驟.story: A horse that breaks into speed. Of weather: 驟雨, rain that comes at a gallop, and, says passage 23, is gone within the day.

骨.def: bone; skeleton; frame, framework; Kangxi radical 188
骨.shuowenEn: The kernel of the flesh. From 冎 (bare bone) with 肉 (flesh).

parts.m: bare bone; the dome of the skull

骨.story: The Shuowen compares bone to the stone of a fruit: the hard part inside the soft. The oldest Chinese writing is cut on bone and shell, 甲骨文. The Laozi has the word twice. The sage strengthens the bones (3). The infant’s bones are weak and its sinews soft, and yet its grip is firm (55). In later Chinese, 骨 is also a quality: 骨氣 is backbone in a person, and in calligraphy a stroke with inner strength is said to have bone.
骨.gap: English “bone” is dry and dead: bare bones, bone-tired. 骨 is the living frame, the part of a person that holds and does not scheme.

高.def: high, tall; lofty, elevated; Kangxi radical 189

鬼.def: ghost; spirit of dead; devil; Kangxi radical 194; 23rd lunar mansion, determinative star θ Cancri
senses: a ghost: the spirit of a dead person
the dead as powers that can help or harm
鬼.shuowen: 人所歸爲鬼。从人，象鬼頭。鬼陰气賊害，从厶。
鬼.shuowenEn: What a person goes home to be is a 鬼. From 人 (person), and it shows a ghost’s head. The dark breath of ghosts harms by stealth, so it has 厶.
鬼.story: The Shuowen defines the ghost by a pun on 歸, “to go home”. In early China the dead were ancestors if they were fed and dangerous if they were not; a murdered or forgotten ghost came back. The Laozi names 鬼 only in passage 60: where the Dao presides, the ghosts have force and do not wound, and the 德 of both sides comes home, 歸.
鬼.gap: “Ghost” in English is a tale for children, and “demon” is evil. 鬼 is one’s own dead, who have claims.

魄.def: vigor; body; dark part of moon
senses: pò: the bodily soul, tied to flesh, senses, and bones
the dark or faint part of the moon’s disc
魄.shuowenEn: The yin spirit. From 鬼 (ghost), with 白 for the sound.

parts.m: a ghost; a spirit of the dead

魄.story: One of a person’s two souls. The 魄 comes with the body’s first shaping and stays with the bones; the 魂, the cloud-soul, is added after and can wander. At death the 魂 rises and the 魄 sinks into the earth. The same word names phases of the moon in early bronze inscriptions. In the Laozi it stands once, in the first question of passage 10: carrying the 魄 and holding the One, can there be no parting? In modern Chinese 魄力 is boldness, and 落魄 is to be down and out: to have dropped one’s 魄.
魄.gap: “Soul” in English is one, immaterial, and immortal. 魄 is one of two, close to the flesh, and it does not outlast the body for long.

魚.shuowen: 水蟲也。象形。魚尾與燕尾相似。
魚.shuowenEn: A water creature. A picture. The tail of 魚 is like the tail of 燕 (the swallow).
魚.story: A picture of a fish, upright: head, scaled body, forked tail. The four dots of the modern form are the tail and not fire. The Laozi has two fish. One must not slip out of the deep (36). The other is small and in a pan: to govern a great state is like cooking small fish (60); stir too much and they break. In both lines the fish stands for that which is ruined by too much handling.
魚.gap: None in the word itself. The gap is in the image: English readers think of fishing; the line thinks of the fish.

鮮.shuowen: 魚名。出貉國。从魚，羴省聲。
鮮.shuowenEn: The name of a fish. It comes from the land of the Mo. From 魚 (fish), with a short form of 羴 for the sound.

parts.m: sheep; short for 羴, which gives the sound

鮮.story: A fish and a sheep. Readers like to see a feast in it, but the Shuowen says that it names one kind of fish and that the sheep marks the sound. It came to mean fresh fish, and then “fresh”. The Laozi uses it once: to rule a great state is like cooking 小鮮, small fresh fish, which are cooked whole and must not be stirred (60).
鮮.gap: “Fish” loses the freshness; “delicacy” loses the fish. The word also hides a second reading, “rare”.

黑.def: black; dark; evil, sinister; Kangxi radical 203
senses: what is out of sight, unnoticed
黑.shuowen: 火所熏之色也。从炎，上出𡆧。𡆧，古窻字。
黑.shuowenEn: The colour that fire smokes on. From 炎 (flames), which go up and out through 𡆧. 𡆧 is the old graph for “window”.

parts.m: a smoke hole, a window (as the Shuowen reads the top)

黑.story: The Shuowen pictures black as soot round a smoke hole above a fire; scholars read the oldest forms in several other ways. Soot is also what Chinese ink is made of, and 墨, ink, is “black” over “earth”. In Laozi 28 the black is what one keeps to after one knows the white: the unlit place, out of the glare. It is close to 玄, the deep dark of passage 1, and it carries no sense of evil.
黑.gap: In English, black against white is sin against purity. In the Laozi, 黑 is only the dim and unseen, and it is the side to stay on.

齊.def: even, uniform, of equal length; Kangxi radical 210

齒.def: teeth; gears, cogs; age; Kangxi radical 211
